cases.promptMarkdown:
Review this copy. The device is a Class IIa continuous ECG patch. Intended
purpose as assessed: "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the
supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac
arrhythmias."

Copy: "The X100 patch records your heart rhythm for 14 days straight. New parents love
it for keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight — just peel, stick, and sleep."

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
The device's assessed intended purpose is continuous single-lead ECG recording **in
adults**, **under healthcare-professional supervision**, for **detecting cardiac
arrhythmias**. The copy sells overnight breathing monitoring of a **newborn** by a
**parent**.

PASS requires:
(1) The newborn breathing-monitoring use is flagged as a breach of **MDR Art. 7(d)** —
    suggesting a use outside the assessed intended purpose. Art. 7(d) must be named.
(2) It is NOT treated as a truthfulness problem, and NOT said to be curable by evidence
    or substantiation. The cure is narrowing the claim or extending the conformity
    assessment.
(3) At least one of the three drifts is named explicitly: newborn vs "in adults";
    breathing vs cardiac-arrhythmia ECG; unsupervised parental use vs HCP supervision.

Also flagging Art. 7(a) or 7(b) alongside (d) is correct and does not cost the pass —
respiration monitoring is not in the assessed purpose, and positioning the patch as an
infant breathing monitor creates a false impression regarding diagnosis.

Note for the judge: the reference file's own limb (d) example uses a different scenario.
Do not look for that wording; judge whether the reasoning is applied to THIS copy.

Additionally, no market is stated in this prompt. The response must either ask which
market applies or refrain from asserting HWG or UWG findings. Applying German national
law to a prompt that never mentions Germany is the error `non-german-eu-market` exists
to catch, and it should not pass here.

# Device Claims Review: X100 patch — short-form consumer copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** X100 continuous ECG patch — Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Publikum. "your heart rhythm", "New parents", "peel, stick, and sleep" address the lay reader directly — not Fachkreise.
**Markets:** EU assumed (MDR Art. 7 applies regardless). **Germany not confirmed** — HWG and UWG items below are marked as contingent. Tell me if DE is a target market and I will promote them.

## Summary

5 claims reviewed. 2 cut, 2 reword, 1 verify.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

The second sentence is the whole problem. It markets an adult cardiac arrhythmia device as an infant respiration monitor. That is a different population and a different indication from the one assessed, and it is the kind of drift that **evidence cannot cure** — no study makes an off-label claim on-label. It comes out or the conformity assessment changes.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d), 7(a), 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** Four separate failures in one phrase.
- **7(d) — population.** The assessed intended purpose is "in **adults**". A newborn is outside it.
- **7(d) — indication.** The assessed purpose is "detection of **cardiac arrhythmias**" by ECG. Respiration is a different indication, "other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out".
- **7(a).** Respiration monitoring is a function the device, as assessed, does not have — the intended purpose describes single-lead ECG recording and nothing about breathing.
- **7(b).** "Keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight" creates a false impression of a protective monitoring function. The reader takes it as apnoea watching.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Cured by cutting the claim, or by a conformity assessment covering infant respiration monitoring, which is a new intended purpose rather than a copy fix.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 1 (Wirkungen die sie nicht haben); UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit) — both if the copy targets Germany `[verified]`
**Call:** **Cut.** Highest priority item in this review — the failure mode a parent experiences is a device that was never designed to detect the event they are relying on it to catch.
**Suggested fix:** Delete. If infant monitoring is a real product direction, it is a regulatory project, not a sentence.

---

**Claim:** "New parents love it"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`
**Why:** A testimonial that suggests a use is still suggesting a use. Art. 7(d) reaches the endorsement framing, not just the direct claim — social proof for an off-label population is the same breach delivered indirectly.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — the problem is the use endorsed, not whether parents said it.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 11(1) no. 11, if DE. Note the qualifier: third-party statements are **not** flatly prohibited for devices, only where "missbräuchlich, abstoßend oder irreführend". This one is irreführend because of what it endorses — a testimonial for the on-label use would be fine. `[verified]`
**Call:** **Cut** (falls with the sentence above).

---

**Claim:** "just peel, stick, and sleep"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`
**Why:** The assessed purpose is recording "**under the supervision of a healthcare professional**". "Just peel, stick, and sleep" positions the device as self-applied consumer wellness with no clinician in the loop, and drops the fact that output requires clinical interpretation. Supervision is part of the assessed purpose, so copy that writes it out suggests a use outside it.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by restoring the supervision framing.
**Also engaged:** if DE — HWG § 11(1) no. 7 (health "durch die Verwendung verbessert", and its mirror: that unattended overnight sleep is safe *because of* the device, impaired without it); HWG § 3 no. 2(a) (Erfolg mit Sicherheit) — "sleep" as an instruction reads as an assurance the device will not miss anything. The no. 2(a) point is the weaker of the two and depends on the sentence it sits in; it largely dissolves once the newborn claim is gone. `[verified]`
**Call:** **Reword.**

---

**Claim:** "The X100 patch records your heart rhythm"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Accurate to the assessed function. Flagging for coherence only: the second-person consumer address is what makes the missing "under the supervision of a healthcare professional" read naturally, so it should change with the fix above. On its own it is not a breach — a patient wearing a prescribed patch does record *their* rhythm.
**Call:** **Reword** (drafting, not compliance).

---

**Claim:** "for 14 days straight"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Nothing misleading on the material supplied. The assessed purpose says "continuous" without stating a duration, so 14 days is an open question for the technical file, not a breach.
**Evidence needed:** validated maximum wear time and continuous recording duration from the technical documentation, plus adhesive/skin-contact wear-duration data. If the file supports less than 14 days — or 14 days only under conditions — this becomes MDR Art. 7(a), and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 in DE.
**Call:** **Verify.**

---

### On limb (c) — an open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation at all. I am not raising 7(c) as a breach, for a reason worth stating: 7(c) is scoped to "a likely risk associated with the use of the device **in line with its intended purpose**". The alarming risk here — a parent relying on an ECG patch to catch a breathing event — arises from use *outside* the intended purpose, which is (d), (a) and (b) territory, already flagged above. I do not have the IFU, so I cannot name a likely in-purpose risk from supplied material, and inferring one from the device category would make the finding unfalsifiable.

> Worth checking against the IFU: skin irritation or adhesive reactions over a 14-day wear, contraindications, and whether the IFU records that results require clinician interpretation. If any of those are there, the rewrite needs an IFU pointer to clear 7(c).

## Suggested replacement copy

Paste-ready, tracking the assessed intended purpose:

> **The X100 is a single-lead ECG patch that records continuously for up to 14 days.** Prescribed by your doctor and reviewed by your care team to help detect cardiac arrhythmias. For adults only — the X100 does not monitor breathing and is not an infant or apnoea monitor. Read the instructions for use.

Two notes on that draft: "up to 14 days" is deliberate until the wear-time data is confirmed — switch to "for 14 days" if the technical file supports it unconditionally. And the explicit "does not monitor breathing" line is there because the original copy has presumably been in market; if so, a plain negation does more than silent deletion.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "14 days straight" | Validated continuous recording duration and maximum wear time | Regulatory / technical documentation owner |
| "14 days straight" | Adhesive and skin-contact data over the full wear period | Biocompatibility / technical file |
| (c) open question | IFU: contraindications, known limitations, interpretation requirement | Regulatory |
| Market scope | Is Germany a target market? | Marketing |
| Distribution | Has this copy already run? Where? | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Reference file |
|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]` |
| HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 2(a) | `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` |
| HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 11 | `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` |
| UWG § 5(2) no. 1 | `references/uwg.md` `[verified]` |

UWG § 6 not engaged — no comparison in this copy. HWG § 3a not cited: it is limited to Arzneimittel and does not apply to devices.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

Two things I'd want to know: **is Germany a target market** (it moves four contingent items into live findings), and **has this copy already been published** — if it has, the newborn sentence is worth escalating internally today rather than handling as a routine copy revision.

I read the three reference files and ran the claim-by-claim pass. Both anchors are settled: the intended purpose was supplied, and the audience is unambiguously Publikum.

# Device Claims Review: X100 patch — short-form copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** X100 continuous ECG patch — Class IIa (as stated)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias"
**Audience:** Publikum — "your heart rhythm", "new parents", "peel, stick, and sleep" are consumer-directed. HWG § 11 (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only) would apply.
**Markets:** EU assumed. **Whether this targets Germany is not established** — the copy is in English. MDR Art. 7 findings below stand regardless; HWG/UWG items are recorded as `Also engaged` with that condition named.

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 2 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

The second sentence is the problem, and it is not a wording problem. It relocates a prescription-grade adult cardiac device into unsupervised infant respiratory surveillance — a different population, a different setting, a different physiological signal, and a different indication. That is four simultaneous departures from the assessed intended purpose in eleven words. Limb (d) breaches of this kind are **not curable by evidence**: no dataset makes the claim lawful, because the conformity assessment did not cover the use. The fix is to cut it or to extend the assessment.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a), 7(b) and 7(d) `[verified]`
**Why:**
- **(d)** — "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out". The assessed purpose is *adults*, *under HCP supervision*, for *arrhythmia detection*. This suggests newborns, unsupervised, for respiration. Every element of the assessed purpose is displaced.
- **(a)** — "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". The assessed purpose is single-lead **ECG**. Breathing is not an ECG output. Unless respiration monitoring is a validated, assessed function, the copy ascribes a function the device does not have.
- **(b)** — "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis". Overnight infant breathing surveillance carries an unmistakable apnoea/infant-death-prevention implication for the reader. That is a clinical benefit the device is not assessed to deliver, and reliance on it is the failure mode that makes this the highest-severity item in the asset.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Only cut, or an extended conformity assessment covering paediatric respiratory monitoring.
**Also engaged (if DE market):** HWG § 3 no. 1 — "Wirkungen beigelegt [...], die sie nicht haben" `[verified]`. HWG § 11(1) no. 7 — the framing implies a newborn's breathing goes unwatched without the device, which is the "Gesundheit durch die Nichtverwendung beeinträchtigt" shape `[verified]`. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit" `[verified]`.
**Call:** **Cut.**

---

**Claim:** "New parents love it"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`
**Why:** The endorsement is what carries the off-purpose use — it presents paediatric home use as established practice among an existing user base, which is itself the suggestion limb (d) prohibits. It also asserts a fact about adoption that I have no basis for.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the (d) point. If a reworked endorsement is kept for the on-purpose use, the adoption claim needs a source.
**Also engaged (if DE market):** HWG § 11(1) no. 11 — "Äußerungen Dritter [...] wenn diese in missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender Weise erfolgen" `[verified]`. Testimonials are **not** banned for devices; this one is engaged specifically because the use it endorses is outside the intended purpose, which puts it in the *irreführend* branch.
**Call:** **Cut** as written.

---

**Claim:** "just peel, stick, and sleep"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`
**Why:** The assessed purpose is conditioned on use "under the supervision of a healthcare professional". This presents the device as a three-step self-service consumer product with no clinician in the loop, which suggests a use — unsupervised self-application and self-monitoring — outside the assessed purpose. The supervision condition is not decoration; it is part of what was assessed.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by restoring the supervision condition, not by data.
**Also engaged (if DE market):** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann" `[verified]`. Arguable rather than clear-cut: standing alone "peel, stick, and sleep" is application-convenience copy, but sitting directly after an infant-breathing-surveillance promise it reads as an assurance that the parent may safely stop watching. If the newborn sentence goes, this concern goes with it.
**Call:** **Reword** — keep the ease-of-use point, restore the clinician.

---

**Claim:** "records your heart rhythm for 14 days straight"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Continuous recording of cardiac rhythm is squarely the assessed purpose. "14 days straight" is a duration claim I have not seen substantiated, but an unverified duration is an open question for the technical file, not a breach.
**Evidence needed:** Validated maximum wear/recording duration from the technical documentation, and confirmation that 14 days is continuous rather than cumulative or battery-typical. Adhesive wear-time data and any skin-tolerance limit should be checked at the same time.
**Also engaged (if DE market):** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — "wesentliche Merkmale [...] von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" `[verified]`, if the validated duration is shorter than 14 days or conditional.
**Call:** **Verify.**

---

**Open question — limb (c).** The copy surfaces no limitation at all. I am not raising a 7(c) breach, for two reasons: I have not seen the IFU, so I cannot name a likely risk from supplied material; and the most serious reliance risk here attaches to the *newborn* use, which is not "use in line with its intended purpose" and so belongs under (d)/(a)/(b) rather than (c). Worth checking the IFU for skin irritation, adhesive reactions, and any statement that recordings require clinical interpretation — if such a limitation is recorded there, benefit-only copy of this kind would need a pointer to it.

## Suggested replacement copy

Paste-ready, pending the 14-day verification:

> The X100 patch records a continuous single-lead ECG for up to 14 days. Your healthcare professional fits it, supervises the recording and interprets the results to help detect cardiac arrhythmias. For adults only. It is not a breathing, apnoea or infant monitor. Peel, stick, and get on with your day.

If 14 days is not validated as continuous wear, substitute the validated figure. If you want to keep an endorsement, attach it to the assessed use and to a real, attributable source.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "14 days straight" | Validated continuous recording/wear duration; adhesive wear-time data | Regulatory / technical file owner |
| Any respiration capability | Whether respiration is an assessed, validated output — if not, the newborn line cannot be rehabilitated at all | Regulatory |
| Paediatric use | Whether the conformity assessment covers any paediatric population (assume not, on the purpose supplied) | Regulatory / notified body |
| "New parents love it" | Source for any retained adoption or endorsement claim | Marketing |
| Limitations for 7(c) | IFU: contraindications, skin reactions, need for clinical interpretation | Regulatory |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 11 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

Two things would sharpen this: confirmation of whether the copy runs in Germany (it decides whether the HWG/UWG items are live or hypothetical), and the IFU for the limb (c) question.

# Device Claims Review: X100 patch — short-form consumer copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** X100 continuous ECG patch — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** **Publikum.** "your heart rhythm", "New parents", "peel, stick, and sleep" — this is consumer-facing, not Fachkreise. HWG § 11 (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only) applies if the copy runs in Germany.
**Markets:** EU assumed. **German market not confirmed** — the German overlay is shown under `Also engaged:` with that condition named. Tell me if DE is in scope and those move to `Breach:`.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 2 reword, 0 substantiate, 0 OK.**

The copy breaches three of the four Art. 7 limbs in 34 words. The newborn sentence is the serious one: it moves the device into a population the assessment did not cover (adults), asserts a function the device does not have (respiration), and does both inside a testimonial. **That one cannot be fixed with evidence** — no study makes a newborn-breathing claim lawful for an adult-indicated ECG recorder. It is cured by deleting it or by extending the conformity assessment.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "New parents love it for keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight"
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(d)**, **MDR Art. 7(a)**, **MDR Art. 7(b)** `[verified]`
**Why:**
- **(d)** — "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out": the assessed purpose is **adults**; a newborn is a different population, and overnight infant monitoring is a different use entirely.
- **(a)** — "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have": the device records **single-lead ECG**. Breathing is respiration. Unless the technical documentation carries a validated respiration-derived output (and the intended purpose as supplied does not mention one), the device does not have this function.
- **(b)** — "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis": "keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight" reads as apnoea surveillance. The clinical impression is that a parent can rely on it to detect a newborn who stops breathing.

**Evidence needed:** n/a — **cannot be cured by evidence.** Limb (d) is not a truthfulness test. Only narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment to a neonatal respiration indication cures it, and that is a new intended purpose, not a marketing edit.
**Also engaged** (if the copy targets Germany):
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 11** `[verified]` — "Äußerungen Dritter ... wenn diese in missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender Weise erfolgen". "New parents love it" is a third-party endorsement, and it is *irreführend* because the use it endorses is one the device does not have. Testimonials are not banned for devices — this one fails on the misleading qualifier.
- **HWG § 3 no. 1** `[verified]` — Wirkungen beigelegt, die sie nicht haben.
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** `[verified]` — the sentence implies an infant's health is safeguarded by use / at risk without it.
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** `[verified]` — "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse". This is the Abmahnung hook.

**Call: Cut.** Delete the sentence. Do not attempt to soften it with a hedge — the population problem survives any hedge.

---

**Claim:** "just peel, stick, and sleep"
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(d)** `[verified]`
**Why:** The assessed purpose is recording "**under the supervision of a healthcare professional**". "Peel, stick, and sleep" positions the device as lay self-application and unsupervised self-use, with no clinician in the loop at fitting or at interpretation. That is a use outside the assessed intended purpose even though every word of it is literally true.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by restoring the supervision condition, not by data.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — "Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit", if DE.
**Call: Needs rewording.**
**Suggested fix:** "Fitted and reviewed under the supervision of your healthcare professional — comfortable enough to wear day and night."

---

**Claim:** "The X100 patch records your heart rhythm for 14 days straight."
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(d)** `[verified]` — narrow point only: the second-person, standalone framing drops the supervision condition and the arrhythmia-detection purpose, presenting the device to a consumer as a self-directed heart-rhythm recorder. The recording function itself is squarely within the intended purpose.
**Why:** "continuous single-lead ECG recording" is what was assessed; "records your heart rhythm" is an acceptable lay rendering of it, but detached from the HCP supervision and the arrhythmia-detection indication it drifts in the same direction as the sentence above.
**Evidence needed:** the **14-day** figure. Confirm the validated maximum wear duration in the technical documentation (adhesive, battery, signal quality over the full period) supports "14 days straight" without qualification. If the file supports "up to 14 days", the copy must say "up to".
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "wesentliche Merkmale … von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse", if DE and the 14-day figure is a typical-case rather than guaranteed duration.
**Call: Needs rewording + Verify.**

---

### Open question — limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation: no mention that the recording requires clinical interpretation, no wear-site or skin-reaction caution, no adults-only statement. I am **not raising (c) as a breach**, because the only material I have is the intended purpose, and it does not name a likely risk. Check the IFU: if it records a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose — skin irritation from prolonged adhesive wear is the usual candidate for a 14-day patch — then benefit-only copy of this kind omits it, and an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix.

## Paste-ready rewrite

> **The X100 patch records a single-lead ECG continuously for up to 14 days.** Fitted and reviewed under the supervision of your healthcare professional, it captures your heart rhythm day and night so your clinician can review the recording for arrhythmias. **For adults only. Not a breathing, apnoea or infant monitor.** Read the instructions for use.

Changes made: newborn/breathing testimonial deleted; supervision condition restored; arrhythmia-detection purpose stated; "14 days" qualified to "up to" pending the technical file; adults-only and an explicit negative scope line added to close off the reading the original invited. The negative line is optional if the newborn claim never appeared publicly — keep it if this copy has already run.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "14 days straight" | Validated maximum continuous wear duration — adhesive, battery, signal quality across the full period. Does the file support an unqualified 14 days, or "up to 14 days"? | Regulatory / technical documentation owner |
| Respiration monitoring | Confirm the technical documentation contains **no** validated respiration output (I am assuming it does not, from the intended purpose supplied). If it somehow does, the population problem for newborns still stands. | Regulatory affairs |
| Limb (c) omission | Does the IFU record a likely risk — skin reaction on prolonged wear, or a limitation requiring clinical interpretation — that consumer-facing copy should surface? | IFU / technical file |
| Market scope | Is Germany in scope for this copy? Four additional provisions attach if so. | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Tier | Reference file |
|---|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (d) | `[verified]` | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` |
| HWG § 3 no. 1 | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 11 | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| UWG § 5(2) no. 1 | `[verified]` | `references/uwg.md` |

Not cited and deliberately so: HWG § 11(1) no. 12 (under-14 targeting) — this copy targets parents, not children; HWG § 3a — Arzneimittel only; UWG § 6 — no comparison in the copy.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

## Verdict: do not publish. Two sentences contain three claims that fall outside the assessed intended purpose.

Assuming EU MDR 2017/745 (Class IIa terminology). The governing provision is **Article 7** — promotional material must not mislead as to intended purpose, safety or performance, and specifically must not "ascribe functions and properties to the device which the device does not have." Annex I §23 and Article 10(1) additionally require all supplied information to be consistent with the intended purpose used for conformity assessment.

---

### Critical

**1. Neonatal population — outside the assessed population.**
Intended purpose says *adults*. The copy markets use on a newborn. This is not a borderline overreach; it is promotion to a population the device was never assessed for, and an adult single-lead patch raises separate GSPR questions for neonates (adhesive on neonatal skin, electrode geometry relative to chest size, leakage current limits). If you actually want this population, it is a new intended purpose requiring fresh clinical evaluation and re-notification, not a copy change.

**2. Respiration monitoring — a function the device does not have.**
"Keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing" claims a physiological parameter the device does not measure. ECG-derived respiration is a distinct validated function; arrhythmia detection is not it. This is the textbook Article 7(d) violation.

**3. Implied infant apnea / overnight safety monitoring.**
"Keeping an eye on breathing … and sleep" reads, to the intended reader, as an infant apnea monitor. In the EU that is a different and higher-risk device type, and the safety exposure is asymmetric: a parent who relies on this and loses a child produces a vigilance event, a liability claim, and a plausible finding that your own marketing induced the reliance. This is the single line I would treat as unshippable regardless of what else changes.

### Major

**4. "Just peel, stick, and sleep" removes the healthcare professional.**
HCP supervision is a *condition* of the intended purpose, not a detail. Copy that positions the device as self-directed consumer use contradicts the assessed use context. Replace with language that names the prescribing/reviewing clinician.

**5. "New parents love it" — unsubstantiated testimonial-style claim.**
Needs documented evidence, and in several member states testimonials in medical device advertising are separately restricted. It also compounds finding 1 by signalling the target user is a parent, not a patient under care.

### Minor

**6. "14 days straight" must match the validated wear duration** in the technical documentation and IFU exactly — including whether 14 days is continuous or cumulative across electrode changes. If the IFU says "up to 14 days," the copy cannot say "14 days."

**7. Missing limitations.** No statement that the device does not detect all arrhythmias, is not for emergency use, and that recordings require clinician interpretation.

---

### Suggested compliant rewrite

> The X100 patch records a continuous single-lead ECG for up to 14 days, so your clinician can review your heart rhythm over days rather than minutes. Applied once and worn discreetly under clothing, it captures arrhythmias that a short in-clinic ECG can miss.
>
> For adults, prescribed and reviewed by a healthcare professional. The X100 does not detect all arrhythmias and is not for use in emergencies. It does not monitor breathing and is not a safety or infant monitoring device.

Two notes on the rewrite: I kept the "days rather than minutes" framing because the clinical advantage over a resting ECG is a legitimate, substantiable performance claim and it's the real selling point the original copy buried. The explicit breathing/infant disclaimer is there because the original claim may already be in market — if so, the negative statement is worth carrying for a cycle rather than silently dropping the claim.

Confirm "up to 14 days" and "discreetly under clothing" against the IFU before this goes anywhere; I've assumed both are supported.

This is a claims review against the intended purpose you gave me, not legal advice or a substitute for your regulatory affairs sign-off.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

**Do not publish.** Two sentences, and the second one is an off-label claim for a population the device was never assessed for, on a physiological parameter it doesn't measure. This is the kind of copy that draws a notified body finding, a competent authority advertising complaint, and — if a baby comes to harm — product liability exposure that the CE mark will not shield.

---

## Findings

### 1. Newborn breathing monitoring — Critical

> *"New parents love it for keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight"*

Three separate breaches in one clause:

- **Wrong population.** Intended purpose is *adults*. Newborns were not in the clinical evaluation, the usability engineering, or the risk file. Adhesives, skin integrity, electrode geometry and signal processing validated on adult torsos do not transfer.
- **Wrong parameter.** The device records ECG. It does not measure respiration. Even if a respiratory signal could be derived from thoracic impedance or R-R modulation, that function wasn't assessed and cannot be claimed.
- **Wrong risk class.** Monitoring a newborn's breathing overnight is, in substance, an apnea monitor — a vital-parameter monitor where variation implies immediate danger. Under MDR Annex VIII Rule 10 that is Class IIb, not IIa. You would be advertising a device outside the conformity assessment actually carried out.

This maps directly onto **MDR Article 7(a), (b) and (d)**: ascribing functions the device does not have, creating a false impression regarding diagnosis, and suggesting uses other than the assessed intended purpose.

The clinical hazard is false reassurance. A parent who believes the patch is watching the baby's breathing may not check on the baby. That is a foreseeable-misuse pathway to an infant death, and this copy would be Exhibit A in establishing that the misuse was not merely foreseeable but induced by the manufacturer.

### 2. Supervision requirement dropped — Major

> *"just peel, stick, and sleep"*

The intended purpose says **"under the supervision of a healthcare professional."** The copy positions the device as a self-applied consumer product with no clinician in the loop. Omitting a condition of safe use that forms part of the assessed intended purpose engages **Article 7(c)** (failing to inform of likely risk in line with intended purpose) and conflicts with the labelling obligations in Annex I, Ch. III, §23.

### 3. Diagnostic purpose absent — Major

The copy never says what the device is *for*: detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Under-claiming isn't itself unlawful, but here the vacuum gets filled by the newborn-breathing claim. The reader's takeaway is "baby monitor," not "arrhythmia diagnostic."

### 4. "14 days straight" — Verify before use

Must match the validated maximum wear duration in the technical documentation, including adhesive and battery performance at the upper bound. If the claim is *up to* 14 days under stated conditions, say "up to." "Straight" implies uninterrupted recording with no gaps — confirm that data integrity across the full period is substantiated.

### 5. "New parents love it" — Major

A testimonial-style popularity claim. It needs documented substantiation under **Article 7**, and several Member States restrict testimonials in medical device advertising outright. Here it also compounds finding 1 by implying an established base of infant users.

### 6. "records your heart rhythm" — Minor

Acceptable lay phrasing, but omitting *single-lead* slightly overstates capability against multi-lead comparators. Retain "single-lead" where space allows.

---

## Rewrite

**Long form:**

> The X100 is a single-lead ECG patch that records continuously for up to 14 days, helping your doctor detect cardiac arrhythmias. Applied and worn under the supervision of a healthcare professional. For use in adults.

**Short form:**

> Up to 14 days of continuous single-lead ECG, to help your clinician detect arrhythmias. For adults, under healthcare professional supervision.

Any lifestyle framing ("peel, stick, and forget it's there") is fine only if it describes wearing comfort and sits alongside the supervision statement — not as a substitute for it.

---

## Two things to action beyond the copy

1. **Risk file.** Paediatric and infant respiratory-monitoring use should be captured as reasonably foreseeable misuse, with mitigations — including explicit contraindication in the IFU and labelling.
2. **Marketing sign-off.** If this draft reached review in this state, the promotional material approval route needs a mandatory RA/QA gate before external release, per Article 10(9) QMS obligations.

Worth having your regulatory lead confirm the Rule 10 classification point against your notified body's position before you rely on it in any internal escalation.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict: do not publish

Two of the three sentences promote a use outside the assessed intended purpose. This isn't a wording fix — the newborn/breathing claim would need to be deleted, not softened.

## Findings

**1. Off-label population and function — MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (d) — critical**

"keeping an eye on a newborn's breathing overnight" fails on both axes at once:

- **Population:** intended purpose is *adults*. Neonates are outside the assessed population, and you almost certainly have no paediatric clinical evidence, no neonatal adhesive/skin biocompatibility data, and no validated signal performance at neonatal heart rates.
- **Function:** the device records ECG. It does not measure respiration. Ascribing a function the device does not have is the textbook Art. 7(a) violation.

Worse, the implied use case is neonatal apnoea/SIDS surveillance. Parents will read it that way. That is a safety claim on which an infant's life depends, made for a device that cannot deliver it. If you *did* intend that purpose, it would be monitoring of vital physiological parameters where variation implies immediate danger — Rule 10, **Class IIb**, not IIa — so the existing certificate wouldn't cover it either way.

**2. Drops the HCP supervision condition — Art. 7(d) — high**

"just peel, stick, and sleep" positions the device as consumer self-application. The intended purpose is conditioned on healthcare-professional supervision; that condition is part of what was assessed. Also check whether direct-to-consumer promotion of an HCP-supervised device is permitted in each target member state — national advertising rules vary and are not harmonised by the MDR.

**3. "keeping an eye on" implies real-time monitoring — Art. 7(b) — high**

The device is a *recorder*: data is analysed retrospectively. The copy implies live surveillance with alerting. It will not wake anyone up.

**4. No risk information — Art. 7(c) — medium**

Nothing on adhesive-site skin irritation, on the fact that the device does not detect all arrhythmias, or that it is not for emergency use. Art. 7(c) treats omission of likely risks as itself misleading.

**5. "New parents love it" — testimonial — medium**

Beyond the off-label content, lay-directed testimonials for medical devices are restricted in several member states (e.g. Germany, HWG §11). Check per market.

**6. "14 days straight" — substantiation — low**

Fine if your technical documentation supports 14 days of continuous wear as validated maximum, including adhesive performance and battery. If 14 days is the ceiling rather than the typical, say "up to 14 days."

## Suggested rewrite

> The X100 is a single-lead ECG patch that continuously records your heart rhythm for up to 14 days. Applied and monitored under the supervision of your healthcare professional, it captures the data your clinician reviews to help detect cardiac arrhythmias.
>
> For use in adults only. The X100 records your ECG for later clinical review — it does not monitor breathing, and it does not provide alarms or emergency alerts. Mild skin irritation may occur at the adhesive site.

## One process point

If marketing is actively pursuing the new-parent segment, that's a signal worth escalating rather than just editing out of a draft. Pursuing it would require a changed intended purpose, paediatric clinical evidence, likely reclassification to IIb, and a new conformity assessment. Better to establish that now than to keep catching it at copy review.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: gated procurement page — testimonial + install-base line

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Surgical navigation system — Class IIb
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (hospital procurement, clinical engineering; credentialed login) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply. HWG § 3 does.
**Markets:** DE (copy states DACH — see Claim 3)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.

**No breaches identified on the face of this copy.** Both rewording calls are risk reduction against provisions that bite only if a fact I don't have goes the wrong way — not cures for an existing breach. Do not read "no breach" as "no exposure": this copy is 27 words carrying three unbounded factual assertions, and every one of them is checkable by a competitor.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "It took two steps out of every registration."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Presented as one named clinician's account of his own site. As a bounded first-person statement it asserts nothing false on the material supplied. The exposure is in two words: *every*, and the unstated baseline.
**Evidence needed:** What the two steps were; which registration workflow (the device presumably supports more than one); whether the reduction holds across case types, imaging modality and configuration, or only in his setup.
**Also engaged:**
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** ("von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse") — if the step reduction is configuration-dependent and a procurement reader would take "every registration" as the result to expect at their site.
- **MDR Art. 7(a)** — same condition; ascribing a property that holds only under conditions the copy doesn't state.
- **UWG § 6(2) no. 2** — **if** the baseline is a competitor's navigation system rather than a manual or prior in-house workflow. DACH surgical navigation is a small vendor field; "erkennbar" under § 6(1) does not require naming anyone. If it is comparative, an undefined comparator fails *nachprüfbar* on the face and **no amount of internal data cures it** — the fix is to name the comparator and publish the basis, or keep the baseline explicitly non-comparative.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** see revised copy below — bind the claim to his workflow and name the baseline.

---

**Claim:** "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A verifiable factual assertion about installed base and duration. Nothing misleading on what I have.
**Evidence needed:** Live sites in each of DE, AT and CH; continuous use since 2024 (not one 2024 install plus a gap); and that "routine use" means clinical routine, not evaluation, pilot, or study use. If any site is a pilot, "routine use" is the word that breaks.
**Also engaged:**
- **HWG § 3 no. 3(b)** and **UWG § 5(2) no. 3** — if the count is stale or counts pilots/evaluations as routine use. Track-record overstatement is the classic Abmahnung target because a competitor can check it.
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 4** — if "routine use" spans indications or procedures outside the certificate scope, the phrase implies coverage the device doesn't hold.
- **MDR Art. 7(d)** — same condition; cannot be assessed without the intended purpose.
**Call:** Verify, then reword for precision

**On "DACH" specifically:** Switzerland is outside the EU/EEA. Whether asserting Swiss routine use implies Swiss market access turns on the Swiss MedDO regime and the CH-REP requirement, which this skill does not verify. I'm flagging it as an open question rather than stating a rule I can't cite. If the device isn't on the Swiss market, drop "DACH" and name the countries — that removes the question entirely.

---

**Claim:** "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd" (attributed endorsement)
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Audience is Fachkreise, so HWG § 11(1) no. 11 is out of scope here. And § 11 no. 11 does not ban testimonials for devices in any event — only abusive, repulsive or misleading ones. This one is none of those on its face.
**Evidence needed:** Written consent from Prof. Ellwanger **and** from the institution for use of both names in advertising; accuracy of title and affiliation; and whether there is a financial or contractual relationship (advisory board, investigator fees, equity, discounted install).
**Also engaged:** **HWG § 3 no. 3(b)** — "Angaben über die Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung oder Erfolge [...] der für sie tätigen oder tätig gewesenen Personen." If Prof. Ellwanger is compensated by or contracted to the manufacturer, presenting the quote with no disclosure is capable of deceiving as to who is speaking.
**Call:** Verify
**Note (not a statutory finding):** "Universitätsklinikum Süd" is not a real institution name I can place — if it is an anonymisation, say so explicitly. An anonymised reference site sitting next to a named professor reads as evasive, and a procurement reader cannot check it.

**One thing I will not tell you:** whether adopting a customer's quote makes the manufacturer liable for the claim as if it had made it itself. That is a *Zu-eigen-machen* question decided by case law, which this review does not assess. It matters a lot to how Claim 2 is scored, so put it to counsel rather than treating my "no breach" as settling it.

---

### On MDR Art. 7(c) — an open question, not a finding

The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I am not raising (c), because I have not seen the IFU and I will not infer a likely risk from "surgical navigation" as a category.

But this copy makes the check unusually specific, and it is grounded in the copy itself rather than in the device class: **the claim is that steps were removed from registration.** If any of those steps were verification or accuracy-confirmation steps, or if the IFU records registration accuracy verification as a required step with an associated risk, then advertising their removal is a materially different asset from advertising a time saving. Check the two steps against the IFU before this goes live. If they were verification steps, this is not a rewording problem.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "two steps out of every registration" | Identity of the two steps; which workflow; whether removal is configuration-dependent | Clinical/product, then cross-check against IFU |
| "two steps" | Whether the baseline is a competitor system or a prior in-house/manual workflow | Prof. Ellwanger's site / sales |
| "routine use since 2024" | Site list per country with go-live dates; routine vs. pilot/evaluation status | Sales ops |
| "DACH" | Swiss market access status (CH-REP) | Regulatory |
| Testimonial | Written consent (individual + institution); any financial relationship | Legal / marketing |
| Whole asset | Intended purpose as assessed, and certificate scope | Regulatory (DoC / technical documentation) |

## Revised copy (paste-ready)

Baseline explicitly non-comparative, claim bound to the site, install base precise:

> Prof. [full name], [role], Universitätsklinikum Süd, on the change to his department's workflow: "It removed two steps from our registration procedure compared with the manual workflow we used before."
>
> In clinical routine use at [N] hospitals in Germany and Austria since [month] 2024.
>
> [Prof. [name] receives no compensation from [manufacturer]. / Prof. [name] is a paid clinical advisor to [manufacturer].]

Three changes and why each one is there:

1. **"compared with the manual workflow we used before"** — names the baseline. If the real baseline is a competitor product, do not substitute a vague phrase; either name it and publish the basis, or drop the comparison. Swapping one undefined comparator for another gains nothing.
2. **"[N] hospitals in Germany and Austria"** — a countable, checkable assertion instead of a region. Add Switzerland back only once regulatory confirms market access.
3. **Disclosure line** — pick whichever is true. Costs nothing with a Fachkreise audience, and closes the § 3 no. 3(b) route.

**Gating caveat:** this review assumes the credentialed login is real and enforced. If any of this copy is lifted to the public site, a trade-show panel, a press release or a LinkedIn post, the audience becomes Publikum, HWG § 11(1) nos. 7 and 11 come into scope, and it needs re-reviewing as a different asset.

**Language:** the copy came to me in English. HWG applies to the German-language asset as published — have the German version reviewed on its own text, not as a translation note. "Routinemäßig im Einsatz" and "in klinischer Routine" do not carry identical weight.

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Reference file | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` | [verified] |
| HWG § 3 no. 3(b) | `references/hwg.md` | [verified] |
| HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 11 (scope only — not applicable to this audience) | `references/hwg.md` | [verified] |
| UWG § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4 | `references/uwg.md` | [verified] |
| UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 | `references/uwg.md` | [verified] |
| Swiss MedDO / CH-REP | — | [verify] — not covered by this skill |
| *Zu-eigen-machen* of third-party statements | — | [verify] — case law, not assessed |

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

**Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is not assessed:** I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, and here it matters specifically because "routine use" is doing unexamined work — routine use *for what*. Paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

graders.evidence:
I've read all three reference files. Here's the review.

---

# Device Claims Review: gated procurement page — testimonial + install-base line

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Surgical navigation system — Class IIb
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** **Fachkreise.** Credentialed login, hospital procurement and clinical engineering. HWG § 11 does **not** apply; § 3 does. See the gating caveat at the end.
**Markets:** DE (primary) — copy also asserts AT and CH reach

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 2 verify, 0 clean.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

The copy contains nothing false on its face. Its exposure is structural: a quantified delta with no stated baseline, and two status words ("routine use", "DACH") that assert more than they look like they assert.

---

## Findings

### 1. The step-reduction quote

**Claim:** "It took two steps out of every registration."
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" `[verified]`
**Why:** "Two steps out of" is a delta with no referent. Two steps fewer than what — the site's prior manual workflow, a competitor system, an earlier version of yours? A procurement reader takes it as a property of the product they are buying; if the two steps were removed relative to one hospital's idiosyncratic prior setup, the statement is zur Täuschung geeignet about the results that reader can expect. "Every" universalises a single-site observation.
**Evidence needed:** The workflow comparison the professor is describing — which baseline, which registration mode, whether the reduction holds in the standard configuration you ship.
**Also engaged:**
- **UWG § 6(2) no. 2** `[verified]` — if the unstated baseline is an identifiable competitor product, this is comparative advertising under § 6(1) ("erkennbar" does not require naming), and an undefined comparator fails *nachprüfbar* on the face of the copy. That defect is **not curable by evidence** — only by naming the baseline or dropping the comparison. If the baseline is your own predecessor version or manual workflow, § 6 is not engaged and § 5 alone governs.
- **MDR Art. 7(d)** `[verified]` — conditional on the intended purpose. If those two steps were removed by deviating from the registration procedure in the IFU, publishing the result suggests an off-IFU workflow. Check what the professor actually did before you check whether it is true.

**Call:** Needs rewording.

### 2. "In routine use"

**Claim:** "In routine use ... since 2024."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 3(b) (Erfolge des Herstellers) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — if any of the DACH deployments are pilots, evaluations, loan units, or sites under clinical investigation. "Routine use" asserts settled, non-investigational deployment, and procurement buys on exactly that word.
**Evidence needed:** Site list with go-live dates and contract status; confirmation that the 2024 installations ran the same configuration and the same certificate scope as the product on this page (relevant if any part of the fleet was on a legacy certificate under the MDR transitional arrangements).
**Call:** Verify.

### 3. "across the DACH region"

**Claim:** "across the DACH region"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 — "Zulassung ... der Waren" `[verified]`. DACH includes **Switzerland, which is outside the EU**. A CE mark alone does not place a device on the Swiss market. If you do not have compliant Swiss market access for this device, "in routine use across DACH" implies an authorisation status the device does not hold — a § 5 finding independent of whether every performance claim is accurate.
**Evidence needed:** Swiss market-access status; installed sites per country. Note the Swiss regime is national law outside what this review verifies — confirm with your regulatory function `[verify]`.
**Call:** Verify — and name the countries instead of the acronym.

### 4. The attribution

**Claim:** "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd"
**Breach:** none. HWG § 11(1) no. 11 (third-party statements) does not apply — audience is Fachkreise. Note also that § 11 no. 2, the professional-endorsement item, does **not** apply to medical devices at all `[verified]`; a testimonial from a named clinician is not prohibited here on either route.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]` — deceptive statements about persons acting for the manufacturer. If Prof. Ellwanger is a paid advisor, consultant, KOL, or holds equity, presenting the quote as an unaffiliated user's report is capable of deceiving. Disclose the relationship inline.
**Evidence needed:** Signed quote-approval, current title and department, institutional permission to use the hospital's name, and the compensation relationship. Also confirm "Universitätsklinikum Süd" is the institution's actual registered name and not an internal anonymisation that survived into the draft.
**Call:** Verify.

### Considered and not raised

**HWG § 3 no. 2(a) (Erfolg mit Sicherheit):** "every registration" is absolute phrasing, but it asserts a workflow step-count, not certainty of therapeutic success. Not cited.

**MDR Art. 7(c) — open question, not a finding.** The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I cannot name a likely risk from anything supplied, so I will not flag (c) on inference. But the check is unusually pointed here: registration accuracy is the safety-critical function of a navigation system, and this copy's single claim is that steps came out of registration. If the IFU carries a registration-accuracy verification requirement, copy that reads as "fewer steps in registration" should not leave a clinical engineer thinking those steps are optional. Worth putting the IFU in front of whoever signs this off.

---

## Suggested fix — paste-ready

> Prof. [full name], [department], Universitätsklinikum [name]: "Compared with the [named baseline — e.g. our previous manual registration workflow], it removed two steps from our standard patient registration." Single-site experience; registration steps and accuracy verification per IFU § [x].
>
> In clinical use at [N] hospitals in Germany and Austria since [month] 2024.
>
> [If applicable:] Prof. [name] is a paid clinical advisor to [company].

Four changes: the baseline is named (kills the § 6(2) no. 2 exposure and grounds the § 5 delta), the claim is scoped to one site rather than "every", "routine use across DACH" becomes a countable statement about countries you can evidence, and the IFU pointer keeps the workflow claim inside the assessed procedure.

If Switzerland is in fact covered, add it back explicitly — "Germany, Austria and Switzerland" — rather than restoring the acronym.

---

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "two steps out of every registration" | The baseline being compared against; whether the reduction holds in shipped standard configuration | Product / clinical applications |
| Same | Whether the professor's workflow matches the IFU registration procedure | Regulatory / clinical affairs |
| "routine use" | Site list, go-live dates, pilot vs. contracted status | Sales ops |
| "since 2024" | First install date; certificate scope and configuration at that date | Regulatory |
| "DACH" | Swiss market-access status | Regulatory |
| Attribution | Quote approval, current title, hospital name permission, compensation disclosure | Marketing / legal |
| Limb (d) | **The intended purpose as assessed**, verbatim from the DoC or technical documentation | Regulatory |

**Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is not assessed:** I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, and here there is a specific reason to look, since the only substantive claim is about how the registration procedure is performed. Paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

---

## One caveat on the gating

The Fachkreise finding depends entirely on the gate being real and staying real. Hospital procurement and clinical engineering behind a credentialed login is squarely Fachkreise, so § 11 is out. But if this quote is later lifted into an ungated brochure, a trade-show panel, a press release, or the public site, § 11 reopens — no. 11 (third-party statements where misleading) and no. 9 (promotional purpose not clearly recognisable) would both need re-checking against the copy as it appears there. Worth tagging the asset internally as gated-only.

Separately, a drafting note rather than a finding: this is English copy for a German-market page. Language requirements for advertising are not in the provisions this review verifies — check separately with your regulatory function `[verify]`.

graders.evidence:
## Device Claims Review: gated procurement page — testimonial + install-base line

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Surgical navigation system — Class IIb (as stated)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (credentialed gate, procurement + clinical engineering) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply; § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (copy also asserts AT and CH placement — see Claim 3)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 2 substantiate, 0 clean.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

Two framing points before the findings:

**The testimonial does not insulate the performance claim.** MDR Art. 7 prohibits the use of "text, names, trademarks, pictures and figurative or other signs that may mislead" in advertising `[verified]`. Quoted text placed in your advertising is your text. The quantified claim inside the quotation marks is assessed exactly as if you had written it in your own voice.

**The Fachkreise finding depends on the gate actually holding.** Hospital procurement is Fachkreise on the reference's own list, so § 11 is out — including no. 11 (testimonials) and including no. 2 (professional endorsements), which does not apply to devices at all `[verified: HWG § 11(1) closing sentence — "Für Medizinprodukte gilt Satz 1 Nr. 7 bis 9, 11 und 12 entsprechend"]`. If the page is search-indexed, or credentials are self-service rather than vetted, the audience is arguably Publikum and § 11 nos. 7, 9 and 11 come back into scope. Confirm with whoever owns the gate.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "It took two steps out of every registration."
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "wesentliche Merkmale … Vorteile … von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse"
**Why:** The reader cannot evaluate the claim because the baseline is missing on both ends: two steps out of *what* prior workflow, and two out of *how many*. Removing 2 of 4 steps and 2 of 15 steps are different products. A quantified benefit whose denominator and comparator are both absent is zur Täuschung geeignet as to expected results, and it is material — workflow time is a live procurement criterion, so it is squarely "geeignet, den … Marktteilnehmer zu einer geschäftlichen Entscheidung zu veranlassen".
**The bigger problem is "every".** A single clinician's experience at a single site is being stated as an invariant property of the device across all registrations. That is limb (a) territory — ascribing a property the device does not have — unless the technical documentation supports step reduction as a general performance characteristic rather than one site's observation `[verified: MDR Art. 7(a)]`.
**Evidence needed:** The prior workflow this is measured against, the total step count, and whether the reduction is a general performance characteristic in the technical file or a single-centre observation. Evidence fixes the substantiation; it does **not** fix "every" — that is cured by narrowing the wording.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 `[verified]` — if the unstated baseline is an identifiable competitor system (§ 6(1) "erkennbar" is broad; naming is not required), the comparison rests on a characteristic the reader cannot check, which breaches no. 2 **on the face of the copy**. That one cannot be cured by any amount of internal data — only by naming the comparator and publishing the basis, or dropping the comparison. If the baseline is genuinely your own earlier workflow, say so, and § 6 stays out.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** see the paste-ready block below.

---

**Claim:** "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Not misleading on its face, but it rests on three things I have not seen: that deployments are *routine clinical use* rather than pilots, evaluations or loaner installs; that they span all three DACH countries rather than Germany alone; and that the start date is accurate. "Routine use" counting pilots is the classic version of this overstatement.
**Evidence needed:** Site list by country with go-live dates and use category (routine vs. pilot/evaluation).
**Also engaged:**
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "Verfügbarkeit" `[verified]` — if pilots are being counted as routine use, or if "DACH" is really Germany plus one Austrian site.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 4 `[verified]` — "Zulassung des Unternehmers oder der Waren". The line asserts lawful placement on three markets. If the Class IIb certificate scope or the market-access arrangements did not cover all three from 2024, the claim implies an authorisation status the device did not hold. **Switzerland is the one to check specifically** — it is outside the EU, and its device market-access requirements are outside what these reference files verify, so I am flagging the question rather than stating the rule.
**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd" (the attribution itself)
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Naming a clinician and institution is permitted, and § 11 no. 11 is off because the audience is Fachkreise. Three conditional exposures:
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]` — "unwahre oder zur Täuschung geeignete Angaben … über die Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung oder Erfolge des Herstellers, Erfinders **oder der für sie tätigen oder tätig gewesenen Personen**". Two conditions. (i) If the title or affiliation is inaccurate or out of date. (ii) If Prof. Ellwanger is a paid consultant, advisory board member, investigator or shareholder, they are a person "tätig für" the manufacturer, and presenting the quote as an unaffiliated clinician's view is capable of deceiving as to whose voice this is. Disclose any financial relationship inline.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 4 `[verified]` — "Aussagen oder Symbole, die im Zusammenhang mit direktem oder indirektem Sponsoring stehen", on the same undisclosed-relationship condition.
- The institution name does independent work. "Universitätsklinikum Süd" reads as institutional endorsement, not one surgeon's opinion. If the Klinikum has not endorsed the product, attribute to the individual and their department, and confirm the Klinikum has consented to use of its name. (Consent and name-use rights are personality and trademark questions, not claims law — outside these reference files, raised so it does not get lost.)
- If the quote was originally spoken in German, the English rendering is your text under Art. 7. Keep the German original on file and make sure the translation does not sharpen it.
**Call:** Verify

---

## Paste-ready revision

Fill the bracketed values from the technical file and the site list; do not publish with brackets in place.

> Prof. [Vorname] Ellwanger, [Funktion], [Klinik/Abteilung], Universitätsklinikum Süd: "In unserem Ablauf entfielen zwei der [N] Schritte unserer bisherigen Registrierungsroutine."
>
> Erfahrungsbericht eines einzelnen Zentrums; keine kontrollierte Studie. Die Schrittzahl hängt vom jeweiligen Workflow und Eingriff ab. [Prof. Ellwanger berät [Hersteller]. / Es besteht keine finanzielle Beziehung zu [Hersteller].]
>
> [Produkt] ist seit [Monat] 2024 an [N] Kliniken in Deutschland und Österreich im klinischen Routineeinsatz. [+ Schweiz, only if market access there is confirmed for the stated period.]

English equivalent, if the page runs in English:

> Prof. [First name] Ellwanger, [role], [department], Universitätsklinikum Süd: "In our workflow, two of the [N] steps in our previous registration routine were eliminated."
>
> Single-centre user experience, not a controlled study. Step count varies by workflow and procedure. [Prof. Ellwanger is a consultant to [manufacturer]. / No financial relationship with [manufacturer].]
>
> [Product] has been in routine clinical use at [N] hospitals in Germany and Austria since [month] 2024. [+ Switzerland only if confirmed.]

Four changes, each doing specific work: "in our workflow" retires the universal "every"; the denominator makes the benefit checkable; the single-centre qualifier stops one site's observation reading as a device property; naming the countries and site count replaces "DACH" with something a procurement reader can verify.

## Open question I could not resolve — limb (c)

The copy surfaces no limitation. Registration is the step where a navigation system's accuracy is established, so a claim about removing steps from it is the kind of copy where a (c) omission would matter most — but I have no IFU or technical documentation, and I will not infer a likely risk from the device category and then flag you for omitting it. That would be unfalsifiable.

The concrete question for whoever holds the IFU: **do any of the removed steps correspond to a verification, check or confirmation step recorded in the IFU?** If they do, the copy advertises the removal of a safety check, and limb (c) `[verified: MDR Art. 7(c)]` bites — the proportionate fix on a page this short is an IFU pointer, not patient-facing safety text.

## Limb (d) — not assessed

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

Two specifics I would check against it once supplied: whether registration-workflow efficiency is within the assessed intended purpose and performance claims at all, and whether the procedures in routine use across those sites sit inside the indication the conformity assessment covered.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "two steps out of every registration" | Prior workflow definition, total step count, whether reduction is a general performance characteristic or single-centre observation | Clinical affairs / RA |
| "two steps out of every registration" | Whether the unstated baseline is your own prior workflow or an identifiable competitor system | Product marketing |
| "routine use … since 2024" | Site list by country, go-live dates, routine vs. pilot classification | Sales ops |
| "routine use across DACH" | Certificate scope and market-access position for DE, AT and **CH** for the stated period | RA |
| "Prof. Ellwanger" | Current title and affiliation; any consultancy, investigator, equity or advisory relationship | Medical affairs / legal |
| "Universitätsklinikum Süd" | Written consent for name use; confirmation the quote is attributed to the individual, not the institution | Legal |
| Removed steps | Whether any correspond to an IFU verification step | RA / IFU owner |
| Audience | Whether the gate is vetted-credential and non-indexed | Web / digital |

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Source file | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7 chapeau, (a), (c) | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` | `[verified]` |
| HWG § 3 no. 3(b) | `references/hwg.md` | `[verified]` |
| HWG § 11(1) closing sentence (scoping, applied to exclude § 11) | `references/hwg.md` | `[verified]` |
| UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1 and 4 | `references/uwg.md` | `[verified]` |
| UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 | `references/uwg.md` | `[verified]` |
| Swiss device market-access requirements | — not in references | `[verify]` — flagged, not stated |

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---
