graders.evidence:
## The gate buys you less than you think

Credentialed access to Fachkreise (hospital procurement and clinical engineering both qualify under § 2 HWG — the hospital is an *Einrichtung, die der Gesundheit von Menschen dient*) switches off **§ 11 HWG**, the layperson restrictions. That's real but narrow. Still fully in force on a gated page:

- **MDR Art. 7** — misleading claims, no audience carve-out
- **§ 3 HWG** — Irreführungsverbot, applies to Fachkreiswerbung
- **§ 6 HWG** — Gutachten/Zeugnisse rules, applies to Fachkreiswerbung
- **UWG §§ 5, 5a, 6** — B2B advertising is squarely covered

Also worth naming: a competitor (Brainlab, Stryker, Medtronic all sell into this market) can obtain procurement credentials trivially, and the Wettbewerbszentrale acts on member referrals. Gated ≠ unobserved. Abmahnung risk is live.

## Blocking

**1. "Took two steps out of every registration" — no denominator, no baseline, no substantiation.**

Two of four is a 50% reduction; two of twenty is noise. Reduced *versus what* — your previous generation, or a competitor's workflow? If the implied comparator is a competitor, this is vergleichende Werbung under **§ 6 UWG** and must be objective and verifiable; as written it is neither. German courts apply the strict *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis* standard to health-related claims, and the burden sits with you. One clinician's recollection does not meet it for a quantified performance claim.

**2. The safety question underneath it — this is the one I'd resolve first.**

Which two steps? In surgical navigation, registration sequences typically include accuracy verification. If the omitted steps were verification steps, or if this workflow isn't the one in your validated Zweckbestimmung and IFU, the copy promotes off-label use of a Class IIb device and engages **MDR Art. 7(c)** (failing to inform of a likely risk) and **7(d)** (suggesting uses outside the assessed intended purpose). A quote celebrating a surgeon skipping steps is a bad artifact to have in discovery if a registration-accuracy complaint ever surfaces. If the shortened workflow *is* validated and in the technical file, say so explicitly and the problem largely dissolves.

**3. "Universitätsklinikum Süd" doesn't match any German university hospital.**

German Unikliniken are named for their city (Heidelberg, Freiburg, Tübingen) or are institutionally distinct (Charité, MHH). "Klinikum Süd" exists in Nürnberg but is municipal, not a Uniklinik. So this is either a placeholder that survived into review copy, or an anonymisation. If it's anonymisation, it's incoherent — you've named the professor, which identifies the institution anyway. Pick one: fully attributed with consent, or fully de-identified ("a German university hospital").

**4. "DACH ... since 2024" has a Switzerland problem.**

Since the EU–Swiss MRA lapsed for medical devices in May 2021, CE marking alone doesn't permit Swiss placement. You need a **CH-REP** and **MepV** compliance. Confirm the device is lawfully on the Swiss market and was so in 2024 before claiming routine use there. Separately, confirm the CE certificate date precedes "2024" in each of the three countries — if any DACH use predates lawful placement, the claim documents it.

## Fix before publishing

**Substantiate "routine use."** It implies established, broad adoption. Three pilot sites won't support it. State installed base and procedure volume with a data source and date — that's both defensible and more persuasive to this audience than the adjective.

**Disclose the relationship (§ 5a UWG).** If Prof. Ellwanger is a consultant, KOL, investigator on the underlying study, or if the site is a reference/discounted installation, that must be visible. Undisclosed commercial relationships are also where **§§ 299a/299b StGB** and the BVMed/MedTech Europe codes bite — and procurement committees specifically look for this.

**§ 6 HWG attribution.** A named clinician's testimonial needs the speaker's qualification and the date of the statement. Add month/year and full title.

**Consent, in writing, from two parties.** The professor personally, and the Klinikum for use of its name (§ 12 BGB, § 5 MarkenG). Many German university hospitals flatly prohibit commercial use of their name; several require press-office sign-off. Public-sector professors may additionally need a Nebentätigkeitsgenehmigung. Verbal agreement at a congress booth is not sufficient.

**Missing device identification.** No intended purpose, manufacturer, CE/Notified Body number, or IFU pointer anywhere. Even for Fachkreise this is standard and its absence is conspicuous.

**Language.** If this is the German-market page, it should be in German. Not strictly an HWG requirement for Fachkreise, but labelling and IFU must be German under MPDG/MPBetreibV, and an English-only procurement page reads as untranslated global collateral.

## Suggested rewrite

> **[Device name]** reduces the patient registration workflow from [N] to [N−2] steps compared with [our previous-generation system / the standard paired-point workflow], while maintaining the registration accuracy specified in the instructions for use. Source: [PMCF report / validation study ref, date].
>
> Prof. Dr. med. [Full name], [role], Universitätsklinikum [City], [Month] 2025: "It took two steps out of every registration."
> *Prof. [name] [is a paid consultant to / received no compensation from] [Manufacturer].*
>
> In clinical use at [N] sites in Germany, Austria and Switzerland; first clinical use [Month] 2024, [N] procedures to [date].
>
> [Device], Class IIb medical device. CE [NB number]. Manufacturer: [X]. Intended purpose: [...]. Observe the instructions for use.

## What I need from you to finish this

1. Which two steps were removed, and is the shortened sequence in the validated IFU workflow?
2. The baseline the reduction is measured against.
3. Is "Universitätsklinikum Süd" a placeholder, or an anonymisation of a real site?
4. Swiss CH-REP status and CE certificate date.
5. Installed base and procedure count per country.
6. Nature of the financial relationship with Prof. Ellwanger and the site.

Answer 1 and 2 and most of the regulatory exposure resolves into an ordinary substantiation exercise. If the answer to 1 is "the surgeon developed a faster workflow himself," pull the quote entirely — you can't build a Class IIb procurement page on a workflow you haven't validated.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Bottom line

The gating is doing real work here — it legitimises the testimonial, which would be flatly prohibited in public-facing copy. But the copy still has three substantiation gaps that MDR Art. 7 and § 3 HWG apply regardless of audience, plus one likely factual error. Don't publish as written; the fixes are mostly additive.

(Not legal advice — this needs your regulatory affairs and legal sign-off before it goes live.)

---

## What the gating buys you

Hospital procurement and clinical engineering staff qualify as **Fachkreise** under § 2 HWG — they're employees of "Einrichtungen, die der Gesundheit von Mensch oder Tier dienen," and clinical engineering applies/maintains devices in the exercise of its profession. HWG applies to medical devices (§ 1 Abs. 1, referencing Art. 2(1) MDR).

That matters because **§ 11 Abs. 1 HWG only restricts advertising *außerhalb der Fachkreise*.* Behind a proper gate, you escape:

- **Nr. 2** — statements that a device is medically recommended, tested, or used by physicians
- **Nr. 11** — third-party statements, especially testimonial or endorsement letters

Publicly, "Prof. Ellwanger says…" is exactly what Nr. 2 and Nr. 11 prohibit. Gated, it's permissible.

**Two conditions on that, though:**

1. **The gate must verify institutional affiliation, not self-declaration.** A credentialed login is defensible; a "I confirm I am a healthcare professional" checkbox is contested in German case law and would likely fail if challenged. Keep audit logs of credential verification — you'll want them if the Wettbewerbszentrale or a competitor sends an Abmahnung.
2. **Any leakage collapses the protection.** If this quote appears in a press release, LinkedIn post, trade-show handout, un-gated teaser text, or a search-indexed page fragment, § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2/11 snap back and the testimonial becomes prohibited Publikumswerbung. Flag the asset as *Fachkreise-only* in your DAM and brief marketing accordingly. This is the single most likely way this copy gets you in trouble.

---

## Issues to fix

### 1. "Universitätsklinikum Süd" — likely not a real institution (high)

I'm not aware of a German university hospital by that name. Either it's a placeholder that survived into the draft, or it's an anonymisation. Both are problems:

- If placeholder: replace with the real site.
- If anonymised: naming the professor while obscuring the institution is incoherent and reads as evasive. Procurement and clinical engineering will notice immediately, and a non-verifiable attribution attached to a verifiable name is itself arguably misleading under § 3 HWG.

Name the real hospital and department, or drop the attribution entirely and present the claim as internal data.

### 2. Consent and the physician's own professional exposure (high)

You need, in writing:

- **Prof. Ellwanger's consent** to the verbatim quote, the name, and the title as used.
- **The Klinikum's consent** to use its name. German university hospitals are typically restrictive about endorsement use; many prohibit it outright in Nebentätigkeit rules.
- **Verbatim accuracy.** If the quote was originally German, quote the German and keep the English as a marked translation. "It took two steps out of every registration" reads like a rendering of something like *"Das hat uns bei jeder Registrierung zwei Schritte erspart"* — a translated testimonial that drifts is a § 3 HWG problem.

Separately: **§ 27 Abs. 3 MBO-Ä** bars physicians from lending their name and professional title to commercial purposes in an unfair manner. That's the professor's exposure, not yours — but it creates a real takedown risk mid-campaign if their Ärztekammer or employer objects, and your procurement audience knows the rule exists.

### 3. Undisclosed financial relationship (high, if applicable)

If Prof. Ellwanger is a paid consultant, speaker, advisory-board member, or their department received discounted or loaned equipment, disclose it. Omission is misleading under § 3 HWG and § 5a Abs. 1 UWG (withholding material information), and undisclosed commercial testimonials can qualify as *getarnte Werbung* (UWG Anhang Nr. 11). The **BVMed-Kodex Medizinprodukte** and the **MedTech Europe Code of Ethical Business Practice** both require transparency in HCP engagements — FSA/AKG don't cover devices, so these are your applicable codes.

Disclosure also *helps* with this audience. Procurement discounts un-disclosed praise anyway.

### 4. "Two steps out of every registration" — unsubstantiated absolute, and it's the safety-critical step (high)

Three distinct problems:

**"Every" is an absolute you cannot support.** One clinician's routine in one specialty at one site. Step count varies by procedure type, reference array, patient anatomy, and IFU configuration. Scope it: which procedures, which workflow, how many cases, what period.

**No comparator.** "Took two steps out" is implicitly comparative. State the baseline. If it's your own predecessor system, say so. If it's a **named competitor**, § 6 UWG (vergleichende Werbung) kicks in — the comparison must be objective, verifiable, and address products meeting the same need. An unnamed-but-identifiable competitor is worse than a named one.

**Registration is the accuracy-determining step in surgical navigation.** A fewer-steps claim invites the inference that accuracy is unaffected or improved. If you have no data supporting accuracy equivalence, the omission risks MDR Art. 7(1)(a) — ascribing performance the device does not have. Pair the workflow claim with your registration accuracy specification (TRE/FRE) and state explicitly that it is unchanged.

**And check what the two steps were.** If either is a verification or accuracy-check step, and the described workflow deviates from the IFU, you are promoting off-label use — MDR Art. 7 plus intended-purpose breach. Confirm the workflow Prof. Ellwanger describes is the IFU workflow before quoting it.

### 5. "Across the DACH region" — Switzerland is the problem (high)

Switzerland is not in the EU and CE marking alone is not sufficient. Under the **MepV**, you need a **CH-REP**, Swiss registration, and Swiss language requirements met. Confirm with Swissmedic documentation that the device is lawfully placed on the Swiss market.

If it isn't, "DACH" is a false availability claim — and clinical engineering readers in Switzerland will be the ones who catch it.

Also substantiate the geography itself: if this is four sites in Germany and one in Austria, "across the DACH region" overstates adoption. Give the actual numbers per country. Specific counts are more persuasive to procurement than regional hand-waving anyway.

### 6. "In routine use … since 2024" (medium)

- "Routine use" is vague and edges toward implying standard of care. Prefer "in clinical use at [n] hospitals."
- Verify the first commercial installation date against your CE certificate validity. If you're running on a legacy MDD certificate under Art. 120 transitional provisions, confirm no significant design or intended-purpose changes have occurred since.
- "Since 2024" also implies real-world evidence exists. Procurement will ask. Have your PMCF data and PSUR ready — for Class IIb these are required anyway, and referencing them is a selling point.

### 7. Missing device identification (medium)

There's no § 4 HWG mandatory-particulars equivalent for devices, but for a Class IIb system addressing procurement and clinical engineering, omitting these is both a credibility gap and an avoidable Art. 7 exposure:

- Product name and device class
- CE mark with notified body four-digit number
- Legal manufacturer name and address
- Intended purpose (verbatim from the IFU)
- "Gebrauchsanweisung beachten"

### 8. Language (medium)

Market is Germany; the copy is in English. English is often tolerated for Fachkreise, but hospital procurement files and tender documentation run in German, and comprehensibility feeds into § 3 HWG. Produce a German primary version.

---

## Suggested rewrite

**German (primary):**

> **Nur für Fachkreise**
>
> Prof. Dr. med. [Vorname Nachname], [Klinik für …], [Universitätsklinikum …, Stadt]:
> „[Verbatim German quote — z. B.: In unserem kraniellen Workflow entfallen mit [Produkt] gegenüber [Vorgängersystem] zwei Schritte der Registrierung.]"
>
> Erfahrungsbericht eines Anwenders, monozentrisch, [n] Eingriffe, [Zeitraum]. Die Anzahl der Arbeitsschritte hängt von Eingriff, Referenzbasis und Konfiguration gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung ab; Ergebnisse an anderen Standorten können abweichen. Die Spezifikation zur Registrierungsgenauigkeit ist unverändert (Gebrauchsanweisung, Abschnitt [x]).
>
> Prof. [Nachname] ist [entgeltlich als Berater für [Firma] tätig / erhielt keine Vergütung].
>
> Seit [Monat] 2024 im klinischen Einsatz an [n] Kliniken in Deutschland und [n] in Österreich. [Schweiz nur nennen, wenn CH-REP und MepV-Registrierung bestätigt.]
>
> [Produkt] — Medizinprodukt der Klasse IIb. CE [NB-Nr.]. Hersteller: [Name, Adresse]. Zweckbestimmung: [wortgetreu aus der Gebrauchsanweisung]. Gebrauchsanweisung beachten.

**English (secondary, same gate):** direct translation of the above, with the German quote retained and the English marked as a translation.

---

## Before publishing

- [ ] Written consent: professor (quote + name + title), hospital (name use)
- [ ] Verify the hospital name is real and correctly stated
- [ ] Quote verbatim in source language; translation checked
- [ ] Financial relationship determined and disclosed
- [ ] Step-reduction claim: comparator named, case count and period documented, claim file opened
- [ ] Confirmed the described workflow is IFU-conformant
- [ ] Accuracy-equivalence data attached or accuracy spec stated as unchanged
- [ ] Swiss market status confirmed (CH-REP, MepV registration) or Switzerland removed
- [ ] Per-country site counts substantiated
- [ ] Gate verifies institutional affiliation; credential logs retained
- [ ] Asset tagged Fachkreise-only; no reuse in press, social, or un-gated pages
- [ ] Page excluded from search indexing (`noindex`, robots.txt); no pre-login teaser text
- [ ] Regulatory affairs and legal sign-off recorded

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Bottom line

Two sentences, three claim types, and each one has a gap. Nothing here is unfixable, but as written I'd hold it. The gating helps less than you probably think, and the strongest exposure isn't the testimonial — it's "routine use across the DACH region."

*(Flagging for regulatory affairs / counsel sign-off, not substituting for it.)*

---

## 1. What the login gate actually buys you

Credentialed login is a reasonable basis for treating this as **Fachkreiswerbung** under §§ 1, 2 HWG — hospital procurement and clinical engineering staff plausibly qualify as persons who handle medical devices in the course of their profession. That switches off most of § 11 Abs. 1 HWG, including the restrictions on third-party statements and on "is professionally recommended / used by professionals." Good.

But:

- **§ 6 HWG still applies** — it is not limited to public-facing advertising. If Prof. Ellwanger's statement is treated as a *Zeugnis*, you must give the author's **name, profession and position**, and the **date the statement was made**. You currently have a surname and an institution. Add full name, title, department, role, and a statement date.
- **MDR Art. 7 still applies.** It covers advertising with no professional-audience carve-out. Every substantiation problem below survives the gate untouched.
- **The gate must be real and leak-free.** Self-declaration checkboxes have been held insufficient; credentialed login is stronger, but it fails if the quote appears anywhere outside the wall. Check: `noindex` on the gated page, no quote text in meta descriptions or OG/social cards, no crawlable teaser, no preview in email campaigns or PDF landing pages, and access logging so you can later evidence who the audience was.

---

## 2. "It took two steps out of every registration."

**The comparator is missing.** Two steps out of *what* baseline — your previous release, the site's prior landmark-based workflow, or a competitor's system? Readers will fill that in themselves, and if they read it as a competitor comparison you're into § 6 UWG territory, which demands objective and verifiable comparison. Name the baseline explicitly.

**"Every" is an absolute claim on single-site anecdotal evidence.** One user's experience cannot support universality. Either evidence it (procedure count, period, site) or let the quote stand as what it is: one centre's experience, labelled as such.

**Quotation marks do not transfer liability.** Under German practice you adopt a quoted claim as your own (*zu eigen gemacht*). You are on the hook for its accuracy exactly as if you'd written it in your own voice.

**Watch the implied safety claim.** "Fewer steps" invites the inference of fewer opportunities for error — i.e. better registration accuracy. For a navigation system that's the claim that matters commercially, and it's the one you almost certainly haven't evidenced for this statement. If accuracy or outcome benefit isn't in the clinical evaluation, add an explicit negative disclaimer rather than leaving the inference open. Confirm the workflow claim is inside the intended purpose and traceable to the CER / technical documentation — promotional material consistency is auditable under your QMS obligations.

**Don't try to fix a weak claim with fine print.** German misleading-advertising doctrine works on overall impression (*Gesamteindruck*); a prominent headline claim can't be rescued by a footnote if the headline itself overstates. Qualify the frame around the quote — never edit the quote itself to soften it.

---

## 3. "Prof. Ellwanger at Universitätsklinikum Süd"

- **Written consent** from the individual for this exact wording, plus separate institutional permission for use of the *Universitätsklinikum* name. University hospitals are typically restrictive here, and unauthorised use is a Namensrecht/trademark problem independent of HWG. Naming a person is also processing personal data — you need a DSGVO legal basis on file.
- **Disclose any financial relationship.** Consultancy, investigator fees, honoraria, travel, discounted or loaned equipment — all of it. Undisclosed material connections are misleading by omission (§ 5a UWG) and breach the MedTech Europe Code and the BVMed Kodex Medizinprodukte.
- **Corruption exposure.** A compensated endorsement aimed squarely at purchasing decision-makers deserves a § 299a/b StGB look from counsel. Not automatically a problem; worth documenting that it isn't one.
- **Tender hygiene.** German public hospitals procure under VgV/GWB. If this clinician could sit on an evaluation panel, featuring them by name in procurement-facing material is awkward at best. Worth a commercial-side check.
- **Is "Universitätsklinikum Süd" the real name?** It reads like a placeholder. If it's an anonymisation, say so; if it's real, verify spelling and the department.

---

## 4. "In routine use across the DACH region since 2024." ← biggest risk

- **Switzerland is a third country.** The device must be lawfully on the Swiss market under MepV with a CH-REP appointed and Swiss labelling in place. If it isn't, this sentence is false and arguably an implicit offer into a market you're not cleared for. Same check for Austria.
- **"Routine use" is undefined and implies established adoption.** If the installed base is a handful of sites, "routine use across the DACH region" overstates materially — and procurement is precisely the audience that will ask for the number and hold it against you in a tender. Replace with counts: sites, procedures, per country, as of a stated date.
- **"Since 2024" must reconcile with your certificate history.** Confirm the MDR certificate date for the Class IIb configuration being advertised, and don't let MDD-era market presence blur into an MDR "since 2024."

---

## 5. Missing scaffolding

No intended purpose is stated anywhere. Under MDR Art. 7 claims are read against intended purpose, so state it once, verbatim from the IFU, before the claims. Also add device name/configuration, CE mark reference with notified body number, and — for a German-market page — a German-language version. Advertising language isn't mandated the way labelling is, but an English-only quote in German procurement material is a practical own-goal.

---

## Suggested rework

> **[Device name]** — [intended purpose, verbatim from the IFU].
>
> **Prof. Dr. med. [First Last]**, [role], Klinik für [Fach], Universitätsklinikum [Name], on [workflow step], statement of [DD.MM.YYYY]:
>
> *"It took two steps out of every registration."*
>
> Basis: single-centre user experience, [n] procedures between [month/year] and [month/year], compared with [named baseline]. Individual user experience; not a claim of improved registration accuracy or clinical outcome.
>
> Prof. [Name] [has a paid consultancy agreement with / received no compensation from] [Company] [since YYYY].
>
> CE-marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745, Class IIb; notified body [name, NB-####], certificate valid since [date]. Placed on the market in Germany and Austria since [month/year]; in Switzerland since [month/year] under MepV, CH-REP [name]. As of [date]: [n] installed sites and approx. [n] procedures in DE/AT/CH.

Heavier than your original, but this is the audience that rewards specificity. If the layout can't carry it, the attribution block and relationship disclosure must stay adjacent to the quote — those two can't go behind a hover or a footnote. The market and installed-base figures can.

---

## What I need to finish this

1. The clinical evaluation section supporting the workflow claim — is "steps removed" in there, and against what comparator?
2. Prof. Ellwanger's written approval of this wording, the statement date, and the institutional permission.
3. The financial relationship, if any.
4. Swiss and Austrian regulatory status, plus CH-REP.
5. Installed sites and procedure counts per country, with an as-of date.
6. MDR certificate date for this configuration.

Give me 1–6 and I'll produce a final German and English version with the placeholders closed.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: consumer web page copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Home blood-pressure monitor — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum — ungated public consumer page, so HWG § 11 applies (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only)
**Markets:** DE (and EU, via MDR Art. 7)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

The fear framing is the problem, and it is not a close call: HWG § 11(1) no. 7 is written for exactly this shape of sentence, and this page is Publikum. The Schmidt endorsement is *not* prohibited — § 11(1) no. 2 (endorsements by health professionals) does not apply to devices — but it carries verification duties.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** § 11(1) no. 7 prohibits Publikumswerbung "die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit durch die **Nichtverwendung** ... beeinträchtigt ... werden könnte" — this sentence says not measuring is a gamble with your heart, which is that proposition in plain words. Paired with "check your pressure daily" it also creates a false impression regarding treatment (Art. 7(b)): a monitor measures blood pressure, it does not protect the heart, and the copy implies the act of measuring averts cardiac risk. Under UWG § 5(2) no. 1 that same implication is an Angabe capable of deceiving about "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse".
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Even a device that measures perfectly does not make "don't gamble with your heart" lawful Publikumswerbung; the defect is the fear framing, not the data.
**Call:** Cut.
**Suggested fix:** see the paste-ready copy below.

A weaker secondary reading is available — that "don't gamble" implies using the device removes the uncertainty, engaging HWG § 3 no. 2(a) (Erfolg mit Sicherheit). I am not recording it as a breach; the no. 7 finding disposes of the sentence either way.

---

**Claim:** "check your pressure daily"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]` — in combination with the preceding sentence
**Why:** no. 7 has a second limb: health "durch die **Verwendung verbessert** werden könnte". Standing alone, an instruction to measure daily asserts no health improvement and would likely be fine. Following "don't gamble with your heart", it reads as the remedy to the stated danger, which is the improvement-by-use proposition.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the § 11 point. Separately, confirm that a daily self-measurement regime is what the IFU actually specifies — a measurement schedule is a clinical instruction, and if the IFU specifies something else the copy contradicts the labelling.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) — if the assessed intended purpose or the IFU does not cover routine daily self-measurement by consumers, a daily-use instruction suggests a use beyond it. Cannot be assessed without the intended purpose.
**Call:** Needs rewording.

---

**Claim:** "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** HWG § 11(1) no. 2 — advertising with recommendations by members of the health professions — does **not** apply to medical devices; § 11(1) sentence 2 limits devices to nos. 7 to 9, 11 and 12. The applicable item is no. 11, and it prohibits third-party statements only "wenn diese in missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender Weise erfolgen". A genuine, accurately described recommendation is not caught. Nothing in front of me shows it is false.
**Evidence needed:** written confirmation from Schmidt of the recommendation and its scope; proof of the professorship and of Facharzt für Kardiologie status, with first name and institution; and the nature of any commercial relationship with the manufacturer.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 and § 3 sentence 1 `[verified]` — if the recommendation was not actually given, is stated more broadly than given, or the title/specialty is inaccurate, the Äußerung Dritter becomes irreführend.
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]` — if Schmidt is a person "für sie tätig" (advisory board, medical director, paid consultant to the manufacturer), then statements about their Vorbildung and Befähigung fall under this provision directly and must be exact.
- UWG § 5(1) `[verified]` — a paid endorsement presented as independent is an irreführende geschäftliche Handlung, and an endorsement is plainly geeignet to drive a purchase decision.
**Call:** Verify.

Two drafting notes, not findings. "Professor Schmidt" with no first name and no institution is unidentifiable — Schmidt is among the commonest German surnames — which does nothing for you legally but makes the claim impossible to defend quickly if an Abmahnung arrives. And whether an endorsement with no disclosed basis is misleading *per se* turns on case law this review does not assess; I am not stating a rule on it.

---

## Paste-ready replacement copy

English:

> Recommended by Prof. [first name] Schmidt, consultant cardiologist at [institution]. [Paid partnership.] Measure your blood pressure at home and discuss your readings — and how often to measure — with your doctor.

German, which is the version that will actually publish and should be the one counsel reviews:

> Empfohlen von Prof. Dr. [Vorname] Schmidt, Facharzt für Kardiologie, [Klinik/Institution]. [Bezahlte Kooperation.] Messen Sie Ihren Blutdruck zu Hause. Besprechen Sie Ihre Messwerte und die passende Messhäufigkeit mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt.

What the rewrite does: removes the not-using-harms-you framing entirely (§ 11(1) no. 7); drops the implication that measuring itself protects the heart (Art. 7(b)); hands the measurement frequency back to the treating physician instead of asserting a daily regime the IFU may not support (Art. 7(d)); makes the endorser identifiable; and includes a disclosure line to be kept only if a commercial relationship exists — delete the bracket if Schmidt is independent, since a false disclosure has its own problems.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| Schmidt recommendation | Signed confirmation of the recommendation and its exact scope | Prof. Schmidt / medical affairs |
| "Professor", "cardinologist" | Verification of professorship and Facharzt für Kardiologie registration; first name and institution | Medical affairs / HR |
| Independence of endorsement | Contracts, honoraria, advisory-board membership, equity | Legal / finance |
| "daily" | IFU text on measurement frequency for the self-measurement user group | Regulatory affairs |
| Limb (d), unassessed | Intended purpose verbatim from the DoC / technical documentation | Regulatory affairs |

## Not assessed

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

On limb (c): the copy surfaces no limitation at all. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — for instance anything about cuff fit, measurement conditions, or acting on readings without clinical advice. Worth checking against the IFU; I have not raised (c) as a finding because I cannot point to the risk in supplied material.

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Reference file |
|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(b), 7(c), 7(d) | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]` |
| HWG § 3 sentence 1, § 3 no. 2(a), § 3 no. 3(b) | `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` |
| HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 11, and sentence 2 device-scoping rule | `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` |
| UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1 | `references/uwg.md` `[verified]` |

UWG § 6 is not engaged — there is no comparison in this copy.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

# Device Claims Review: consumer web page copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Home blood-pressure monitor — Class IIa (as stated)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum (public consumer page, no gating) — HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 in scope
**Markets:** EU + DE

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed. The headline hook breaches HWG § 11(1) no. 7 on its face, and the fix is not a wording tweak.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]`
**Why:** § 11(1) no. 7 prohibits, outside Fachkreise, "Werbeaussagen, die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit durch die **Nichtverwendung** … beeinträchtigt … werden könnte". "Gamble with your heart" states the consequence of *not* measuring as cardiac risk taken on. That is the prohibited framing, and § 11 applies because the page is ungated Publikumswerbung.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. The defect is the framing, not its truth.
**Call:** Cut
**Suggested fix:** see paste-ready copy below.

---

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart — check your pressure daily." (read as a whole)
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`; HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]`; HWG § 11(1) no. 7 second limb `[verified]`
**Why:** The sentence links daily use of the device to protection of cardiac health. A blood-pressure monitor measures; it does not treat or prevent. Art. 7(b) prohibits "creating a false impression regarding treatment", and § 3 no. 1 prohibits attributing "therapeutische Wirksamkeit oder Wirkungen … die sie nicht haben". The same construction is the "durch die **Verwendung verbessert**" half of § 11(1) no. 7 — health improved by use.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the framing. Outcome data on managed hypertension would substantiate a claim about *clinical management*, not about the monitor conferring the benefit.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** see paste-ready copy below.

---

**Claim:** "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Note what does **not** apply. § 11(1) no. 2 (endorsements by healthcare professionals) is **not** in force for medical devices — the closing sentence of § 11(1) limits devices to nos. 7 to 9, 11 and 12. Expert recommendations are not per se prohibited here. No. 11 reaches third-party statements only "wenn diese in missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender Weise erfolgen", and nothing in the quote is abusive or repulsive. No. 9 does not bite either: on a product page the promotional purpose is plainly recognisable.
**Evidence needed:** Written confirmation of the recommendation; the person's full name, institution and current cardiology qualification; whether they are or were engaged or compensated by the manufacturer.
**Also engaged:**
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 11** `[verified]` — if the title, specialty or the recommendation itself is inaccurate, or if a commercial relationship is material to how a consumer reads "recommended" and is not surfaced, the irreführend limb is what carries it.
- **HWG § 3 no. 3(b)** `[verified]` — if Prof. Schmidt is a person "für sie tätig" (engaged by the manufacturer), statements about their "Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung" are directly caught, so the professorship and the cardiology credential must be current and accurate.
- **UWG § 5(2) no. 3** `[verified]` — reaches this only if the copy is read as a claim about the *trader's* own qualifications or affiliations rather than an independent third party's view.

**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** name the person fully and identifiably, and state the relationship: "Empfohlen von Prof. Dr. [Vorname Nachname], Kardiologe/Kardiologin, [Klinik/Institution]. [Bezahlte Kooperation | Unabhängige Empfehlung, keine Vergütung]." A recommendation the reader cannot attribute to an identifiable person is the version most exposed under no. 11.

---

### Limb (c) — open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — I'm not going to infer one from the device category and flag you for omitting it. Worth checking the IFU for anything on cuff sizing, arrhythmia affecting measurement accuracy, or self-interpretation of readings; if the IFU records such a limitation, benefit-only copy plus a 14-word hook is where Art. 7(c) usually bites, and an IFU pointer is normally the proportionate fix.

## Paste-ready replacement copy

The asset is 14 words, so here is the actual revised text rather than a description.

**English:**
> Blood-pressure measurement at home — as often as your doctor recommends. Your readings support your doctor's assessment; they do not replace it. Please read the instructions for use.

**German (for the DE market page):**
> Blutdruckmessung zu Hause – so häufig, wie Ihre Ärztin oder Ihr Arzt es empfiehlt. Die Messwerte unterstützen die ärztliche Beurteilung, ersetzen sie aber nicht. Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung.

Test the German wording on its own, not as a translation pass — § 11(1) no. 7 catches the published phrasing, and fear framing reappears easily in German rewrites ("Gehen Sie kein Risiko ein…" is the same defect).

Two constraints on the replacement: "as often as your doctor recommends" replaces a fixed daily regimen, which keeps the frequency inside whatever the IFU says instead of asserting one; and the readings sentence removes the treatment implication while keeping the reason to buy.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" | Full name, institution, current cardiology qualification, written consent to the recommendation | Marketing / the individual |
| Same | Whether the person is or was engaged or compensated by the manufacturer | Legal / commercial |
| Measurement frequency | What the IFU says about how often to measure, and on whose instruction | Regulatory / technical file |
| Limb (c) | Whether the IFU records a likely risk or limitation for use in line with the intended purpose | Regulatory / technical file |

## Limb (d) — not assessed

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

Specifically, "check your pressure daily" is the phrase to re-test once you supply it. If the assessed intended purpose frames measurement as taken on medical instruction, an advertised standing daily self-measurement regimen is intended-purpose drift, and that is cured by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment — not by data. My replacement copy is already drafted to survive that check.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 3(b) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 9, 11, and the device-scoping sentence "Für Medizinprodukte gilt Satz 1 Nr. 7 bis 9, 11 und 12 entsprechend" — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) no. 2 — cited only to record that it does **not** apply to devices `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 3 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

UWG § 6 is not engaged: the copy makes no comparison.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

Two things worth flagging beyond the blocks. The endorsement is the item most people expect to be the problem and it isn't — the § 11(1) no. 2 endorsement ban that would have killed it applies to medicinal products, not devices, so it survives as a Verify. The hook everyone reads as harmless marketing atmosphere is the actual breach. And since HWG is enforced privately through UWG, the realistic failure mode here is an Abmahnung from a competitor over the "don't gamble" line, which arrives faster than any regulator would.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed.

The second sentence carries the problem. It is a textbook HWG § 11(1) no. 7 shape and it also implies a clinical outcome a measuring device does not deliver. The first sentence is not prohibited as such — but it rests on facts I cannot see.

---

## Findings

### 1. "Don't gamble with your heart"

**Claim:** "Don't gamble with your heart"
**Breach:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** § 11(1) no. 7 prohibits Publikum advertising "die nahelegen, dass die Gesundheit durch die **Nichtverwendung** [...] beeinträchtigt [...] werden könnte". The sentence's entire function is to say that not measuring puts your heart at risk — that is the operative words, almost literally. Art. 7(b) is engaged in parallel: paired with "check your pressure daily", the line creates a false impression that using the device protects the heart. A BP monitor measures; it does not treat, prevent or reduce cardiac risk. That is the "outcome implication from a monitoring-only device" shape.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. The defect is the fear framing, not an unproven figure.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` — "Erfolg mit Sicherheit" — arguable on the reading that "don't gamble" implies use removes the element of chance. I would not lead with this; the no. 7 finding is far cleaner and the fix disposes of both. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse") is the enforcement route for the same defect.
**Call:** Cut
**Suggested fix:** see the paste-ready copy below.

### 2. "check your pressure daily"

**Claim:** "check your pressure daily"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** A measurement-frequency instruction is not misleading in itself. But two things sit unresolved. First, a daily self-measurement regimen directed at the general public is a **use direction**, and whether it falls inside the assessed intended purpose is exactly the limb (d) question I cannot answer without the intended purpose. Second, standing next to sentence 1 it also supplies the "durch die **Verwendung verbessert**" half of § 11(1) no. 7 — health improved by use. Isolated from the fear framing, that half is much weaker; the fix below separates them.
**Evidence needed:** the intended purpose as assessed, plus whatever the IFU says about measurement schedules.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]` — if the assessed intended purpose frames measurement as clinician-directed rather than routine daily self-screening. If that is the case, this is **not** curable by evidence; it is cured by narrowing the claim.
**Call:** Needs rewording

### 3. "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."

**Claim:** "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** **This is not a prohibited endorsement.** HWG § 11(1) no. 2 (professional endorsements) does **not** apply to medical devices — § 11(1) closes with "Für Medizinprodukte gilt Satz 1 Nr. 7 bis 9, 11 und 12 entsprechend." The applicable item is no. 11, and it bans third-party statements only "wenn diese in **missbräuchlicher, abstoßender oder irreführender** Weise erfolgen". Nothing on the face of this line is abusive or misleading. But it is bare — no first name, no institution, no specialty board, no statement of what was recommended and no disclosure of any commercial relationship — so I cannot confirm the facts it rests on.
**Evidence needed:** written, dated consent from the named individual; verification that the Professor title and the cardiologist qualification are current and correctly stated; disclosure of any payment, advisory role, shareholding or other relationship.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 `[verified]` — if the recommendation was not given, was given for a different product or indication, or is presented in a way that conceals a paid relationship, it becomes *irreführend* and the safe harbour closes.
- HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]` — "über die Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung oder Erfolge des Herstellers [...] oder der **für sie tätigen** [...] Personen". If Prof. Schmidt is engaged by or paid by the manufacturer, he is a person acting for them, and any overstatement of his credentials lands here directly.
- UWG § 5(1) `[verified]` — the enforcement route; an endorsement is plainly capable of causing a purchase decision the consumer would not otherwise make, so the § 5(1) materiality filter is satisfied.

**Call:** Verify

---

## Paste-ready revised copy

Matching the register and length of the original, in English as supplied:

> **Recommended by Prof. Dr. [full name], cardiologist at [institution]. [Paid advisor to / Compensated by] [company].**
> **Blood pressure changes without symptoms. Measure at home and share your readings with your doctor.**

The substantive changes: the fear appeal is gone, the benefit is reframed from "protect your heart" to what the device actually does — produce readings for a clinician — and the measurement cadence is no longer asserted by the advertiser. The endorsement is kept, because it is lawful, but it is made checkable and the relationship is disclosed.

A German rendering will need a native-speaker pass before it goes live — § 11(1) no. 7 turns on phrasing, and a direct translation can reintroduce the fear framing. As a starting point, not a sign-off:

> **Empfohlen von Prof. Dr. [Name], Kardiologe an [Institution]. [Bezahlter Berater von / Vergütet durch] [Unternehmen].**
> **Bluthochdruck verläuft oft ohne Symptome. Messen Sie zu Hause und besprechen Sie Ihre Werte mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt.**

---

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Recommended by Professor Schmidt" | Signed, dated consent; scope of what was recommended | Marketing / the individual |
| "Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" | Verification of title and specialty qualification, currently held | Regulatory / legal |
| Any relationship with Prof. Schmidt | Contract, advisory agreement, payment records — to determine what must be disclosed | Legal |
| "check your pressure daily" | Intended purpose as assessed; IFU wording on measurement frequency | Regulatory / technical file |

---

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Status | Reference file |
|---|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(b) | `[verified]` | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` |
| MDR Art. 7(d) | `[verified]` | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` |
| HWG § 3 no. 2(a) | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| HWG § 3 no. 3(b) | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| HWG § 11(1) no. 7 | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| HWG § 11(1) no. 11 | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1 | `[verified]` | `references/uwg.md` |

---

## Open questions I could not close

**Limb (c) — failing to inform of a likely risk.** The copy surfaces no limitation at all: nothing about readings requiring clinical interpretation, nothing about conditions affecting measurement accuracy. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs in consumer-facing copy. Worth checking against the IFU. I am not recording it as a breach, because I cannot point to the risk in material you supplied, and a (c) finding built by inference from the device category would be unfalsifiable.

**Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is not assessed:** I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, and here it bears directly on "check your pressure daily", so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

---

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

## Verdict: do not publish as written

Both sentences carry per‑se prohibitions under German advertising law for medical devices. This isn't a "soften the wording" fix — the professional endorsement has to come out entirely, and the fear hook has to be rebuilt.

Relevant frame: the HWG (Heilmittelwerbegesetz) applies to medical devices (§ 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG, referencing MDR Art. 2 Nr. 1), and because the page is public and ungated, the stricter *Publikumswerbung* rules in § 11 apply with no availability of professional‑audience carve‑outs. Germany also has an active private enforcement market (competitors, Wettbewerbszentrale, vzbv), so the practical exposure is an Abmahnung with costs and a cease‑and‑desist undertaking, not just regulator attention.

---

### Finding 1 — "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" (critical)

**§ 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 2 HWG** bans advertising outside professional circles with statements that the product "ärztlich … empfohlen oder geprüft ist oder angewendet wird." The provision expressly covers "der Gegenstand," i.e. devices, not just medicinal products. This is an absolute prohibition — no disclaimer, no substantiation and no disclosure of the relationship cures it. It applies whether or not Professor Schmidt genuinely holds that view.

Secondary exposure:
- **§ 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 4 HWG** if any accompanying image shows a person in professional clothing or practising as a health professional (white coat, stethoscope, clinic setting) — so also check the visual treatment, not only the words.
- **MBO‑Ä § 27** (model professional code for physicians): the physician themselves risks professional sanction for lending their name and title to commercial advertising. Flag this to Professor Schmidt if the arrangement is already in place.
- **UWG § 5a** if a paid or equity relationship exists and is undisclosed — an additional, independent violation layered on the HWG one.

**Action:** remove. If you have genuine clinical credibility to convey, route it to facts about the device rather than a person: independent validation status, the validation standard, peer‑reviewed data. Physician endorsement can only live in genuinely gated Fachkreise material, and "ungated public page" is stated here, so that route is closed.

### Finding 2 — "Don't gamble with your heart" (critical)

**§ 11 Abs. 1 Satz 1 Nr. 7 HWG** prohibits advertising statements apt to create or exploit fear (*Angstwerbung*). A gambling metaphor applied to cardiac risk is close to a textbook case: the persuasive mechanism *is* the implied threat of a cardiac event.

The same phrase also suggests health will be impaired by not using the product, which compounds the problem under Finding 3.

**Action:** rewrite around benefit, not dread. Convenience, accuracy, continuity of data for the doctor, understanding your own trend.

### Finding 3 — implied clinical benefit beyond the intended purpose (high)

Taken together, the two sentences assert that daily use of this monitor protects cardiac health. A blood‑pressure monitor's intended purpose is *measurement*. It does not diagnose hypertension, and it does not prevent cardiovascular events.

- **MDR Art. 7(a)/(b):** claims must not ascribe functions beyond the intended purpose or create a false impression regarding treatment or prevention.
- **UWG § 3 Abs. 3 in conjunction with Anhang Nr. 17:** untrue claims that a product cures or prevents illness are per‑se unfair, with no balancing test.
- Every retained claim must be supported in the clinical evaluation and technical documentation (**MDR Annex XIV**). "Clinically validated accuracy," if you use it, needs a specific basis — typically ISO 81060‑2 validation, ideally a STRIDE BP listing you can cite.

### Finding 4 — "check your pressure daily" (medium)

This is a usage instruction, and it needs to match the IFU and prevailing clinical guidance. ESH guidance for home monitoring is built around 7‑day measurement schedules (morning and evening, two readings each) around clinical appointments, not indefinite daily self‑measurement — which in some patients drives measurement anxiety and over‑monitoring.

**Action:** verify against your IFU. If the IFU doesn't prescribe daily use, the advertising contradicts the approved instructions. Safer framing: "as often as your doctor recommends."

### Gaps to close before publication

- **Language:** copy for the German market should be in German. (Strictly an MDR requirement for labelling and IFU under Annex I § 23, but for advertising it's a practical and consumer‑protection expectation.)
- **No substitute for medical advice / consult your physician** signposting, given the copy currently nudges toward self‑management.
- **Manufacturer identity and CE conformity** presentation consistent with the rest of the site; nothing implying the CE mark or the notified body endorses the product.
- Confirm the ungated page carries no content that would only be lawful for Fachkreise.

---

### Suggested rewrite

**German (primary):**
> Klinisch validierte Messgenauigkeit für Zuhause. Behalten Sie Ihre Blutdruckwerte im Blick und besprechen Sie sie mit Ihrer Ärztin oder Ihrem Arzt.

**English (reference):**
> Clinically validated accuracy at home. Keep track of your blood pressure readings and discuss them with your doctor.

This keeps the value proposition — accuracy, home use, useful data for the clinical relationship — while dropping the endorsement, the fear appeal, the implied prevention claim, and the unsanctioned daily‑use instruction. "Klinisch validiert" still needs the validation record behind it; if you don't have ISO 81060‑2 validation you can point to, drop that phrase and lead with a feature that is documented.

If you want a variant that still conveys expert credibility, the compliant path is institutional and impersonal — e.g. referencing the validation standard or an independent validation registry — rather than any named clinician.

One flag: I've written this against the current HWG structure as I understand it, and § 11 has been amended repeatedly. Have German regulatory counsel confirm the exact provision wording before you rely on the citations in a written position; the substantive conclusions on Findings 1 and 2 are well settled regardless of numbering.

## Verdict: do not publish. Both sentences carry hard-law problems for an ungated German consumer page.

### 1. "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" — prohibited outright

§ 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 HWG bans advertising *außerhalb der Fachkreise* that references a recommendation by scientists or persons working in healthcare. The prohibition is categorical: it doesn't matter whether Prof. Schmidt exists, whether the recommendation is sincere, or whether you disclose payment. No disclaimer cures it.

Medical devices are in scope via the § 11 Abs. 1 chapeau ("Gegenstände oder andere Mittel") together with § 1 HWG. Note the nuance worth confirming with counsel: Nr. 2's own wording ends on "zum Arzneimittelverbrauch anregen," and its application to devices rests on the chapeau rather than the subsection text — the prevailing reading applies it, but have your regulatory lawyer confirm the exact current numbering and the device analysis.

Secondary exposure:
- If Schmidt is a paid KOL and that's undisclosed → § 5a Abs. 4 UWG (failure to identify commercial intent).
- If Schmidt is composite or illustrative → § 5 UWG and Art. 7(a)/(b) MDR (false impression).
- Any accompanying image of a person in a white coat or clinical setting triggers § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 4 HWG separately.

**Practical risk:** Germany's Abmahnung ecosystem (Wettbewerbszentrale, VSW) actively polices HWG § 11. Realistic outcome is a cease-and-desist demand with costs and a penalty-bearing Unterlassungserklärung, not a regulator letter.

**If you want the endorsement at all:** it can only live behind verified HCP gating (Fachkreise), and the brief says no gating — so drop it.

### 2. "Don't gamble with your heart" — fear-based appeal

§ 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 7 HWG prohibits advertising statements apt to create or exploit anxiety. "Don't gamble with your heart" does exactly that: it frames non-purchase as a wager with cardiac consequences. This is the textbook Angstwerbung pattern.

(Art. 7 MDR is about misleading claims and doesn't itself contain a fear clause — the exposure here is HWG, not MDR.)

### 3. "Check your pressure daily" — intended-purpose and evidence problems

- **IFU conflict.** If the IFU directs measurement as advised by a physician, promotional copy prescribing a different regimen risks Art. 7(d) MDR (suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose). Check the actual IFU wording before any rewrite ships.
- **Not guideline-aligned.** ESH guidance for home BP is a structured 7-day series (duplicate morning and evening readings) around clinical decision points — not indefinite daily self-measurement, which is associated with health anxiety and over-reaction to single readings.
- **Implied self-management.** The copy positions the device as a standalone decision tool with no clinician in the loop.

### 4. Missing

No device identification ("Medizinprodukt"), no IFU reference, no statement that it doesn't replace medical assessment. Confirm with counsel whether a mandatory warning line is required for this device category in DE ads — I'd rather you verify than take my recall on it.

---

## Suggested rewrite

**DE:**
> Blutdruck zu Hause messen – klinisch validiert nach ISO 81060-2.
> Messen Sie so, wie es Ihre Ärztin oder Ihr Arzt empfiehlt.
> Medizinprodukt der Klasse IIa. Gebrauchsanweisung und Sicherheitshinweise beachten. Ersetzt keine ärztliche Untersuchung oder Diagnose.

**EN gloss:** *Measure your blood pressure at home — clinically validated to ISO 81060-2. Measure as your doctor advises. Class IIa medical device. Read the instructions for use and safety information. Does not replace medical examination or diagnosis.*

What changed and why: the named-clinician endorsement is replaced with an objective, substantiable validation fact (only use the ISO line if the device genuinely holds that validation — otherwise substitute your real evidence); the fear frame is replaced with a neutral capability statement; the frequency instruction is redirected to the user's own physician, which is both guideline-consistent and outside the § 11 Nr. 2 problem, since it's not a product endorsement.

This is a compliance review, not legal advice — have German regulatory counsel sign off before launch, particularly on the § 11 device-scope point and the mandatory-warning question.

## Verdict

Both halves of this line are problems for a public, ungated German page. I'd not ship it as written. (Not legal advice — this needs your regulatory/legal sign-off, but here's what a reviewer will hit.)

---

### 1. "Recommended by Professor Schmidt, cardiologist" — the expert endorsement

**Why it's a problem**

- **HWG § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2** prohibits, in advertising directed at the general public, statements that a product is "ärztlich … oder anderweitig fachlich empfohlen oder geprüft." Note: the post-2012 wording of Nr. 2 says *Arzneimittel*, and whether it extends to Medizinprodukte is genuinely contested in the commentary. Do not treat that ambiguity as a green light — German practice is conservative here, and a competitor or Wettbewerbszentrale abmahnung will test it.
- **MBO-Ä § 27** (berufswidrige Werbung): a physician generally may not lend their name and title to commercial product advertising. The doctor carries that exposure; you can be pulled in via **UWG § 3a** for inducing the breach.
- **"Professor Schmidt"** is unverifiable — no first name, no institution, no specialty board, no basis for the recommendation. A generic authority cue like this is exactly what reads as misleading under **UWG § 5** / **HWG § 3** even before the Nr. 2 question.
- If the endorsement is paid or otherwise compensated, non-disclosure is a separate hit (**UWG § 5a Abs. 4**), and naming a real person requires documented written consent (GDPR + Persönlichkeitsrecht).

**Fix:** remove the named-clinician endorsement from ungated consumer copy. If you want it, put it behind a genuine Fachkreise gate — and even then, verify the physician's own professional-conduct position first. For the public page, replace authority with substantiable fact: clinical validation protocol, ISO 81060-2 conformity, independent test results. Those carry more weight and are defensible.

### 2. "Don't gamble with your heart" — the fear appeal

**Why it's a problem**

- **HWG § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 7** bars advertising with statements "die geeignet sind, Angstgefühle hervorzurufen oder auszunutzen." This clause is *not* limited to Arzneimittel — it applies to your device. "Don't gamble with your heart" is a textbook Angstwerbung construction: it frames non-use as risking a cardiac event.
- **MDR Art. 7** independently prohibits claims that create a false impression regarding the device's function or the benefit it delivers. The implied proposition here is that using the monitor protects your heart. It doesn't — it measures blood pressure. The causal jump from measurement to cardiac protection is an unsupported clinical-benefit claim.

**Fix:** state the information gap neutrally rather than the catastrophe. Hypertension being asymptomatic is a factual, non-fear-based hook and it does the same persuasive work.

### 3. "check your pressure daily" — the usage instruction

Lower-severity, but flag it. This is a medical usage recommendation delivered in marketing copy, and blanket daily measurement for the general population isn't what ESH/ESC guidance says — HBPM is specified as structured protocols (e.g. 7 days, morning and evening, duplicate readings) around diagnosis and treatment adjustment. Two consequences:

- It must be consistent with your **IFU and stated intended purpose** (MDR Art. 7, Art. 10(11)). Marketing copy that prescribes a different regimen than the IFU is an off-label promotion problem.
- Encouraging undirected daily self-measurement in asymptomatic users is also the kind of thing that compounds the anxiety finding above.

**Fix:** defer frequency to the IFU or to the user's physician.

---

## Suggested rewrite

> **High blood pressure usually has no symptoms.** Clinically validated measurement accuracy (ISO 81060-2) — so you and your doctor can see the full picture. Follow the measurement schedule in the instructions for use or the one your doctor recommends.

Or shorter, if the slot is tight:

> **You can't feel high blood pressure. You can measure it.** Clinically validated accuracy for use at home.

Both drop the endorsement, replace the fear frame with the asymptomatic fact, and route frequency to the IFU.

## Before you publish

- Confirm the ISO 81060-2 / clinical-validation claim is actually true for *this* device and that you hold the report — I've written it in as a placeholder because it's the natural substitute for the endorsement, not because I've verified it.
- Check the full page for the same two patterns elsewhere; single lines rarely offend alone.
- Route through regulatory/legal — the HWG § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2 scope question for Medizinprodukte in particular is one they should take a documented position on.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: CGM consumer copy (20 words)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Continuous glucose monitor — Class IIa (as stated by you)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes; readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change."
**Audience:** Publikum — assumed. "Straight to your phone", "your glucose", "dose" all address the patient directly. Confirm; if this is trade press or an HCP-gated channel, the HWG § 11 line below drops out.
**Markets:** EU assumed. **You have not told me whether this targets Germany.** MDR Art. 7 findings below stand either way; HWG and UWG points are marked as conditional on DE.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed plus one asset-level omission. **1 cut, 1 reword, 1 verify, 1 asset-level reword.**

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

The intended purpose you supplied contains an express carve-out for treatment decisions. The copy's closing line asserts exactly the use the carve-out excludes. That is a limb (d) breach and it is not curable by data.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(d)** `[verified]`, and **Art. 7(b)** `[verified]`
**Why:** Art. 7(d) prohibits "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out". Your intended purpose states readings "are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for **treatment decisions**". Insulin dosing is the treatment decision. The copy suggests the device as the basis for it, with no carve-out for rapid change. Art. 7(b) is engaged in parallel: "confidence" attached to dosing creates a false impression regarding treatment that the device's own intended purpose disclaims.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — **cannot be cured by evidence.** A MARD figure or a dosing study does not fix this. It is cured by narrowing the claim, or by extending the conformity assessment to cover a non-adjunctive dosing indication. If the device *is* already assessed for non-adjunctive dosing, then the intended purpose you gave me is the wrong one and this finding changes — send the current one.
**Also engaged:** **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** `[verified]` — "fälschlich der Eindruck erweckt wird, daß ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann" — if the market is DE. "With confidence" is certainty framing over an outcome the intended purpose expressly qualifies. This limb is additive; MDR Art. 7 has no guarantee prohibition. Also **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** `[verified]` ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse") if DE.
**Call:** **Cut**

---

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(b)** `[verified]`
**Why:** The device measures **interstitial** glucose — that word is in the intended purpose and it is load-bearing, because the entire treatment-decision carve-out exists on account of the interstitial-to-blood relationship. Unqualified "your glucose" collapses the distinction and creates a false impression about what is being measured. "At a glance" compounds it by implying the reading needs no context or confirmation.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the interstitial point — that is a wording fix, not a data question.
**Also engaged:** **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** `[verified]` — health "durch die Verwendung verbessert" framing — only if DE **and** Publikum. I rate this weak on this line alone; I flag it because no. 7 is the highest-frequency § 11 item for devices and the rewritten headline should not drift toward it.
**Call:** **Reword**

---

**Claim:** "Real-time readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone."
**Breach:** **none** on the material supplied.
**Why:** A factual capability and delivery claim. Nothing in it conflicts with the intended purpose. Two things to check rather than two breaches: (1) "real-time" is an established term of art for rtCGM, but your intended purpose's rapid-change carve-out implies a physiological lag between interstitial and blood glucose — confirm "real-time" is the term used in your IFU and technical documentation, and that it is not doing work the lag contradicts; (2) confirm the 5-minute interval is the assessed sampling/display interval, not a best case.
**Evidence needed:** IFU terminology for the reading cadence; the sampling interval as stated in the technical file. Both should be a one-line check.
**Also engaged:** **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** `[verified]` — "wesentlichen Merkmale" — only if the 5-minute figure is not the assessed interval, and only if DE.
**Call:** **Verify** — no rewrite needed if both check out.

---

**Asset-level finding — the whole 20 words**
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(c)** `[verified]`
**Why:** Art. 7(c) is an omission test: "failing to inform the user or the patient of a **likely** risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose". I am not inferring this risk from the device category — **you supplied it.** Your own intended purpose records that readings do not replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid change. That is a named limitation on in-purpose use, in the material you gave me. The copy is benefit-only and surfaces none of it, while simultaneously inviting the excluded use. In a 20-word patient-facing asset, a short confirmatory-testing pointer is the proportionate fix; a full IFU pointer would be proportionate on a longer page.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — this is a drafting fix.
**Also engaged:** **HWG § 3 no. 2(b)** `[verified]` — "bei bestimmungsgemäßem oder längerem Gebrauch keine schädlichen Wirkungen eintreten" — if DE. Benefit-only framing around a dosing decision edges toward the no-harm impression. Additive to Art. 7; no MDR equivalent.
**Call:** **Reword** (satisfied by the rewrite below)

---

## Paste-ready revision

> **Know your glucose trends at a glance. Interstitial glucose readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. When your glucose is changing fast, confirm with a fingerstick before dosing.**

What each change does:

- **"glucose trends"** and **"interstitial glucose readings"** — closes Art. 7(b). Tracks the assessed intended purpose word-for-word.
- **"When your glucose is changing fast, confirm with a fingerstick before dosing"** — closes Art. 7(d) and Art. 7(c) together. It keeps dosing in the copy, which is what the marketing intent wants, but positions the device the way the conformity assessment covers it. It also disposes of the HWG § 3 no. 2(a) and no. 2(b) exposure, because there is no longer a certainty or no-harm impression to rebut.
- **"every 5 minutes, straight to your phone"** — kept verbatim, subject to the verification below.

If the marketing team pushes back on losing "Dose with confidence": the substitute for it is not a softer synonym. Anything that makes the device the basis for the dosing decision without the rapid-change condition reopens limb (d), regardless of phrasing.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Real-time" | Terminology as used in the IFU and technical documentation; confirmation that the interstitial-to-blood lag does not contradict it | Regulatory affairs / technical file owner |
| "every 5 minutes" | Assessed sampling and display interval, not best case | Regulatory affairs |
| "Dose with confidence" | The **current** intended purpose from the DoC — if the device has since been assessed for non-adjunctive dosing, the limb (d) finding changes | Regulatory affairs |
| Whole asset | Whether the IFU records further likely risks (e.g. compression lows, warm-up period, interfering substances) that belong in patient-facing copy | IFU / risk management file |

## Two things I need from you

1. **Is this DE-market copy?** If yes, the HWG § 3 no. 2(a) and no. 2(b) points move from "Also engaged" to live breaches on the original text, and the Abmahnung route opens via UWG. The rewrite above already handles them, so this changes the risk narrative more than the fix.
2. **Is the channel gated to Fachkreise?** "Straight to your phone" says no, but confirm. If it is ungated public web, HWG § 11 applies in full (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only).

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Tier | Reference file |
|---|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(b), (c), (d) | `[verified]` | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` |
| HWG § 3 no. 2(a), no. 2(b) | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| HWG § 11(1) no. 7 | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| UWG § 5(2) no. 1 | `[verified]` | `references/uwg.md` |

Not engaged, for the record: UWG § 6 (no comparison in the copy), UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4 (no certification, class or notified-body claim made — the Class IIa status you told me is not asserted in the copy), HWG § 3a (Arzneimittel only, never applies to devices).

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.
