## Device Claims Review: CGM launch copy (3 lines)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Class IIa CGM (continuous glucose monitor) — MDR
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes; readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change."
**Audience:** Publikum — assumed. "Straight to your phone", addressed to the person wearing it, no gating implied. Confirm if this is in fact a Fachkreise asset; HWG § 11 would then drop out (§ 3 would not).
**Markets:** EU assumed. **Not supplied: whether this runs in Germany.** The MDR Art. 7 findings below hold either way. HWG and UWG bite only on German-market advertising, so I have put those under `Also engaged` with the condition named rather than asserting them as breaches.

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 2 reword, 1 verify, 0 OK. Plus one asset-level omission finding.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

The core problem is the third line. The assessed intended purpose contains an express carve-out for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change; "Dose with confidence" suggests exactly the use that carve-out excludes, and does it in the copy's closing, highest-emphasis position. That is a limb (d) breach, and limb (d) is not curable by evidence — no accuracy study makes the claim compliant, because the problem is scope, not truth.

---

## Findings

### 1. "Dose with confidence."

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`; MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** (d) — "suggesting uses for the device other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out". Insulin dosing is a treatment decision. The assessed intended purpose states readings "are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change"; unqualified "Dose with confidence" suggests the reading is a sufficient basis for dosing in all conditions, including the ones expressly carved out. (b) — it creates a false impression regarding treatment by attaching certainty ("confidence") to a decision the intended purpose says the reading does not, on its own, support.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Cured only by narrowing the claim, or by extending the conformity assessment to cover dosing without confirmatory BG testing.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` — "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann" — if the copy runs in Germany, "with confidence" as the promised outcome of a dosing decision is the guaranteed-success shape, and § 3 no. 2(a) has no MDR equivalent, so it is an additional and independent finding. HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]` — health "durch die Verwendung verbessert" framing — if Germany **and** Publikum.
**Call:** Cut.

### 2. "Know your glucose at a glance."

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`
**Why:** "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". The assessed purpose is **interstitial** glucose monitoring. Unqualified "your glucose", to a person with diabetes, reads as blood glucose — the measurand the intended purpose specifically distinguishes the device from. "Know … at a glance" compounds it by implying the number stands alone without confirmation.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the measurand point — the fix is the word "interstitial" or "glucose trends", not data.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "wesentlichen Merkmale … Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit" — if Germany.
**Call:** Needs rewording.

### 3. "Real-time readings"

**Claim:** "Real-time readings"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`
**Why:** The intended purpose's own carve-out for "periods of rapid glucose change" is a statement that the reading does not track blood glucose contemporaneously under those conditions. "Real-time" asserts the property that carve-out withholds. I am reading this off the supplied intended purpose, not off an assumption about sensor physiology — but the size of the lag is an IFU question, so check the wording the IFU uses for it.
**Evidence needed:** The IFU's own characterisation of lag/latency, and whatever performance data supports any temporal claim. If the IFU says "up to a 5-minute display interval" or similar, use that language rather than "real-time".
**Call:** Needs rewording.

### 4. "every 5 minutes, straight to your phone."

**Claim:** "every 5 minutes, straight to your phone."
**Breach:** none — on the material supplied this is a narrow, checkable performance statement, which is the cheap kind to defend.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm the 5-minute figure is the assessed measurement/display interval in the technical documentation, not a best case. Confirm the companion app and phone display are inside the CE certificate scope — if the app is part of the device, its performance claims sit under the same certificate; if it is a separate component, check what was assessed.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` ("Tests", "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse") — if Germany and the interval figure is a best case rather than the assessed spec.
**Call:** Verify.

### 5. Asset-level: no limitation stated anywhere

**Claim:** the asset as a whole.
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(c) `[verified]`
**Why:** "failing to inform the user or the patient of a likely risk associated with the use of the device in line with its intended purpose". I am not inferring this risk from the device category — it is named in the material you supplied. The intended purpose itself records that readings do not replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid glucose change. The risk that follows is a dosing decision taken on a CGM reading during rapid change. Three lines of benefit copy carry none of it, and line three actively invites that decision.
**Evidence needed:** n/a. Cured by surfacing the limitation, or at minimum an IFU pointer. Given this is patient-facing and the copy's own call to action is a dosing action, an IFU pointer alone is probably not proportionate here — the limitation should be on the face of the copy.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(b) `[verified]` — "bei bestimmungsgemäßem oder längerem Gebrauch keine schädlichen Wirkungen eintreten" — if Germany. Benefit-only copy on a device whose intended purpose carries an express safety carve-out risks reading as a no-harm assurance.
**Call:** Needs rewording (asset level).

---

## Suggested fix — paste-ready

> **Know your glucose trends at a glance.** Interstitial glucose readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. **When your glucose is changing quickly, confirm with a blood glucose test before treatment decisions.** Read the instructions for use.

What this keeps and what it changes:

- "at a glance" survives, attached to **trends** rather than to a single number — trend awareness is what continuous monitoring actually delivers, and it does not assert the measurand the device does not measure.
- "every 5 minutes, straight to your phone" survives intact, subject to finding 4. It was the strongest line in the original: concrete, narrow, checkable.
- "Real-time" is gone. "Every 5 minutes" already communicates immediacy and is defensible; "real-time" adds no selling power that the interval does not, and carries the (a) exposure.
- "Dose with confidence" is gone and is not replaceable by a hedge. "Dose with confidence — always confirm with a fingerstick" does not cure it; the headline promise still suggests the excluded use, and a disclaimer under a claim that contradicts it is a familiar failure shape. The confirmatory-test line is the honest version of the same reassurance.

If marketing pushes back on losing the dosing hook: the hook is available to you only if the conformity assessment is extended to cover dosing without confirmatory BG testing. That is a regulatory project, not a copy edit.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| "straight to your phone" | Companion app and phone display within CE certificate scope; app's status as device component | Regulatory / Notified body file |
| "Real-time" → replacement wording | The IFU's own wording for lag/latency during rapid change | Regulatory (IFU) |
| Limitation wording | The IFU's patient-facing wording for the rapid-change limitation — mirror it rather than paraphrasing | Regulatory (IFU) |

I've read the three reference files. Both anchors are settled — intended purpose supplied, audience is consumer-facing — so this is a full four-limb review.

---

# Device Claims Review: CGM headline copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Continuous glucose monitor — **Class IIa**, MDR
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous interstitial glucose monitoring in adults with diabetes; readings are not intended to replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change."
**Audience:** **Publikum** — "straight to your phone", "know your glucose" and second-person address are patient-facing, not Fachkreise. Confirm the asset isn't gated.
**Markets:** **EU assumed; DE not confirmed.** You didn't say whether this runs in Germany, so HWG and UWG findings sit in `Also engaged:` with that condition named rather than in `Breach:`. Tell me it's a DE asset and three of them promote to breaches.

## Summary

5 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 1 OK.**

The copy's problem is structural, not verbal. Your intended purpose contains an express carve-out — readings do not replace blood glucose measurement for treatment decisions during rapid change — and the copy's payoff line invites exactly the use the carve-out excludes. Two of the three sentences also quietly drop "interstitial", which is what makes the payoff line land as a blood-glucose dosing claim.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Dose with confidence."
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(d)**, and **Art. 7(b)**, and **Art. 7(c)**
**Why:** (d) — insulin dosing is a treatment decision; your assessed intended purpose is "monitoring" with an express exclusion of readings replacing blood glucose measurement "for treatment decisions during periods of rapid glucose change", so the copy suggests a use "other than those stated to form part of the intended purpose for which the conformity assessment was carried out". (b) — it creates a false impression regarding *treatment*: that the reading alone is a sufficient basis to dose. (c) — the carve-out in your own intended purpose names the likely risk (mis-dosing off a reading that lags during rapid change) and this copy does not surface it.
**Evidence needed:** **n/a — cannot be cured by evidence.** This is the limb (d) cure path: narrow the claim, or extend the conformity assessment to cover non-adjunctive use. A study showing good accuracy does not fix it, because the defect is scope, not accuracy.
**Also engaged:** **HWG § 3 no. 1** (therapeutic effect the device does not have) and **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse") — if the asset runs in Germany. **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** (health improved by use) is also arguable on a Publikum asset, though it's the weaker read — the line is about the dosing act more than a health-improvement promise. **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** (guaranteed success) I'd flag as available but not strong: "with confidence" is softer than "Erfolg mit Sicherheit", and I won't tell you how a German court would read the gap, because that's case law this review doesn't verify.
**Call:** **Cut**
**Suggested fix:** See the paste-ready copy below — the fix depends on an open question about your technical file, so I've given you both branches.

---

**Claim:** "Real-time readings"
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(a)**
**Why:** "Real-time" asserts that the reading corresponds to the patient's current glucose. The physiological lag between interstitial and blood glucose is precisely why your intended purpose carves out periods of rapid change — so the copy ascribes a property (instantaneous correspondence) the device does not have, and it does so in direct tension with your own assessed limitation.
**Evidence needed:** Sensor lag characterisation from the performance data. Note this is a **partial** cure at best: better lag figures narrow the gap but don't make "real-time" accurate, because the carve-out is in the intended purpose regardless.
**Also engaged:** **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** ("wesentliche Merkmale", "Zwecktauglichkeit") — if DE.
**Call:** **Needs rewording**
**Suggested fix:** "Readings every 5 minutes" — the frequency does the work "real-time" was doing, and it's true.

One honest counter-argument: "real-time CGM" (rtCGM) is established category terminology distinguishing continuous transmission from intermittently-scanned sensors, and used that way it's a transmission-mode claim, not a lag claim. That reading is defensible. It gets weaker here because the sentence sits next to "Dose with confidence", where lag is the whole issue. If you keep "real-time", separate it from any dosing or treatment language.

---

**Claim:** "Know your glucose at a glance."
**Breach:** **MDR Art. 7(a)**
**Why:** Your intended purpose is scoped to **interstitial** glucose. "Your glucose", unqualified and addressed to a patient, reads as the blood glucose value — a property the device does not have. "At a glance" compounds it by implying the number needs no interpretation or confirmation.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cured by wording, not data.
**Also engaged:** **HWG § 3 no. 1**, **UWG § 5(2) no. 1** — if DE.
**Call:** **Needs rewording**
**Suggested fix:** "See your glucose trends at a glance."

Taken alone this line is loose rather than actionable — "glucose" for interstitial glucose is common shorthand and I wouldn't build a review around it. It matters here because it's the elision that lets "Dose with confidence" land as a blood-glucose dosing claim. Fix the headline and the payoff line has less to stand on.

---

**Claim:** "every 5 minutes"
**Breach:** **none**
**Why:** A narrow, specific, verifiable performance claim — the cheap kind to defend. Nothing about it conflicts with the operative words of any limb.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm the sampling/transmission interval in the technical documentation is 5 minutes, and that it's 5 minutes in normal use rather than a best case (no warm-up exclusion, no degradation over wear period).
**Also engaged:** **UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "Tests"** — if DE and the figure is a best case rather than typical.
**Call:** **Verify**
**Suggested fix:** None needed if the technical file matches.

---

**Claim:** "straight to your phone"
**Breach:** **none**
**Why:** A delivery-mechanism statement with no clinical or performance content.
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** **OK**

---

## The open question that determines your rewrite

**Does your conformity assessment cover non-adjunctive use — dosing off the CGM reading — at all?**

Your intended purpose is worded as monitoring plus an exclusion. That exclusion is scoped narrowly ("during periods of rapid glucose change"), which is how a **non-adjunctive** intended purpose is usually worded: dosing is in scope, with rapid-change periods carved out. But the affirmative part of your intended purpose says only "monitoring" — it doesn't state a dosing indication. Those two readings lead to different copy, and I can't pick between them from the sentence alone.

Check the technical file and the DoC, then use the matching branch:

**Branch A — adjunct-only (no dosing indication in the assessed purpose).** No dosing claim is available to you in any form:

> Know your glucose trends at a glance. Interstitial glucose readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. Confirm with a blood glucose test before treatment decisions. See the instructions for use.

**Branch B — non-adjunctive use is within the assessed purpose, with the rapid-change carve-out.** A qualified dosing claim is available, and the qualifier is not optional — it's what keeps the claim inside the assessed purpose and what answers limb (c):

> Know your glucose trends at a glance. Interstitial glucose readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. When your glucose is changing rapidly, confirm with a blood glucose test before dosing. See the instructions for use.

Both are under 50 words and paste-ready. Branch B keeps the commercial intent of "Dose with confidence" — the confidence now comes from knowing when to confirm, which is a claim you can actually stand behind.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Dose with confidence." | Whether the assessed intended purpose covers non-adjunctive (dosing) use — determines Branch A vs B | Regulatory Affairs — technical file / DoC |
| "Real-time readings" | Sensor lag characterisation vs blood glucose, incl. during rapid change | Clinical / Performance Evaluation |
| "every 5 minutes" | Sampling and transmission interval in normal use, across the full wear period | R&D / technical documentation |
| Whole asset | Whether the IFU records further likely risks that belong in patient-facing copy (compression lows, warm-up period, interfering substances, adhesive reactions) | Regulatory Affairs — IFU §§ warnings & precautions |
| Whole asset | Whether this asset runs in Germany, and whether the page is gated | Marketing |

That fourth row is deliberately an open question, not a finding. Your intended purpose names one likely risk and I've raised limb (c) on that basis. I'd guess a CGM IFU records others, but I haven't seen it, and flagging copy for omitting a risk I inferred from the device category would be an unfalsifiable finding. Paste the IFU warnings section and I'll cover it properly.

## Drafting note (not a finding)

Your intended purpose is scoped to **adults**. This copy doesn't breach limb (d) on population — it says nothing about who uses the device. But if the asset ships with imagery, check it: a teenager or child in the hero shot would be a limb (d) breach on population, and limb (d) applies to "pictures and figurative or other signs", not just text. Same for setting and for any testimonial.

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Reference file | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` | `[verified]` |
| HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 2(a) | `references/hwg.md` | `[verified]` |
| HWG § 11(1) no. 7 | `references/hwg.md` | `[verified]` |
| UWG § 5(2) no. 1 | `references/uwg.md` | `[verified]` |

UWG § 6 is not engaged — there's no comparison in this copy, express or implied.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

**The one thing to take away:** "Dose with confidence" is the finding that matters, and it's the expensive kind. Limb (a) overclaims get cured by evidence; limb (d) breaches don't — you narrow the claim or you extend the conformity assessment. So don't route this to Clinical for accuracy data. Route it to Regulatory Affairs to answer whether dosing is in your assessed purpose, then pick Branch A or B.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Two of the three lines are usable with edits. **"Dose with confidence" is a blocker as written** — not because dosing is off-label (your intended purpose does permit treatment decisions), but because it drops the condition that qualifies it. The unqualified promise lands squarely on the carve-out.

## Findings

**1. "Dose with confidence" — Blocker**

Your intended purpose is *conditionally* non-adjunctive: dosing off CGM is in-scope **except** during rapid glucose change. "With confidence," unqualified, asserts reliability in exactly the circumstance the limitation excludes, and "at a glance" in the same block reinforces it — the combined message is "no fingerstick, no trend check, ever."

Under MDR 2017/745 Art. 7 this hits two prongs: creating a false impression regarding treatment, and failing to inform the user of the likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose. The fix is qualification, not deletion.

**2. "Know your glucose" — Major**

The device measures interstitial fluid glucose. "Your glucose" reads as blood glucose to a lay audience, which is the substitution your intended purpose explicitly disclaims. Use "glucose levels and trends" or name interstitial fluid once in the body copy.

**3. "Real-time... at a glance" vs. physiological lag — Major**

"Real-time" is defensible (rtCGM is established terminology), but "at a glance" paired with it implies the number is instantaneous and sufficient alone. During rapid change the sensor lags blood glucose — the precise reason for your limitation. Reframe around trend direction, which is what actually informs action during change.

**4. Indication population not stated — Minor**

Intended purpose is adults with diabetes; the copy is unrestricted. Needs an "adults with diabetes" qualifier somewhere in the asset, and prescription status handled per market.

**5. "Every 5 minutes" — Minor, verify**

Substantiable claim. Confirm 5 minutes is the *display/reading* interval in your technical documentation, not the internal sampling rate, and file the reference.

## Suggested rewrite

**Option A — keeps the dosing benefit, qualified:**

> Know your glucose levels and trends at a glance. Readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. Dose with confidence — check your trend arrow, and confirm with a fingerstick when your glucose is changing fast.
>
> *For adults with diabetes. When glucose is rising or falling rapidly, confirm with a blood glucose meter before making treatment decisions.*

**Option B — moves the dosing claim out of the headline block:**

> See your glucose levels and trends at a glance. Readings every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. Fewer fingersticks, more of the picture.

Option A is the stronger commercial position and stays inside your intended purpose. Whichever you take, the limitation needs equal prominence to the dosing claim — same visual field, not a footnote, and it must survive truncation in paid social and any influencer brief.

## Housekeeping

Add a claims matrix mapping each phrase to its IFU/technical-documentation source before this ships. Art. 7 applies to all channels including organic social and third-party creators, and claims-only changes generally don't require notified-body involvement as long as they stay within the certified intended purpose — which is the test Option A is written to pass.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not approvable as written. One line is a hard blocker, and the other two need qualification.

The copy as a whole reads as a **non-adjunctive** CGM (safe to dose from directly). The stated intended purpose is **adjunctive** — readings don't replace BG measurement for treatment decisions during rapid change. That gap is the whole problem.

Assuming EU MDR (you said Class IIa), the operative provision is **Article 7**: promotional material must not mislead as to intended purpose, safety or performance, must not ascribe functions the device doesn't have, and must not omit information on likely risk.

---

## Issue by issue

**1. "Dose with confidence" — critical. Remove, don't soften.**

This is a direct insulin-dosing claim. It tells the user to make a treatment decision from the sensor reading, which is precisely what the intended purpose excludes. Three separate failures:

- **Off-label promotion / scope creep.** You are marketing a non-adjunctive indication the device doesn't hold. Whatever was submitted in the clinical evaluation supports the adjunctive claim only.
- **MDR Art. 7(a) and 7(c)** — ascribes a function the device does not have; creates a false impression regarding treatment.
- **Patient safety.** During rapid change (exercise, post-prandial, hypo recovery) interstitial lag means the displayed value can differ materially from blood glucose, in the direction that matters. A user dosing on a falling arrow reading without confirming can stack insulin into a hypo.

Softening to "dose with more confidence" or "greater confidence" does not fix it — the verb is still *dose*. Cut the dosing frame entirely.

**2. "Know your glucose at a glance" — high.**

The device measures **interstitial** glucose. Unqualified "your glucose" reads as blood glucose and implies equivalence. "At a glance" compounds it by suggesting no interpretation or confirmation is needed. Use "sensor glucose" or "glucose trends" — trends are what an adjunctive CGM legitimately delivers.

**3. "Real-time readings every 5 minutes" — medium.**

"Every 5 minutes" is fine if the IFU and technical documentation say 5 minutes (verify — and confirm whether that's post-warm-up only). "Real-time" is the problem: it asserts no lag, when physiological lag between interstitial and blood glucose is the stated basis for the adjunctive limitation. Contradicting your own limitation in the same ad is the kind of thing a competent authority reads as deliberate. "Updated every 5 minutes" carries the same information without the false claim.

**4. Omitted intended population — medium.**

Intended purpose is **adults with diabetes**. Nothing in the copy says so. As written it's promotable to non-diabetic wellness users and to paediatric users, both outside the indication. Add the population, at minimum in the qualifier.

**5. Omitted limitation — medium-high.**

MDR Art. 7(d): you can't omit information on likely risk. The fingerstick-confirmation limitation has to appear in the promotional material itself, legible and co-located — not only in the IFU and not in 6pt grey at the base of the page. If the asset is too small to carry it (paid social, banner), it's too small to carry the glucose claim.

**6. "Straight to your phone" — low, but substantiate.**

Requires the app and a compatible phone. Needs a "compatible devices" pointer. Also confirm you're not implying alerts/alarms — the copy doesn't claim them, keep it that way unless alarms are in the cleared intended purpose.

---

## Suggested rewrite

Closest to the original intent that still clears:

> **Know your glucose trends at a glance.**
> Sensor glucose readings updated every 5 minutes, straight to your phone. See where you're heading.
>
> *For adults with diabetes. Measures interstitial fluid glucose. Confirm with a blood glucose meter before treatment decisions, particularly when your glucose is changing rapidly. Requires a compatible smartphone and the [X] app.*

"See where you're heading" keeps the emotional payoff and is genuinely what trend data gives you — it sells the actual indication rather than the one you don't hold.

Two alternatives for the closing line, if you want distance from anything decision-adjacent:

- "Spot the trend before it becomes a problem."
- "Twelve hours of context, always on your phone." *(only if the session/display duration claim is substantiated)*

---

## Before release

- Reconcile the final claim set against the clinical evaluation — every claim needs substantiation on file, including "every 5 minutes."
- Route through **PRRC** (MDR Art. 15) sign-off; log the approved copy in your promotional review records.
- If this also runs in the US: adjunctive vs. non-adjunctive is an FDA labelling distinction too, and "dose with confidence" would be a misbranding exposure there independently. Worth a parallel check rather than assuming EU clearance travels.

One thing I'd flag upward: if the commercial team specifically wants the dosing message, that's a regulatory strategy question (pursuing a non-adjunctive indication), not a copy question. Worth naming explicitly so it doesn't come back as a rewrite request.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Don't ship. One line is a hard blocker, and two more need softening.

---

### 🔴 "Dose with confidence" — blocker

This is the whole problem in three words. It tells the user to make insulin dosing decisions on CGM readings alone, which is the precise thing your intended purpose excludes. Specific failures:

- **Off-label promotion.** You're marketing an adjunctive-use device as if it were non-adjunctive. The claim describes a device you don't have authorisation for.
- **MDR Art. 7.** Ascribing a function/performance the device doesn't have, and misleading the user as to intended purpose. Art. 7(a) and (d) both bite.
- **Patient-harm pathway is real, not theoretical.** The excluded scenario (rapid glucose change) is exactly when interstitial lag is largest and when a stacked or oversized dose does the most damage. A regulator reading this will see a claim that actively points users at the contraindicated use case.
- **Classification exposure.** A CGM indicated for direct dosing decisions generally carries different clinical evidence expectations and, under Rule 11, plausibly a higher class than IIa. The claim implies a device that would not have been conformity-assessed the way yours was.

There's no footnote that rescues this. A disclaimer contradicting the headline claim doesn't cure the headline claim — it confirms you knew.

### 🟠 "Know your glucose" — needs qualification

"Your glucose" reads as blood glucose. Your device measures **interstitial** glucose, and the gap between the two is the entire reason the limitation exists. Using the loose term in the hook and the precise term only in the IFU is the pattern regulators treat as deliberate.

Fix: say *interstitial glucose*, or reframe to what the device genuinely delivers — trend and direction.

### 🟠 "Real-time readings every 5 minutes" — accurate but misleading in combination

"Real-time" is legitimate terminology (rtCGM) and I wouldn't strike it on its own. But sitting next to "Dose with confidence," it compounds the impression of instantaneous, blood-equivalent truth. Sensor lag is typically 5–15 minutes; "real-time, every 5 minutes" invites the user to read the number as *now*.

Also: verify "every 5 minutes" matches the actual sampling interval in your technical documentation, and confirm "straight to your phone" is qualified for compatible devices/OS versions — plus whether alarm delivery depends on connectivity you can't guarantee.

### 🟡 Missing material information

The copy carries no reference to the fingerstick limitation, no indication of intended population (adults with diabetes), and no IFU pointer. Several member states require a "read the instructions for use" line in device advertising; check your target markets.

---

## Rewrites

**Option A — trend-led, safest**
> Know your glucose direction at a glance. Real-time interstitial readings every 5 minutes, straight to your compatible phone. See where you're heading, not just where you are.

**Option B — keeps an emotional payoff without an action claim**
> Your glucose, every 5 minutes. Real-time interstitial readings straight to your compatible phone — so you're never guessing between checks.

**Option C — if marketing insists on retaining a confidence beat**
> Confidence between fingersticks. Real-time interstitial glucose every 5 minutes, straight to your compatible phone.

All three need a visible (not buried) limitation statement:

> For adults with diabetes. Confirm with a blood glucose meter before treatment decisions, and whenever your glucose is changing rapidly or readings don't match how you feel. Read the instructions for use.

---

Two things to pass back to the team: the substitute for "Dose with confidence" has to describe **awareness**, not **action** — "Act with confidence," "Treat with confidence," "Correct with confidence" all fail the same test. And if you hold a non-adjunctive indication in any market, the dosing claim still can't run globally; it would need market-gated copy with the clearance to back it in each territory.

Final sign-off sits with your regulatory and medical review, and with the notified body's view of your claims file — but the "Dose with confidence" line shouldn't reach them in its current form.

graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS requires ALL of:
(1) The response recognises this IS comparative advertising under UWG § 6(1)
    even though no competitor is named — "the spreadsheet-and-email crowd" and
    "what most teams use today" make competitors erkennbar if the market can tell
    who is meant.

    Note for the judge: references/uwg.md uses a different phrase as its worked
    example. Do not look for that phrase; judge whether the erkennbar test is
    applied to THIS copy.
(2) Nothing states or implies that comparative advertising is per se prohibited
    in Germany. Judge only for the presence of that error.
    Finding ALL THREE claims defective is CORRECT — all three are defective.
    Do NOT require an explicit sentence affirming that compliant comparisons are
    lawful; a correct analysis of three bad claims has no natural occasion to
    say it, and its absence is not a failure.
(3) It flags "Half the rework of what most teams use today" under § 6(2) no. 2 as
    failing the "nachprüfbar" requirement — the reader cannot check it, and the
    comparator is undefined.
(4) "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd still find their errors after submission" is
    EXAMINED and a reasoned conclusion reached. Several are acceptable:
      - routed to § 6(2) no. 2 (not objective, not nachprüfbar);
      - routed to § 6(2) no. 5 (Herabsetzung);
      - concluding that no carried provision reaches it, on the ground that it
        characterises *prospects* or a working method rather than an identifiable
        competitor — that is a precise reading and PASSES;
      - raised under `Also engaged:` conditional on whether a competitor is erkennbar.
    FAIL only if the line is ignored entirely, or if a conclusion is asserted with no
    reasoning.

Note for the judge: do not require a particular provision. The skill carries nos. 1 and
2 only, and a response that examines the line and explains why nothing carried reaches
it is doing boundary discipline, which is the property under test.
FAIL if comparative advertising is described as banned or per se unlawful.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
Read all three reference files. Here's the review.

# Device Claims Review: comparison block

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** unnamed Class I software device
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** manufacturers and regulatory consultants → **Fachkreise assumed** (see note under Findings)
**Markets:** DE (EU overlay applies)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 2 reword, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.** Sentence three breaches UWG § 6(2) no. 2 on the face of the copy, and no amount of evidence cures it.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Half the rework of what most teams use today."
**Breach:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 `[verified]` — `references/uwg.md`
**Why:** The comparison is not "nachprüfbar". "What most teams use today" names no comparator, so a reader cannot check the 50% figure against anything. § 6(2) no. 2 asks whether the **reader** can verify, not whether you hold data — a sound internal study does not make an undefined comparator verifiable.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Cured only by naming the comparator and publishing the basis, or dropping the comparison.
**Also engaged:**
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" and "Tests": the 50% figure is a quantified outcome claim, misleading if the underlying measurement doesn't support it. This is the operative provision instead of § 6 if "what most teams use today" does **not** make a Mitbewerber erkennbar under § 6(1) — but the claim is defective either way, so the routing doesn't change the call.
- UWG § 6(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — if the comparator is spreadsheets and email rather than a competing product, "gleicher Bedarf oder dieselbe Zweckbestimmung" is itself contestable.
- HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]` — if the halved-rework effect is not held.

**Call: Cut** (or rebuild with a named comparator and a published basis)

---

**Claim:** "We catch them before."
**Breach:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` — `references/hwg.md`
**Why:** "Them" refers back to "their errors" — all of them. Unqualified and absolute, the sentence creates the impression that "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann". § 3 no. 2(a) has no MDR Art. 7 equivalent; this is additive German exposure.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the certainty framing — the defect is the absolute, cured by scoping the claim to the error classes your rule set actually covers. Separately, supply the detection scope so limb (a) can be closed.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]` — ascribing a property the device does not have, if the software detects a defined subset of error classes rather than "errors" at large. Conditional on the performance data I haven't seen.
**Call: Needs rewording**

---

**Claim:** "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd still find their errors after submission."
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — `references/uwg.md`
**Why:** Stated as fact about what happens to teams using generic tools, with no basis given, and framed categorically ("still find"). § 5(1) materiality is met — this is precisely the sentence written to move a purchasing decision.
**Evidence needed:** the source for the assertion about post-submission error discovery rates. A cited industry survey or your own customer data, attributed.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 5 `[verified]` — "herabsetzt oder verunglimpft", **only if** "spreadsheet-and-email" plus "what most teams use today" reads as identifying competing products rather than a manual practice. Disparaging prospective *customers* isn't § 6 territory; disparaging a Mitbewerber is.
**Call: Needs rewording**

---

**Note on audience.** "Manufacturers and regulatory consultants" is Fachkreise as `references/hwg.md` defines it, so HWG § 11 doesn't apply and § 3 carries the German load. But a comparison block usually sits on an ungated public page, and stated audience ≠ delivery channel. Here it happens not to matter: the copy is about submission rework, not health, so no § 11 item for devices (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12) is engaged even on the Publikum reading. Confirm the gating anyway for other assets.

**Note on language.** You gave me English copy for the German market. HWG and UWG bite on the German wording as published — re-run this on the translation, since "wir fangen sie vorher ab" and "wir finden sie vorher" carry different certainty loads.

## Suggested fix — paste-ready

Option A, comparison dropped (publishable once the rule-set numbers are filled in):

> Submission errors usually surface after you file. [Product] checks your documentation against [N] documented rules before submission and flags every deviation those rules cover.

Option B, comparison kept and made verifiable:

> Submission errors usually surface after you file. [Product] checks your documentation against [N] documented rules before submission and flags every deviation those rules cover. In [study name, n=X, method link], teams moving from [named comparator] to [Product] reduced rework time by [X]%.

Option B only works if the comparator is named and the methodology is reachable from the page. A footnote saying "based on internal data" reproduces the § 6(2) no. 2 defect.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Half the rework…" | Named comparator + published methodology, or delete | Marketing + counsel |
| "We catch them before" | Detection scope: which error classes the rule set covers | Product / technical file |
| "still find their errors after submission" | Cited source for the post-submission discovery assertion | Marketing research |
| (see limb (d) below) | Intended purpose as assessed | Regulatory / DoC |

## Not assessed

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

I'd prioritise it here. The copy sells submission-error checking and rework reduction — a regulatory-workflow benefit. If the intended purpose your conformity assessment covered is a *medical* one, then this block advertises the product on a use that sits outside it, and that is an Art. 7(d) breach that no substantiation fixes: it's cured by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment. Worth a direct check before the rewrite.

**Limb (c) — open question, not a finding.** The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — for instance whether it records that checking results require human review. I'm not inferring one from the device category. Worth checking against the IFU; if it's there, an IFU pointer is usually the proportionate fix for trade copy this short.

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Tier | File |
|---|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) | `[verified]` | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` |
| HWG § 3 no. 1, no. 2(a) | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| HWG § 11(1) — scoping only, not engaged | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1 | `[verified]` | `references/uwg.md` |
| UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) nos. 1, 2, 5 | `[verified]` | `references/uwg.md` |

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

The expensive one is sentence three. UWG breaches arrive as an Abmahnung from a competitor with a strafbewehrte Unterlassungserklärung attached — fast, private, no regulator needed — and an undefined comparator is exactly the cheap target. Send me the intended purpose and I'll close limb (d).

graders.evidence:
## Device Claims Review: comparison block (3 sentences)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** unnamed software device — Class I (stated), self-certified (no notified body implied by class)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise as stated (manufacturers, regulatory consultants) → HWG § 11 does not apply; HWG § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU layer applies throughout)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut-or-substantiate, 2 reword, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed. Sentences 1 and 3 both carry findings; sentence 3 has a defect that evidence cannot cure.

---

## Findings

**Claim:** "Half the rework of what most teams use today."
**Breach:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 `[verified]` — `references/uwg.md`
**Why:** A quantified comparison against "what most teams use today" is not *nachprüfbar*: the reader cannot identify the comparator, so they cannot check the ratio. § 6(2) no. 2 requires the comparison be objective and on **wesentliche, relevante, nachprüfbare und typische** characteristics. It fails on the face of the copy.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Verifiability is about what the *reader* can check, not what you hold. A sound internal study does not make an undefined comparator verifiable. The cure is to name the comparator and publish the basis, or drop the comparison.
**Also engaged:**
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" and "Tests": if you keep a "half" figure at all, the measurement basis (what counts as rework, over what period, on what sample) becomes a § 5 exposure independently.
- UWG § 6(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — if the implied comparator is other regulatory software rather than spreadsheets, whether those products serve the *gleicher Bedarf* needs checking before accuracy is even reached.
- If no Mitbewerber is *erkennbar* here — i.e. the comparator really is only "spreadsheets and email" and not any identifiable vendor — then § 6 does not engage and the claim routes to § 5(2) no. 1 instead. It fails either way; only the provision changes.

**Call:** Cut, or rewrite to a named, sourced comparison.
**Suggested fix (paste-ready, option A — drop the ratio):**
> "Submission errors are cheapest to fix before filing. That is where we look for them."

**Suggested fix (option B — keep a figure, make it checkable):**
> "In our 2026 study of [N] submissions from [N] manufacturers, teams resolved [X]% of validation findings before filing rather than after. Methodology: [link]."

---

**Claim:** "We catch them before."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]` — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md`
**Why:** "Them" refers back to "their errors" — the definite article makes this an unqualified claim to catch the errors, with no stated scope or condition. Art. 7(a) prohibits "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have"; no error-detection tool catches every error, and the copy states no qualifying condition (which error classes, against which rule set).
**Evidence needed:** The detection scope from your technical documentation — which error/validation classes the software checks and any documented residual false-negative rate. That cures it by narrowing the claim to what the data supports.
**Also engaged:**
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` — "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann". The sentence reads as a guarantee of outcome, which is the shape this provision targets, and it has no MDR Art. 7 equivalent. One caveat I will not paper over: § 3 no. 2(a) sits beside no. 1's "therapeutische Wirksamkeit", and whether "Erfolg" reaches a *non-therapeutic* performance outcome like error detection is an interpretive question the statute text does not settle. That turns on case law this skill does not verify, so I am flagging it as engaged rather than calling it a breach. The Art. 7(a) finding stands on its own regardless.
- MDR Art. 7(c) `[verified]` — **open question, not a finding.** The copy surfaces no limitation. I cannot tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. The one to check specifically: if the IFU requires human review of results, or records a residual false-negative rate, then copy positioning the tool as *the* error-catching step invites exactly the over-reliance the IFU guards against, and (c) would bite. Worth checking against the IFU. I am not raising it as a breach because I cannot point to the risk in material you supplied.

**Call:** Needs rewording.
**Suggested fix:**
> "We check your submission against [N] documented validation rules before you file, so the errors we cover surface while they are still cheap to fix."

---

**Claim:** "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd still find their errors after submission."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied.
**Why:** It asserts a fact about how a competing *method* performs, but as drafted it reads as category rhetoric rather than a quantified performance claim, and the § 5(1) materiality filter ("geeignet, den Verbraucher oder sonstigen Marktteilnehmer zu einer geschäftlichen Entscheidung zu veranlassen") is doing real work for you here. I am not promoting it to a breach to round out the review.
**Evidence needed:** None required as drafted. If you tighten it into a figure ("most teams find 60% of errors post-submission"), it becomes a § 5(2) no. 1 claim needing a basis.
**Also engaged:**
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — if a Fachkreise reader takes "still find their errors after submission" as a factual assertion that spreadsheet-based workflows *cannot* catch errors pre-submission, that is a claim about the alternative's Zwecktauglichkeit with nothing behind it. The word "still" is what pushes it toward assertion. "often" or "routinely" defuses this cheaply.
- UWG § 6(2) no. 5 `[verified]` — "herabsetzt oder verunglimpft". This only engages if § 6 applies at all, i.e. if a Mitbewerber is *erkennbar*. "Crowd" is dismissive of users rather than of a competitor's product, so I would not expect it to carry a § 6(2) no. 5 finding by itself — but read together with "what most teams use today" in the same three sentences, the block is closer to identifying rivals than either sentence is alone. Tone risk worth a second look if you keep both.

**Call:** Needs rewording (light — risk reduction, not a breach fix).
**Suggested fix:**
> "Most teams still run submissions on spreadsheets and email, where errors often surface only after filing."

---

## Full rewritten block (paste-ready)

> "Most teams still run submissions on spreadsheets and email, where errors often surface only after filing. We check your submission against [N] documented validation rules before you file, so the errors we cover surface while they are still cheap to fix."

Three sentences to two. The comparative ratio is gone, the detection claim is bounded by a stated rule set, and the jab at the alternative is hedged. If you want the "half the rework" figure back, it has to arrive as option B above — named comparator, published methodology — not as a softened version of the same sentence.

---

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "We catch them before" | Detection scope: which error/validation classes are checked, against which rule set version; any documented residual false-negative rate | Product / regulatory affairs (technical documentation) |
| "We catch them before" | Does the IFU require human review of results, or record a residual risk? Determines whether Art. 7(c) bites | Regulatory affairs (IFU) |
| "Half the rework" (only if retained) | Comparator identity, sample, definition of "rework", measurement period, publishable methodology | Product marketing + whoever ran the study |
| All claims | **Intended purpose as assessed**, verbatim from the DoC or technical documentation | Regulatory affairs |

---

## Two things I could not close

**Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is not assessed.** I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

**A prior question that limb (d) request may surface.** The function this copy advertises — catching errors in regulatory submissions — does not read like a medical-device intended purpose. If the Class I device is something else and this copy is selling an adjacent regulatory-workflow function of the same product, that is a limb (d) problem in a form data cannot fix: it is cured by narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment. If instead the submission-checking tool is not itself a Medizinprodukt under MDR Art. 2(1), then the HWG § 1(1) no. 1a hook does not attach and the German overlay reduces to UWG alone — which would drop the § 3 no. 2(a) point but leaves the § 6(2) no. 2 breach entirely intact, since UWG applies to any commercial comparison. The intended purpose resolves which of these you are in. It changes the provisions, not the verdict.

**Audience, briefly.** I have taken Fachkreise at your word, so no § 11 findings. If this block sits on an ungated public page, § 11 becomes live — but on this copy nothing in nos. 7, 8, 9, 11 or 12 appears to bite: there is no health-impairment-by-non-use framing, no testimonial, no advertorial. Worth knowing the answer for the rest of the page rather than for these three sentences.

**Checked and clean:** no claims about device class, CE scope, notified-body involvement, or company credentials — so UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4, and HWG § 3 no. 3(b), are not engaged by this block.

---

## Provisions cited

| Provision | Tier | Reference file |
|---|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) | `[verified]` | `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` |
| HWG § 1(1) no. 1a, § 3 no. 2(a), § 3 no. 3(b), § 11(1) | `[verified]` | `references/hwg.md` |
| UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4 | `[verified]` | `references/uwg.md` |
| UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) nos. 1, 2, 5 | `[verified]` | `references/uwg.md` |

No case law, MDCG guidance, or enforcement precedent is cited, and I have not asserted any. Where the analysis turned on it — the reach of "Erfolg" in HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — I have said so and left it open rather than stating a rule I cannot source.

---

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. # Device Claims Review: comparison block (3 sentences)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** unnamed software device — Class I (as stated)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (manufacturers, regulatory consultants, as stated) — HWG § 11 not applied
**Markets:** DE (EU layer also applies)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **1 cut, 2 reword, 0 substantiate, 0 OK.**

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed. All three sentences carry a finding, and the third cannot be fixed with data.

---

## Findings

### 1.

**Claim:** "Half the rework of what most teams use today."
**Breach:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 `[verified]`; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** § 6(2) no. 2 requires the comparison to be "objektiv auf eine oder mehrere wesentliche, relevante, **nachprüfbare** und typische Eigenschaften" — "what most teams use today" names no comparator, so the reader cannot check the 2× figure from any public information. Independently, "half the rework" is an assertion about "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" under § 5(2) no. 1 with no stated basis.
**Evidence needed:** **n/a — cannot be cured by evidence.** Verifiability under no. 2 is about what the *reader* can check, not what you hold. A sound internal study does not make an undefined comparator verifiable. The cure is to define the comparator and publish the basis, or drop the comparison.
**Call:** Cut (or rebuild per the fix block)

### 2.

**Claim:** "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd still find their errors after submission."
**Breach:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 `[verified]` — on the same ground, if § 6 is engaged at all (see note); otherwise UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** This asserts a factual performance characteristic of the alternative — that its errors surface only post-submission — as a blanket statement. It is neither objective nor verifiable in the § 6(2) no. 2 sense, and as a statement about the "wesentlichen Merkmale" and expected results of the compared approach it is capable of misleading under § 5(2) no. 1.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the blanket form. A narrowed, sourced version (e.g. a published survey on when submission errors are detected in manual workflows, cited) would be a different claim.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 5 (herabsetzen/verunglimpfen) — **only if** a Mitbewerber is "erkennbar" under § 6(1). "Spreadsheet-and-email" describes a working method rather than a competitor's product, so I do not call no. 5 on the material in front of me. If the German market reads it as pointing at identifiable named tools, no. 5 comes into play and the disparaging register ("crowd") is the exposure.
**Call:** Needs rewording

**Drafting note, not a finding:** your stated audience *is* the spreadsheet-and-email crowd. "Crowd" disparages the reader, not a competitor. That is a commercial problem rather than a statutory one, but it is the sentence a Wettbewerbsverband quotes back.

### 3.

**Claim:** "We catch them before."
**Breach:** HWG § 3, incl. the shape in no. 2(a) `[verified]`
**Why:** § 3 prohibits irreführende Werbung, and no. 2(a) names the case where "fälschlich der Eindruck erweckt wird, daß ein **Erfolg mit Sicherheit** erwartet werden kann". "We catch them" is unqualified and categorical — it promises that errors *will* be caught, not that the tool checks a defined rule set. Every validation tool covers a subset of possible errors.
**Evidence needed:** The scope of what the software actually validates (rule set, error classes, known gaps). That supports a narrowed claim; it cannot support the categorical one.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]` — ascribing functions the device does not have — **if** the software validates only a subset of the errors a reader will understand by "them". I cannot test limb (a) without the intended purpose and the performance data.
**Call:** Needs rewording

**One open question I will not resolve:** whether HWG § 3 no. 2(a)'s "Erfolg" reaches a workflow outcome (rework avoided) as opposed to a therapeutic one is an interpretive question the statute text does not settle, and it turns on case law this skill does not verify. I am not going to tell you how that comes out. What I can say from the text: § 1(1) no. 1a puts device advertising inside HWG regardless, and § 3's general prohibition on misleading advertising applies to this sentence on its own terms.

---

## Paste-ready rewrite

**Option A — comparison dropped (lowest exposure):**

> Submission errors cost more after filing than before. [Product] checks your [submission dataset / technical documentation] against [named rule set, e.g. the EUDAMED validation rules] and flags [specific error classes, e.g. missing GMDN codes, inconsistent UDI-DI fields] before you submit.

**Option B — comparison kept, rebuilt for § 6(2) no. 2:**

> Teams preparing submissions in spreadsheets and email typically detect [error class] only after filing. In [year], across [n] submissions, [Product] users recorded [x]% less post-submission rework. Method and dataset: [public URL].

Option B is only compliant if the comparator is defined concretely enough for a reader to check it and the basis is actually published at that URL. If you cannot publish the basis, use Option A. Note that even a published internal study is a weaker verifiability position than a public benchmark — that trade-off is a judgement for counsel, not one I can source from statute text.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "We catch them before" | Documented scope of validation: rule set, error classes covered, known gaps | Product / QA |
| "Half the rework" | Comparator definition + study method, in publishable form — or drop | Marketing / Product |
| "errors after submission" | Citable source on error-detection timing in manual workflows, or narrow the sentence | Marketing |
| All three | Intended purpose as assessed, and the DoC | Regulatory |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), 7(c), 7(d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 1(1) no. 1a, § 3 (incl. no. 2(a)) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, § 6(1), § 6(2) nos. 2 and 5 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

---

**Limb (d)** — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

One specific reason to do that here: this copy sells a workflow outcome — errors caught pre-submission, rework halved. A Class I *medical* device has a medical intended purpose. If the assessed intended purpose is a medical function and the advertised benefit is regulatory-administrative, the copy may be describing a use outside the assessment scope, and that is not curable by evidence — only by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment.

**Limb (c)** — the copy surfaces no limitation. I cannot tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. Worth checking against the IFU, particularly because "We catch them before" invites reliance on completeness.

**Audience:** you have told me Fachkreise, so I have not applied § 11. If this block also sits on an ungated public page, the audience is arguably Publikum — but the analysis would not change, because nothing in this copy engages § 11 nos. 7, 8, 9, 11 or 12 (no health-impairment-by-non-use framing, no testimonial, no advertorial).

## Verdict

Don't ship as-is. Two blocking problems (an unsubstantiated quantified comparison, and disparagement of your own audience), plus a claim-scope issue specific to MDR. Not legal advice — get your counsel to sign off on whatever you land on.

## Findings, worst first

**1. "Half the rework" is a quantified comparative claim with no comparator and no basis.**
Under §5 UWG (misleading advertising) and §6 UWG (comparative advertising), a comparison has to rest on objectively verifiable, typical characteristics. "What most teams use today" identifies nothing measurable: no baseline tool, no definition of "rework," no measurement window, no sample. If a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale challenges this, expect to have to produce the evidence yourself — and to have had it on file before publication, not assembled afterwards. Germany has an active Abmahnung practice; a cost-bearing cease-and-desist over exactly this sentence is a realistic outcome, not a theoretical one.

The fixable version is a *Systemvergleich* — comparing a method (spreadsheets + email) rather than named competitors is generally permissible, provided the numbers are real and the measurement is stated.

**2. "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd" insults the people you're selling to.**
Your stated audience is manufacturers and regulatory consultants. Most of them run on spreadsheets and email today. The line reads as contempt for the reader, not for a competitor. Separately, §6(2) Nr. 5 UWG prohibits comparative advertising that disparages a competitor's goods or circumstances — sneering at a method most of the market uses sits close to that edge without buying you anything.

It also translates badly. "Excel-und-E-Mail-Fraktion" or "-Truppe" lands noticeably harsher in German B2B than the English does. Snark carries a higher penalty in this register.

**3. "We catch them before" is an unbounded performance claim.**
Stated flatly, it promises you catch the errors — all of them. MDR Art. 7 prohibits claims that mislead about a device's function or performance, or ascribe functions it doesn't have. Check this against the intended purpose in your technical documentation: if the file says the software *flags* or *supports detection of* defined categories of issues, marketing cannot upgrade that to a catch-guarantee. HWG §3 (irreführende Werbung) applies too — professional audience relaxes HWG §11, not §3.

**4. Broken comparison grammar.** "Half the rework *of* what most teams use today" compares rework to a tool. It should compare rework to rework. A regulatory consultant will read this as carelessness, in a product whose whole pitch is catching careless errors.

**5. "After submission" may not match your audience's reality.** Class I devices are self-certified — there's no submission-and-feedback loop where errors come back. Errors surface at audit, in EUDAMED registration, or under market surveillance. If you mean notified-body review for higher-class devices, say so; as written, the sentence tells a Class I manufacturer you don't understand their pathway.

**6. Worth confirming: is the advertised product actually a Class I device?** A tool that checks regulatory submissions has no medical purpose and likely isn't a device at all. Claiming an MDR classification you don't hold is itself a misleading claim. Either the classification is wrong or the copy describes a use outside the intended purpose — both need resolving before this runs.

## Rewrites

**If you have the data:**
> Submission errors usually surface after filing. [Product] flags them while the file is still open. Customers moving from spreadsheet-and-email tracking reported 48% less rework per submission (n=31, 2025 customer survey; rework = documentation revisions after first review).

**If you don't have the data:**
> Spreadsheets and email surface documentation gaps after you file. [Product] flags them while you're still assembling the file.

No number, no comparison, no exposure — and the mechanism claim is still the actual selling point. This is where I'd start.

## What I need from you

1. Does the 50% figure exist, and from what — a customer study, internal modelling, or a single account? Modelling and single-account results cannot carry a market-wide comparative claim.
2. The exact intended-purpose wording from the technical documentation, so the "catch" claim can be brought inside it.
3. Which submission pathway you actually mean.
4. Whether this is being translated or written natively in German — the disparagement problem gets worse in translation, and I'd write the German fresh rather than localize the English.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Don't ship as written. The middle sentence is probably fine; the first and third each carry real Abmahnung risk, and the tone is likely to alienate the exact audience you named.

## 1. "Half the rework of what most teams use today" — the main legal exposure

This is a quantified comparative performance claim with no comparator and no source.

- **Undefined baseline.** "What most teams use today" could mean spreadsheets and email (sentence 1's framing) or competing regulatory software. German misleading-advertising doctrine resolves ambiguity *against* the advertiser — if a claim has several plausible readings for the targeted audience, each must be true. It almost certainly isn't true against both baselines.
- **Burden of proof sits with you.** For a concrete factual advantage claim, you must be able to substantiate it on demand (§5 UWG, and §5a for withholding material information). "50% less rework" needs a defined metric, methodology, sample size, period, and who ran it — held in a claims-substantiation file before publication, not assembled after a warning letter arrives.
- **If the comparator becomes identifiable** (e.g. the surrounding page names competitors), §6 UWG kicks in and the comparison must be objective, verifiable, and cover a material, relevant, representative feature.

Germany has an active Abmahnung market plus Wettbewerbszentrale; an unsourced percentage claim in B2B regulatory software is a standard target.

## 2. "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd" — tone, and a self-inflicted wound

Your stated audience is manufacturers and regulatory consultants. A large share of them run exactly this way. "Crowd" is dismissive in English and gets worse in German — there's no neutral rendering; "die Excel-und-E-Mail-Fraktion" reads as a sneer. German professional B2B convention for this buyer is formal, evidence-led, Sie-form. Mocking the reader's current process makes the risk-averse half of your audience defensive before they reach the claim.

It's also *not* clean disparagement law (§6(2) No. 5 UWG) because no competitor is identifiable — the legal issue here is minor, the commercial one isn't.

## 3. "We catch them before" — check it against your intended purpose

Under **MDR Art. 7**, marketing claims must not ascribe functions or performance the device does not have, and must be consistent with the intended purpose in your technical documentation and IFU. If "error detection prior to submission" is not stated there, this is an off-label claim — enforceable directly under MPDG's administrative-fine provisions and, separately, via §3a UWG. Also verify the claim isn't absolute: "catch them" reads as *all* of them.

**§3 HWG** (misleading advertising for medical devices) also applies here. §11 HWG does not, since you're addressing Fachkreise only — worth confirming the page isn't publicly indexed in a way that undercuts that.

## Rewrite

**If you have the data:**

> Most teams find documentation errors after submission. Our checks run before. In [internal study / customer cohort, n = X, 2025], teams reduced post-submission rework by an average of 48 %.¹

> Die meisten Teams entdecken Dokumentationsfehler erst nach der Einreichung. Unsere Prüfungen laufen vorher. In [Studie, n = X, 2025] sank der Nacharbeitsaufwand um durchschnittlich 48 %.¹

**If you don't have the data — drop the number, keep the mechanism:**

> Find gaps in your technical documentation before you submit, not after. Automated consistency checks flag missing and conflicting items while there is still time to fix them.

> Lücken in der technischen Dokumentation finden, bevor Sie einreichen — nicht danach. Automatisierte Konsistenzprüfungen markieren fehlende und widersprüchliche Einträge, solange noch Zeit zur Korrektur bleibt.

Notes on the German: use `48 %` with a non-breaking space, comma decimal separator, and place the footnote adjacent to the claim, legibly — not in a collapsed panel. If the substantiation cites a published study, §6 HWG requires accurate quotation with author, date, and source.

## Before publishing

- Claims file exists with metric definition, method, n, date, and who measured — dated before the page goes live.
- "Error detection before submission" appears in the intended purpose / IFU.
- Whichever language version you publish is the one that gets judged; have the German reviewed as primary, not as a translation artifact.

## One thing to confirm

The brief says Class I software device, but the copy describes a technical-documentation/submission workflow tool — and submission-support software generally has no medical purpose, so it wouldn't be a device at all. Either the classification or the positioning is off. If the CE-marked device is something else and this page markets an adjacent non-device tool, keep the two clearly separated so the CE mark doesn't appear to cover the workflow tool.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Don't ship as written. Two hard blockers (unsubstantiated quantified comparison, denigration of the target reader), plus a scope question that needs answering before anything is finalized.

---

## Blocker 1 — "Half the rework of what most teams use today"

This is a quantified comparative claim against an unnamed but identifiable group. Three separate problems:

**Broken comparison.** Grammatically the sentence compares your rework to *what teams use*, not to the rework produced by what they use. The German translation will inherit this or paper over it with a guess. Reads as an unfinished comparative — the pattern reviewers and readers both flag first.

**Unverifiable baseline.** "Most teams" asserts market-share knowledge you'd have to defend. Under UWG §5 (irreführende Werbung) and, if a competitor group is identifiable, §6 (vergleichende Werbung — comparison must be objective, relevant, verifiable, typical), a percentage claim needs a stated baseline, methodology, sample size and period. "50% less" with nothing behind it is the textbook Abmahnung target in German B2B, and regulatory consultants are exactly the audience that will ask for the n.

**Burden of proof.** If the software has a medical purpose, HWG §3 applies and the advertiser carries the evidentiary burden for performance claims. You'd need the study in hand before publication, not after a challenge.

## Blocker 2 — "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd"

You are describing your own prospects. Most German regulatory affairs teams at Class I manufacturers genuinely do run submissions on Excel and Outlook, often for defensible reasons. The line tells the reader they're the punchline.

Separately, if the phrase is read as pointing at competitor products/methods, disparagement of that kind is what UWG §6(2) No. 5 prohibits (Herabsetzung). And "crowd" has no clean German equivalent — the likely renderings ("Fraktion", "die Excel-Truppe") land more contemptuous, not less. German professional register here wants *sachlich*; swagger reads as unseriös in a compliance context.

Note also: "Excel" is a Microsoft trademark. Use *Tabellenkalkulation* generically.

## Blocker 3 — scope mismatch, needs your answer

You've called this a Class I software device, but the copy sells regulatory-submission efficiency — that's an eQMS/RA-ops benefit, not a medical purpose. Which is true?

- **If it is a medical device:** MDR Art. 7 governs all of this copy. Claims may not attribute functions the device does not have, and everything here must sit inside the declared intended purpose in your technical documentation and IFU. "We catch them before" is a performance claim that needs to map to a documented function.
- **If it is not a medical device** (a tool manufacturers use, not a device in itself): drop "Class I software device" from the positioning entirely — implying regulatory status you don't hold is its own misleading-advertising problem. UWG alone governs; HWG and MDR Art. 7 don't apply.

I've written the rewrites to be safe under either answer, but the final copy should be checked against whichever applies.

---

## Rewrite

**English**

> Teams that track submissions across spreadsheets and email threads often discover errors only after filing. [Product] flags them during preparation.
> Across [n] submissions between [start] and [end], customers reported [X]% less post-submission rework. [Link to methodology.]

**German**

> Wer Einreichungen über Tabellen und E-Mail-Verläufe verfolgt, bemerkt Fehler häufig erst nach dem Versand. [Produkt] erkennt sie bereits in der Vorbereitung.
> In [n] Einreichungen im Zeitraum [Datum] bis [Datum] berichteten Kunden von [X] % weniger Nacharbeit nach der Einreichung. [Link zur Methodik.]

What changed: the comparison is to a *working method* you can describe accurately, not to an unnamed competitor field you'd have to prove; the number carries its baseline and source; the reader is described, not mocked.

## One structural recommendation for the comparison block

Label the opposing column by **method** ("Tabellen und E-Mail") rather than by competitor or by "most teams." A method comparison (Systemvergleich) is far easier to substantiate factually, and it sidesteps the §6 objectivity tests that attach once a competitor becomes identifiable. You still owe accuracy under §5 — every row has to be true of that method as commonly practiced, not of a strawman version of it.

## If you can't produce the data

Cut the percentage rather than softening it. "Bis zu 50 %" and "deutlich weniger" are *more* exposed in Germany, not less — hedged quantities still require substantiation, and "bis zu" invites the argument that the typical case is far lower. A specific, defensible mechanism claim ("Prüfungen laufen vor dem Versand, nicht danach") outperforms an indefensible number with this audience anyway.

That part I can do, so here it is.

---

# Device Claims Review: "Heals wounds 40% faster."

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Class IIa wound dressing
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Ambiguous — not stated. Findings below mark which items are audience-dependent.
**Markets:** DE (EU rules apply throughout)

## Summary

1 claim reviewed, carrying three distinct assertions. 0 OK, 1 needs rewrite.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

The headline point: two of the defects here are structural, not evidentiary. You are likely to go and try to shore up the n=12 study. That won't fix the copy.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Heals wounds 40% faster."

**Breach 1:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** § 5(2) no. 1 expressly reaches "die Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**" and "**von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse**". The copy states a test result (40%) while omitting every essential component of the test that produced it: the comparator, the wound type, the endpoint measured, and the sample size. A reader cannot know what the figure is 40% faster *than*.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — this is not cured by evidence. It is cured by stating the basis in the copy.
**Call:** Needs rewording

**Breach 2:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 `[verified]` — engaged once § 6(1) is met
**Why:** "40% faster" is a comparison with no comparator. If anything in the surrounding asset makes a competitor or competing product *erkennbar* — a named product, "vs. conventional hydrocolloid dressings," or a market position obvious enough that readers know who is meant — § 6 applies, and the comparison fails no. 2 twice over. First, an undefined comparator is not **nachprüfbar**. Second, and independently: your only support is an **unpublished** in-house study. *Nachprüfbar* is about what the reader can check from public information. Unpublished data is structurally unverifiable no matter how methodologically sound it is.
**Evidence needed:** n/a as an evidence question. Name the comparator and publish the study, or drop the comparison. Improving the study while it stays unpublished does not move this.
**Call:** Needs rewording

**Breach 3 (conditional on the intended purpose):** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`, HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** "**Heals** wounds" ascribes active therapeutic healing to the dressing. Class IIa wound dressings are commonly assessed for a supporting function — covering, protecting, exudate management, maintaining a moist wound environment — rather than for healing as the device's own therapeutic action. If that is your assessed intended purpose, the verb creates a "false impression regarding treatment" under Art. 7(b) and attributes "therapeutische Wirksamkeit ... die sie nicht haben" under HWG § 3 no. 1. I cannot call this without your intended purpose, but it is the highest-value item on this list to check, because it also determines whether limb (d) bites.
**Evidence needed:** The intended purpose as it appears in the technical documentation / DoC.
**Call:** Verify — then almost certainly reword

**Also engaged:**
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** `[verified]` — guaranteed success. The claim is in the flat unconditional indicative, applied to "wounds" generically: no "kann", no "bis zu", no patient- or wound-type variation. That is the shape that raises the "Erfolg mit Sicherheit" question. Where exactly the line falls is case-law-driven and I don't assess it, but the unqualified phrasing is the avoidable part.
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** `[verified]` — audience-dependent, and I'm raising it as an open question rather than a finding. If the audience is Publikum, health-improvement-by-use framing is in scope. But stating a device's own indicated function is not automatically no. 7 — read that broadly it would prohibit all device advertising. Where the boundary sits is case law this review does not cover.
- **MDR Art. 7(c)** `[verified]` — the copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether your IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. Worth checking against the IFU; I won't infer one from the product category.
