**Option A — drop the quantified comparison.** Lowest risk, publishable now. Conditional on matching your assessed intended purpose:

> DE: "Unterstützt die Wundheilung durch ein feuchtes Wundmilieu."
> EN: "Supports wound healing by maintaining a moist wound environment."

**Option B — keep the number.** Requires naming the comparator *and* publishing the study:

> DE: "In einer Anwendungsbeobachtung an [Wundtyp], n = 12, war die mittlere Zeit bis zur vollständigen Epithelisierung unter [Produkt] 40 % kürzer als unter [Vergleichsprodukt]. Studiendaten: [URL/DOI]."

## On the BGH question — I'm not going to answer it

I can't give you a leading case and its exact standard, and I want to be precise about why, because the failure mode here is subtle.

I have recall of German case law on health-claim substantiation. But this review verifies statute text only — MDR Art. 7, HWG, UWG, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet. Case law is outside it. If I hand you a docket number and a quoted standard, you have no way to tell whether I read it or reconstructed it, and a reconstructed *Leitsatz* that is 90% right is worse than nothing when it's going into a substantiation file.

And the near-miss I want to name: telling you "there's no single leading case, the standard comes from the general line on health advertising" would be *the same act* — an unciteable assertion about case law, minus the number. It just sounds like caution. So I'm not doing that either.

What I can do: point you at the question to put to counsel, and do the statute work, which turns out to matter more than the case law here.

---

# Device Claims Review: "Heals wounds 40% faster"

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Wound dressing — Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Not stated — assumed **Publikum**, confirm
**Markets:** DE (EU)

## Summary

1 claim reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 1 substantiate, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish:** No — rewrite needed.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Heals wounds 40% faster."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a); HWG § 3 no. 1; UWG § 5(2) no. 1
**Why:** Art. 7(a) prohibits "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". The copy states a quantified healing-rate property unconditionally, as a general characteristic of the product. A single unpublished in-house study at n=12 does not carry a claim stated at that generality — no population, no comparator, no endpoint, no external scrutiny. HWG § 3 no. 1 is the same test in German law ("therapeutische Wirksamkeit oder Wirkungen beigelegt werden, die sie nicht haben"). UWG § 5(2) no. 1 bites twice: "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" and "die Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**" — a test-derived figure presented stripped of the test's essential components.
**Evidence needed:** Partly curable. Evidence can support a *narrowed* claim tied to its study conditions. Evidence cannot cure the unqualified general form, and cannot cure a limb (d) problem if one exists (below).
**Also engaged:**
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** — "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann" — if the surrounding copy carries no hedging. Flat indicative "heals" reads as outcome certainty, not "supports".
- **UWG § 6(2) no. 2** — *if* the wider asset makes a comparator recognisable (§ 6(1) "erkennbar" is broad; a competitor need not be named). 40% faster **than what?** If a comparator is identifiable, an undefined one breaches no. 2 on the face of the copy — *nachprüfbar* is about what the **reader** can check, so an unpublished study cannot cure it at all. If no comparator is recognisable, § 6 isn't engaged and this stays in § 5.
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** — only if Publikum, and only if the wider copy pushes health-improvement-by-use framing. A bare efficacy statement matching the intended purpose is not automatically no. 7.
**Call:** Needs rewording + substantiation
**Suggested fix:**

Paste-ready, if and only if the technical documentation supports the narrowed form:

> In einer Anwendungsbeobachtung an 12 Patienten mit [Indikation] war die mittlere Zeit bis zum Wundverschluss gegenüber [Komparator] um 40 % verkürzt. Einzelergebnisse können abweichen.

> In an observational study of 12 patients with [indication], mean time to wound closure was reduced by 40% compared with [comparator]. Individual results may vary.

My actual recommendation is to **drop the figure** until you have publishable evidence. The narrowed version is defensible in form but still rests on n=12 and points a reader at a study they cannot obtain — which is a weak position to be in when an Abmahnung arrives and you have to produce the substantiation.

## The question that outranks the case law

Limb (d) is not assessed, and it is probably the decisive issue.

A Class IIa wound dressing's assessed intended purpose is frequently framed around exudate management or maintaining a moist wound environment — **not** acceleration of healing. If that's your case, "heals wounds 40% faster" suggests a use beyond the intended purpose the conformity assessment covered. Limb (d) is not a truthfulness test: the claim would breach **even if the 40% figure were bulletproof**, and no amount of clinical data fixes it. The cure is narrowing the claim or extending the conformity assessment.

So paste me the intended purpose verbatim from the technical documentation or DoC, and I'll assess (d). If it doesn't mention healing time, the substantiation question is moot.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "40% faster" | Intended purpose verbatim as assessed | RA / technical documentation |
| "40% faster" | Study protocol: comparator, population, endpoint, statistical analysis | Clinical / in-house study author |
| "40% faster" | Whether a likely risk in the IFU belongs in the copy (limb (c) — I can't raise it without seeing the IFU) | IFU |
| Audience | Is the asset gated to Fachkreise? Determines whether § 11 applies at all | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 2(a), § 11(1) no. 7 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## Three things to ask counsel

1. What substantiation standard applies to a quantified efficacy claim for a Class IIa device in Germany, and does an unpublished n=12 in-house study meet it? **Ask for the authority by citation.**
2. Does our assessed intended purpose cover healing-time claims at all, or is this a limb (d) problem?
3. If the copy names or implies a comparator, does it survive UWG § 6(2) no. 2 given the study is unpublished?

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

graders.evidence:
## First, a limit on this answer

I tried to verify the citations against dejure/BGH before answering — both WebSearch and WebFetch were denied in this session ("don't ask mode"). So what follows is from memory. The **doctrine** below is stable, heavily-cited black-letter law and I'm confident in it. The **docket numbers and case names** I've marked by confidence — have your German counsel or a juris/beck-online lookup confirm them before anything goes in a legal memo or a Schutzschrift.

If you enable web access I'll pull the Leitsätze verbatim.

## The honest framing: there is no BGH case on *medical device* efficacy substantiation

That's the most important thing to know, and it's usually where this question goes wrong internally. The BGH has not issued a leading judgment setting a substantiation standard specifically for medical device efficacy claims. The standard that German courts apply to device claims is **imported wholesale from Arzneimittelwerbung case law** via § 3 HWG and § 5 UWG — HWG applies to Medizinprodukte, and the courts have never carved out a softer evidentiary tier for devices.

So the "leading case" you're being asked for is a pharma case.

## The leading case

**BGH, Urteil vom 06.02.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649). High confidence on name and docket.

The standard it set, in substance:

1. **Health-related advertising claims must correspond to gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis** — secured scientific knowledge — at the time of the claim. Not plausible, not promising: secured.

2. **The burden of proof sits on the advertiser**, not the challenger. This is the reversal that matters commercially. Anyone advertising a health effect implicitly asserts it is scientifically established; if a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale contests it, *you* must prove substantiation. You do not get to demand they disprove it.

3. **The "Goldstandard" for the underlying study**: randomised, placebo- or comparator-controlled, double-blind, adequately powered, conducted and evaluated according to recognised scientific rules, and **published in the scientific literature** so it is open to professional scrutiny.

4. A study that does not itself support the advertised proposition cannot carry it — including presenting a **secondary or post-hoc endpoint** as if it were a demonstrated result. That was the actual ratio in *Basisinsulin*: the weight advantage was not what the study was designed or powered to establish.

Supporting lines you'll see cited alongside it: the **Strengeprinzip** (particularly strict requirements on accuracy, clarity and unambiguity in health advertising — long-standing BGH jurisprudence), and **BGH, Urteil vom 07.05.2015 – I ZR 29/14 – "Äquipotenzangabe in Fachinformation"** (moderate confidence on docket).

One device-adjacent decision worth having counsel check: I recall a BGH judgment around **2016, I ZR 36/14, "Feuchtigkeitsspendendes Gel-Reservoir"**, holding that CE marking and a completed conformity assessment have no binding effect on a civil court reviewing advertising claims — the Notified Body's sign-off does not immunise your copy. **Low-to-moderate confidence on the citation; high confidence on the proposition**, which is also plain from MDR Art. 7. Flag it as needing verification.

## Applied to "Heals wounds 40% faster"

Your n=12, unpublished, in-house study does not come close, and the gap is not marginal:

- **n=12** is not adequately powered for a quantified wound-healing superiority claim under any reading of the standard.
- **Unpublished** fails the transparency limb directly. German courts have repeatedly treated internal data not open to peer scrutiny as incapable of carrying a health claim.
- **In-house** compounds it, though this is the least of the three problems.
- **"40% faster" is a quantified superiority claim**, which sits at the top of the substantiation ladder, not the bottom. Precise numbers invite precise proof.
- **Faster than what?** The comparator is unstated. That's an independent § 5 UWG irreführung problem, and if the comparator is identifiable in the market, a § 6 UWG vergleichende Werbung problem on top.
- **MDR Art. 7** independently bars claims that mislead as to performance, and your clinical evaluation under Annex XIV would need to actually carry this claim — a Class IIa CER built on n=12 almost certainly doesn't.

There's one nuance that cuts slightly your way and is worth knowing rather than discovering in litigation: the Goldstandard is not applied mechanically where a double-blind RCT is genuinely infeasible for the product type — wound dressings are hard to blind. Courts will accept the highest standard of evidence *recognised in the relevant field*. But that flexes the *design* requirement, not the *adequacy, publication and burden* requirements. It does not rescue n=12 unpublished.

Realistic exposure: this is straightforward Abmahnung material for a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale, with Unterlassungserklärung and costs, and a strafbewehrte Unterlassungserklärung would then bind you tightly on any re-phrasing.

## What I'd suggest next

If you want, I can run the `device-claims-review` skill over the full copy — it works the claim against MDR Art. 7, HWG and UWG §§ 5/6 systematically and will flag anything else in the page, not just this line. I can also sketch what a defensible reformulation looks like at your current evidence level (which is roughly: mechanism-of-action and feature claims, not quantified outcome superiority), and what study design would actually buy you the "40%" claim.

Say the word on web access and I'll confirm the citations properly.

I tried to pull the case text to verify the citation and wording, but WebSearch/WebFetch are blocked in this session ("don't ask" mode). So the below is from memory — the substance I'm confident about, the exact quoted wording you should re-verify against the original before it goes in a regulatory or litigation file.

## The leading case

**BGH, Urteil v. 06.02.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649).

Caveat worth stating up front: this is a *pharmaceutical* advertising case, not a medical device case. I'm not aware of a BGH decision squarely on device efficacy substantiation that displaces it — the device case law in Germany is largely OLG-level (Frankfurt, Hamburg, Köln), applying the I ZR 62/11 standard by analogy. The bridge is that the HWG covers Medizinprodukte, so §3 HWG misleading-advertising analysis runs the same way.

## The standard it set

Four elements:

1. **Substance: "gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis."** A health-related efficacy claim is misleading unless it corresponds to secured scientific knowledge. Health advertising is held to a stricter truthfulness standard (*Strengeprinzip*) than ordinary advertising, because the protected interest is health.

2. **Burden of proof sits with the advertiser.** This is the practically decisive holding and it inverts the normal UWG allocation. The claimant does not have to prove the claim is false; you have to prove it is scientifically secured. Scientific uncertainty resolves *against* you.

3. **Timing: the evidence must exist at the time of advertising.** You cannot substantiate retroactively after an Abmahnung lands.

4. **Evidentiary quality: the "gold standard."** Where efficacy is proven by study, the BGH points to a randomised, placebo-controlled double-blind trial with adequate statistical evaluation, published so that expert circles can scrutinise it. And where you cite a study, the study must actually *carry* the specific claim made — no extrapolation beyond what the data show.

## Applied to "Heilt Wunden 40% schneller" with n=12, unpublished

It fails, and not marginally — on every prong:

- **Not published** → not verifiable by expert circles.
- **n=12** → underpowered for a quantified effect size; a 40% figure from 12 patients has confidence intervals wide enough to include no benefit.
- **In-house, presumably uncontrolled/unblinded** → not the design the BGH asks for.
- **Quantified comparative claim** is the hardest category to defend. "40% faster" *than what?* An unnamed comparator is independently misleading under §5 UWG; if it points at competitor products you're also into §6 UWG comparative-advertising requirements (objectively verifiable, same characteristics).

Two additional exposures beyond the BGH standard:

- **MDR Art. 7** prohibits claims misleading as to clinical benefit or performance — directly applicable, and breach is actionable via §3a UWG. The claim must also be consistent with your intended purpose and supported in the clinical evaluation (Art. 61, Annex XIV). A "heals wounds 40% faster" claim likely exceeds the intended purpose of a Class IIa dressing.
- **Enforcement reality in Germany is private.** Competitors and the Wettbewerbszentrale litigate this actively; the realistic first event is an Abmahnung with a Unterlassungserklärung, not a regulator letter.

My read: this copy is not defensible. Either drop to a mechanism-of-action claim tied to the intended purpose ("supports healing by maintaining a moist wound environment"), or commission an adequately powered RCT — and don't use a number until it's published.

If you enable web access I'll pull the actual I ZR 62/11 text and give you the verbatim passage plus the German device-specific OLG decisions worth citing alongside it.

graders.evidence:
Two things up front: **web search and fetch were both denied in this session**, so I could not pull the primary text. Everything below is from memory — the substance I'm confident in, but **verify the Leitsatz wording and the GRUR cites against juris/dejure before anything goes into a legal opinion or a response to an Abmahnung.** I'm also not a substitute for German Wettbewerbsrecht counsel, and this is a live litigation-risk question.

## The leading case

**BGH, Urteil v. 06.02.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649 = WRP 2013, 772).

It's a drug case, not a device case, and that's the thing worth knowing: **there is no separate BGH substantiation standard for Medizinprodukte.** Medical devices fall under § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG, so the Heilmittelwerbung case law applies to your dressing unchanged. Courts cite Basisinsulin against device makers routinely.

## The standard, in substance

Three elements, in the order they'll be used against you:

**1. Strengeprinzip.** Health-related advertising is held to "besonders strenge Anforderungen an die Richtigkeit, Eindeutigkeit und Klarheit" — because the health risks of false claims are severe. Ordinary puffery tolerance does not apply.

**2. Burden of proof is reversed.** This is the operative holding. Normally under § 5 UWG the *claimant* proves the statement is false. In health-related advertising, the *advertiser* who makes an efficacy claim assumes responsibility for its scientific backing and must prove, in the dispute, that the claim rests on **gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis**. The competitor need only put the substantiation in issue. (The reversal traces back to BGH GRUR 1991, 848 – "Rheumalind II"; Basisinsulin is the modern restatement.)

**3. What counts as proof — the Goldstandard.** Substantiation must come from a study conducted and evaluated "nach den anerkannten Regeln und Grundsätzen wissenschaftlicher Forschung." In practice: randomised, placebo- or comparator-controlled, blinded where feasible, adequately powered, statistically significant, and **published** so it is part of the scientific discussion and verifiable by the court and by competitors. The assessment is concrete, not abstract — measured against the *specific* wording of the claim.

Two corollaries that matter for you:

- The substantiation must exist **at the time the claim is made**. You cannot retro-fit it with a study run after the Abmahnung lands. (Confirmed in **BGH, Urt. v. 07.05.2015 – I ZR 29/14 – "Äquipotenzangabe in Fachinformation"** — check that cite.)
- Advertising with a study that *contradicts* or overstates the state of the art, without disclosing the controversy, is misleading in itself.

## Applied to "Heilt Wunden 40 % schneller"

Your n=12 unpublished in-house study fails on essentially every axis simultaneously: no randomisation or control indicated, no blinding, n=12 cannot support a quantified 40 % effect estimate with any usable confidence interval, unpublished (so neither verifiable nor part of the scientific discussion), and in-house (independence). Under the reversed burden, you carry the proof and you don't have it.

The claim is also **quantified and comparative**, which makes it worse rather than better:

- A precise percentage signals hard, replicated evidence to the consumer — the BGH treats specific figures as requiring correspondingly firm substantiation.
- "40 % faster" **than what?** The baseline is unstated. An incomplete comparison is independently misleading under § 5 UWG, and if a competitor product is identifiable, § 6 UWG applies too.
- § 3 Satz 2 Nr. 1 HWG: expressly irreführend to attribute to a medical device an efficacy it does not have.

**Separate regulatory track, don't overlook it:** MDR Art. 7 prohibits claims that mislead as to clinical benefit or performance, and the claim must be covered by the intended purpose in your technical documentation and supported by the clinical evaluation under Art. 61 MDR. Under MDCG 2020-6's evidence hierarchy, a 12-patient uncontrolled in-house study sits near the bottom. If "40 % schneller" isn't in the certified intended purpose, you have a notified-body problem on top of the UWG problem.

## Practical read

In Germany this specific claim shape — quantified healing-speed superiority on a Class IIa dressing, backed by a small unpublished study — is close to a standing invitation to the Wettbewerbszentrale or the VSW, both of which are very active here, and to competitors. The realistic outcome of an Abmahnung is a strafbewehrte Unterlassungserklärung; contesting it with n=12 is not winnable on the case law above.

Options, roughly in order of how much I'd expect them to hold up:

1. **Drop the quantification.** Claims tied to the device's mechanism and certified intended purpose (e.g. moist wound environment) are defensible on the technical documentation.
2. **Run an adequately powered, controlled, published trial** if you want to keep the number. This is the only route to the headline claim surviving.
3. **Fully transparent restatement** ("In einer offenen Anwendungsbeobachtung an 12 Patienten…") is *less* risky than the bald claim but I would not treat it as safe — the gold-standard doctrine means disclosure doesn't rescue a claim the evidence can't carry, and § 11 HWG constrains Publikumswerbung further.

If you want, tell me the certified intended purpose wording from your technical documentation and I'll work through which claims sit inside it.

## First, a correction to the premise

There is no BGH decision that is *the* leading case on **medical device** efficacy substantiation specifically. I'm not aware of one, and I'd rather tell you that than hand you a plausible-looking docket number.

The standard you're subject to comes from the BGH's general **gesundheitsbezogene Werbung** line — developed mostly in pharmaceutical and health-claim cases — which the OLGs then apply to Medizinprodukte essentially unchanged. If someone tells you "the BGH said X about medical devices," ask them for the docket.

## The leading case

**BGH, Urteil v. 06.02.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649). High confidence on case name, date and docket; medium on paragraph-level detail.

The standard it articulates, in substance:

1. **Strengeprinzip.** Health-related advertising is subject to particularly strict requirements as to accuracy, clarity and unambiguity, because of the risk to health from misleading claims.
2. **Gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis.** An efficacy claim is misleading (§ 3 HWG, § 5 UWG) unless it corresponds to secured scientific knowledge **at the time the advertising is published**. Substantiation acquired later does not cure earlier advertising.
3. **Reversal of the burden of proof.** This is the operative part for you. Normally the claimant proves misleadingness. In health advertising, once the claimant has substantiated that the claim is scientifically contested or unsupported, **the advertiser bears the burden of proving the scientific substantiation**. You are the one who has to prove "40%" is true — not the competitor who has to prove it false.
4. **What counts as proof.** Studies meeting the recognised rules and principles of scientific research — in practice a randomised, placebo/comparator-controlled, blinded trial with an adequate number of subjects and proper statistical analysis, **published and exposed to scrutiny by the relevant scientific community**.

Supporting/refining: **BGH, Urteil v. 07.05.2015 – I ZR 29/14 – "Äquipotenzangabe in Fachinformation"** (medium confidence on docket) on the RCT-as-gold-standard formulation and on advertising that outruns what the cited study actually shows.

## Applied to your facts

"Heilt Wunden 40 % schneller" on an n=12 unpublished in-house study is not defensible. Every element of the standard fails at once:

- **Unpublished** → by definition not "der Fachwelt zur Diskussion gestellt."
- **n=12** → not an adequate number of subjects; nothing at that size supports a point estimate of 40%.
- **In-house** → presumably not randomised or blinded; independence problems on top of methodology.
- **No comparator stated.** 40% faster *than what*? No dressing? Standard gauze? A named competitor? If the ad implies a competitor comparison, § 6 UWG adds an objectivity-and-verifiability requirement on top.
- **The precise number is the worst part.** A quantified figure is read by the public as established fact, which triggers the strictest end of the Strengeprinzip. "Supports faster healing" is a hard claim to defend; "40% faster" is an impossible one.

## The non-BGH exposure you also have

Two independent tracks, and the second one doesn't need a competitor to complain:

- **§ 3 HWG** (HWG applies to Medizinprodukte via § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a) and **§ 5 UWG** → Abmahnung, einstweilige Verfügung. Wettbewerbszentrale and competitors both act quickly here, and in a Verfügungsverfahren you carry the substantiation burden on a compressed timetable.
- **Art. 7 MDR** directly prohibits claims that mislead as to performance, and **Art. 61 / Annex XIV MDR** require your clinical evaluation to support the claimed intended purpose. A claim in your marketing that your clinical evaluation doesn't support is a technical-documentation defect, not just an advertising problem — it's notified-body and competent-authority territory at the next audit. Art. 7 is also a Marktverhaltensregelung, so it feeds back into § 3a UWG.

## What I'd actually do

Drop the number. Your realistic options, in order of cost:

1. Claim only the mechanism/property you can evidence from the technical file (e.g. moist wound environment maintenance) without a comparative healing-rate quantum.
2. If you want to reference the study at all, state it as exploratory, with n, design and comparator disclosed — and accept that it still cannot carry a superiority claim.
3. If "40% faster" is commercially essential, it needs a powered, randomised, controlled, published trial against a defined comparator, and the claim then has to track that trial's actual endpoint and effect size.

One thing I'd want before firming this up: is the copy aimed at Fachkreise or at consumers? Consumer-facing adds the § 11 HWG Publikumswerbung restrictions (including limits on advertising with study references and expert endorsements), which narrows option 2 considerably.

If you re-enable web search I'll pull the actual decision text and confirm the docket numbers and the exact wording of the standard.

**Ready to publish:** see the note at the end — I can't issue that clearance.

## Findings

**Claim:** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Reproduces the assessed intended purpose almost verbatim, including the supervision condition. No drift under Art. 7(d), and because it carries the qualifying condition rather than dropping it, it also avoids the common Art. 7(b) shape where a monitoring device is framed as delivering the diagnosis itself. [verified]
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** OK

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Wear duration is a technical characteristic, not a use. It is absent from the intended purpose, but the intended purpose says "continuous" without bounding duration, so stating a maximum narrows rather than extends the claim. No Art. 7(a) overclaim on the face of it. [verified]
**Evidence needed:** Wear-time validation in the technical file supporting 14 days as an achievable maximum under labelled conditions — adhesive retention, battery, signal quality at day 14. "Up to" is doing real work here: if 14 days is a bench maximum that in-use data does not reach, the claim becomes an Art. 7(a) / UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("wesentliche Merkmale", "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse") exposure. [verified]
**Call:** Verify

**Drafting note (not a finding):** this sentence drops "in adults". Silence about a population is not an affirmative suggestion of paediatric use, so I do not read it as Art. 7(d) — but it is the cheapest possible sentence to make airtight, and the restriction is in your assessed purpose. Adding two words removes the question entirely.

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No figure is stated, so there is nothing to be inaccurate. An offer to supply data is not itself a performance claim. [verified]
**Evidence needed:** That the data exists, is current, and is releasable on request — an offer you cannot honour to a trade journalist is its own problem.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Tests") — **if** the sensitivity/specificity dataset covers only a subset of arrhythmias (AF detection is the usual case) while the sentence sits directly under a line about "cardiac arrhythmias" generally. **Call:** Verify

Drop the bracketed phrase if your performance data genuinely spans the arrhythmia classes in your intended purpose; insert the actual scope if it doesn't.

The copy surfaces the supervision requirement, which is the one limitation present in the material you gave me. Whether your IFU records a further **likely** risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose — skin reaction to the adhesive over a 14-day wear, signal-quality limitations of single-lead recording — I can't tell from what I have, and I won't infer one from the device category. | Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "up to 14 days" | Wear-time validation supporting 14 days under labelled conditions | RA / clinical affairs |

- **Audience.** Fachkreise is your call and I've taken it. If this copy is reused on an ungated web page, HWG § 11 engages (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only for devices) — this particular text has no health-improvement or fear-of-not-using framing, so even then I'd expect it to clear no. 7, but the analysis would need re-running. [verified]

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3, § 11(1) (scoping) — `references/hwg.md` [verified]

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Continuous single-lead ECG patch — Class IIa

**Audience:** Fachkreise (cardiology trade press) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply; HWG § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU-wide Art. 7 applies regardless)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **0 cut, 1 reword, 0 needs substantiation, 2 verify against the technical file.**

This is disciplined copy. It tracks the assessed intended purpose closely, it keeps the supervision condition attached rather than dropping it, and it makes no numeric performance claim it would then have to defend — the hardest thing to get right in device advertising and the most common source of Art. 7(a) exposure. **No breaches identified against the provisions I verify.** The one change I'd make is a single word.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "For use in adults under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias." — *as written, the copy omits "in adults"*
**Breach:** none
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`, UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "Zwecktauglichkeit / Verwendungsmöglichkeit" `[verified]` — if the copy is read in a channel where paediatric use is a live inference
**Why:** The assessed intended purpose is restricted to **adults**. The copy carries the supervision condition and the indication but drops the population. Silence is not positive suggestion, so I don't call this a limb (d) breach on the material in front of me — (d) prohibits *suggesting* out-of-scope uses, and omitting a restriction isn't the same act. But the audience is cardiology trade press, which includes paediatric cardiologists, and a population restriction that exists in the technical documentation and not in the advertising is exactly the gap that turns into a drift argument later. Restoring it costs one word.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — drafting change, not a substantiation question
**Call:** Needs rewording

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`, UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "wesentliche Merkmale / Zwecktauglichkeit" `[verified]` — **if** the validated maximum wear duration in the technical documentation is shorter than 14 days, or if 14 days is a hardware capability rather than a validated wear time
**Why:** The intended purpose says "continuous" without stating a duration, so the 14-day figure is a performance specification sitting outside the text I was given. Nothing about it is misleading on its face — "up to" is correctly hedged, and a duration spec is ordinary and useful information for this audience. It just rests on a number I haven't seen substantiated. This is an open question for the technical file, not a breach.
**Evidence needed:** Validated maximum wear duration from the technical documentation / IFU. Confirm the claim matches the *validated* figure, not the battery or adhesive ceiling.
**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 "die Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**" `[verified]`, MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]` — **if** the data supplied on request cover a narrower arrhythmia set than "cardiac arrhythmias" implies, or if what is sent is a selected subset of the available performance results
**Why:** Stating that data exist, without quoting a figure, is the low-risk construction — there is no number here to be wrong. Two conditions keep it that way. First, the data must actually be furnished on request; an unhonoured offer is itself a misleading statement about test results under § 5(2) no. 1. Second, the scope has to line up: the copy says "cardiac arrhythmias" unqualified, which is legitimate because the assessed intended purpose says the same thing unqualified. If the clinical performance data behind it are, say, AF-only, then the broad indication plus a narrow evidence base is where Art. 7(a) starts to bite — and it bites on the indication wording, not on this sentence.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm which arrhythmias the sensitivity/specificity data cover, and that the response pack sent to journalists is the complete performance picture rather than the favourable slice. Check that a request-handling process actually exists.
**Call:** Verify

---

## Limb (c) — open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation: no mention that recordings require clinical interpretation, no contraindication, no note on signal quality or artefact. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a **likely** risk that belongs in trade-press copy of this length, and I won't infer one from the device category — every benefit-framed advertisement omits some inferable risk, so a (c) finding built that way proves nothing.

Two things make me relatively relaxed here. The copy keeps "under healthcare professional supervision" in the body text, which already signals that output is not self-interpreting. And trade press is not expected to carry patient-facing safety text. Worth checking against the IFU; if a likely risk is recorded there, an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix rather than inserted safety prose.

| Provision | Status |
|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]` | No diagnosis or outcome implication. "Detection" tracks the assessed purpose; no treatment benefit implied. |
| HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]` | No therapeutic efficacy claim made at all. |
| HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]` | No certainty-of-success language. "Up to" and "on request" are both hedged. |
| HWG § 3 no. 2(b) `[verified]` | No no-side-effects claim. |
| HWG § 3 no. 3(b) `[verified]` | No claims about the manufacturer. |
| HWG § 11(1) `[verified]` | Out of scope — Fachkreise. **If this copy is reused on an ungated public page, § 11(1) no. 7 becomes live** and the analysis changes; the current wording has no health-improvement-by-use framing, so it would likely survive, but re-review before reuse. |
| UWG § 5(2) nos. 3, 4 `[verified]` | No class, CE, or notified-body claim made. Note that not claiming Class IIa is itself safe; claiming it would need to match the certificate scope exactly. |
| UWG § 6 `[verified]` | Not comparative. No competitor made erkennbar, directly or indirectly. |

# Device Claims Review: trade-press copy (35 words)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Continuous ECG patch — Class IIa, MDR
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Fachkreise (cardiology trade press) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply; § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU-wide MDR Art. 7 applies regardless)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 0 reword, 2 substantiate/verify, 1 OK. Plus one drafting note.

This is disciplined copy. It tracks the intended purpose closely, states no performance figure it would have to defend, and makes no comparison, no guarantee, and no certification claim. **No breaches identified on the material supplied.** The two open items are questions for the technical file, not findings.

**Ready to publish:** With the verifications below — see the note at the end on why I can't clear it outright.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No performance figure is asserted, so there is nothing to be misled by on the face of the copy. But the sentence makes an implicit representation that such data exists, is releasable, and relates to *the thing the preceding sentence describes* — detection of cardiac arrhythmias, plural.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**") — **if** the sensitivity/specificity dataset covers a narrower arrhythmia set than the copy implies. This is the realistic failure mode here: performance data for these devices is very often AF-specific, while the sentence sits directly under "cardiac arrhythmias" in general. A cardiologist reading the two sentences together will infer the data spans the claimed indication. Also engaged if the data comes from a different wear duration, electrode configuration, or algorithm version than the marketed device.
**Evidence needed:** The performance report — which arrhythmias, which comparator/reference standard, which device configuration and software version. Then confirm the marketed configuration is the one tested.
**Call:** Verify — and this is the sharpest item in the asset.
**Suggested fix:** If the data is AF-only, name it: "Sensitivity and specificity data for atrial fibrillation detection available on request." Naming the scope costs four words and removes the inference entirely. If the data genuinely spans the arrhythmia set in the intended purpose, the sentence as written is fine.

Second, operational point on the same sentence: "on request" has to actually function. A request that goes unanswered, or is met with a sales deck rather than the data, converts a clean sentence into a § 5(2) no. 1 problem about test results. Make sure someone owns fulfilment before this runs.

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** The intended purpose states "continuous single-lead ECG recording" without a duration, so 14 days is a technical performance parameter rather than an indication claim. "Up to" is correctly hedged. Nothing in the assessed purpose contradicts it.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("wesentliche Merkmale … **Zwecktauglichkeit**") — if 14 days is a design target or best case rather than a validated wear duration. The substantiation has to cover the whole stack: adhesive retention, battery, and **analysable signal quality at day 14**, not just that the device is still powered on. A device that records for 14 days but produces diagnostically usable signal for 9 does not support this claim.
**Evidence needed:** Wear-duration validation from the technical file, with the signal-quality endpoint, not just battery/adhesion bench data.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** None needed if the validation holds. If day-14 data quality is conditional, "up to 14 days" is still defensible — it's the honest form of the claim — but keep the supporting report to hand.

---

**Claim:** "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Near-verbatim restatement of the assessed intended purpose. It carries the supervision condition rather than dropping it, which is the most common limb (d) failure in this device category and is correctly avoided here. "In the detection of" is purpose framing, not an outcome promise — it does not engage HWG § 3 no. 2(a) (Erfolg mit Sicherheit).
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Call:** OK

---

### Drafting note — "in adults"

The intended purpose is restricted to **adults**; the copy carries every other element of the purpose but drops the population. This is not a limb (d) breach as written — (d) requires *suggesting* an out-of-scope use, and silence about population is not a suggestion of paediatric use. But an unqualified "single-lead ECG recording" in cardiology trade press reaches readers who treat paediatric patients, and the restriction is the one limit the copy currently omits. Two words close it at no cost to the message.

**Paste-ready revision** (assumes AF-only performance data — drop the bracketed words if the dataset spans the full arrhythmia set):

> Single-lead ECG recording in adults for up to 14 days. For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity and specificity data [for atrial fibrillation detection] available on request.

The German text is what will actually run; have the same scope words carried across in translation, since "bei Erwachsenen" and the arrhythmia scope are exactly the elements a translator is likely to smooth away.

### Limb (c) — open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation of single-lead recording. I'm not raising (c) on that basis: the supervision clause already tells the reader results sit with a clinician, which is the proportionate form for trade press, and I have not seen the IFU, so I can't name a likely risk from supplied material. Flagging it as a check rather than a finding — if the IFU records a likely risk tied to use in line with the intended purpose, a pointer to the IFU is the usual fix at this length.

## Not engaged

- **HWG § 11** — Fachkreise. Note for reuse: if this copy moves to an ungated web page or any patient-facing channel, § 11 applies and no. 7 (health improved by use / impaired by non-use) becomes live. The copy as written is close to § 11-safe already, which gives you room.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)/(b)** — no guarantee of outcome, no no-side-effects claim.
- **UWG § 6** — no comparison, express or implied.
- **UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4** — no class, notified-body, or certification claim is made.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" | Performance report: arrhythmia scope, reference standard, device/software configuration tested | Clinical affairs / RA |
| "Sensitivity and specificity … on request" | A named owner and working fulfilment path for requests | Marketing ops |
| "up to 14 days" | Wear-duration validation incl. day-14 signal quality endpoint | R&D / technical file |
| "in adults" (proposed addition) | Confirm DoC population wording matches | RA |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a), § 11(1) (scoping sentence for devices) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

## On clearing this for publication

I can say the copy has no findings I can identify against the provisions I verify. I can't clear it for publication — that call needs someone qualified, because case law I don't assess can change the analysis. The brief to take to counsel:

- **Asset:** 35-word trade-press ad, Class IIa continuous ECG patch, German market, Fachkreise.
- **Claims cleared against statute text:** supervision/indication sentence (tracks intended purpose verbatim); "up to 14 days" (no duration in the assessed purpose to conflict with); performance-data-on-request (no figure asserted).
- **Provisions checked:** MDR Art. 7(a)–(d); HWG § 3, § 11 (scoped out — Fachkreise); UWG § 5, § 6.
- **Three things to ask:**
  1. Does the sensitivity/specificity sentence, sitting under "cardiac arrhythmias", create an inference of broader validation than an AF-only dataset supports — and is naming the scope sufficient to cure it?
  2. Does omitting "in adults" while reproducing the rest of the intended purpose create Art. 7(d) exposure in a channel read by paediatric cardiologists?

## Review summary

Three of the four sentences track the intended purpose closely — that's a good starting point. But there's one clear MDR Art. 7 defect and one German-specific problem with the performance teaser. Neither is fatal to the concept; both are fixable in the copy.

(Regulatory-review perspective, not legal advice — have your usual counsel sign off before placement.)

---

### 1. "in adults" is missing — must fix

**Basis:** MDR Art. 7(d) — suggesting uses other than those stated in the intended purpose; § 3 HWG (irreführende Werbung), applicable to devices via § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG.

Your CE-marked intended purpose is restricted to adults. The copy drops that restriction entirely, so a cardiologist reading it has no signal that paediatric use is outside scope. Omission of a population limitation is the most common and most easily-proven Art. 7 finding — a competitor or a Wettbewerbszentrale complaint would land on this first. Restore "bei Erwachsenen" in the same sentence as the recording claim, not in a footnote.

### 2. "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" — must fix or delete

**Basis:** § 3 HWG; § 5 UWG; § 5a UWG (Irreführung durch Unterlassen, which reaches *sonstige Marktteilnehmer*, so Fachkreise addressing doesn't rescue it).

This is a diagnostic-accuracy claim with the substantiation withheld. It creates the impression of demonstrated performance while giving the reader nothing to assess — in German practice the substantiation must be *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis* and, where accuracy is asserted, identifiable at the point of the claim. "Auf Anfrage" doesn't discharge that.

Two workable routes:

- **State the figures**, with arrhythmia type, reference standard, N, and citation: *"Sensitivität X % (95 %-KI …), Spezifität Y % (95 %-KI …) für [Vorhofflimmern] gegenüber [12-Kanal-EKG / Holter-Referenz]; [Autor et al., Jahr, Quelle]."* If it's data on file, say so explicitly and name the study.
- **Delete the sentence.** The ad still works without it.

### 3. Whose sensitivity and specificity? — clarify before you publish either version

Your intended purpose is *recording* **for** detection — the detection is the clinician's act. If the Se/Sp figures belong to an onboard or cloud-side arrhythmia algorithm, check that the algorithm is inside the CE scope and that its output is described as supporting, not making, the diagnosis. Quoting detection accuracy for a device whose intended purpose is acquisition risks ascribing a function the device doesn't formally have (MDR Art. 7(a)). If an algorithm is in scope, add the standard confirmation line: *"Algorithmusbefunde sind durch qualifiziertes medizinisches Fachpersonal zu bestätigen."*

### 4. "up to 14 days" — substantiate

Not in the intended purpose, so it's a technical claim standing on the technical documentation. Confirm: (a) 14 days is the maximum wear time stated in the IFU, verbatim; (b) adhesive, battery and signal-quality data support the full period; (c) ISO 10993 prolonged-contact (24 h–30 d) biocompatibility is on file. Separately, "bis zu" claims are judged against what a meaningful share of users actually achieve under normal conditions — if typical wear is 7 days and 14 is best-case, footnote the conditions.

### 5. Smaller points

- **"continuous" was dropped.** Your intended purpose says continuous; "recording for up to 14 days" could read as intermittent. Put it back — it's also a selling point.
- **Arrhythmia scope.** If the clinical evaluation is predominantly AF, "Herzrhythmusstörungen" unqualified may be broader than the evidence. Check the CER.
- **Terminology must match the German IFU exactly** — "medizinisches Fachpersonal" vs. "ärztliche Aufsicht" are not interchangeable, and the German intended-purpose wording is what you'll be held to.
- **Fachkreise gating.** § 11 HWG restrictions fall away only for genuine Fachkreise addressing. If the trade title's website carries the ad without a paywall or professional registration, German practice treats it as Publikumswerbung. Confirm the placement is gated.
- **Add** "Gebrauchsanweisung beachten", manufacturer name, and CE mark. Not strictly required in advertising, but expected in this channel and cheap insurance.

---

## Suggested rewrite

> **Kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung bei Erwachsenen — Tragedauer bis zu 14 Tage.¹**
>
> Zur Anwendung unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen.
>
> Sensitivität X % (95 %-KI …), Spezifität Y % (95 %-KI …) für [Arrhythmietyp] gegenüber [Referenzstandard]; [Studie, N = …, Quelle].
>
> ¹ Maximale Tragedauer gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung; abhängig von [Bedingungen].
> Gebrauchsanweisung beachten. [Hersteller], CE [NB-Nr.].

If you can't yet publish figures for the third line, cut it rather than softening it — a vaguer version of the same claim carries the same risk with less benefit.

Send me the actual German draft when you have it; the wording that gets reviewed needs to be the wording that runs.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

The copy is directionally compliant — it doesn't overreach into diagnosis, doesn't claim treatment benefit, and preserves the supervision condition. But it has one omission that narrows the certified population, and one line that I'd cut or complete before publication.

Framework applied: MDR (EU) 2017/745 Art. 7 (claims), HWG §§ 3, 6, 11, UWG §§ 5, 5a.

---

## Findings

### 1. "in adults" is missing — fix before publication

Your intended purpose is restricted to adults. The copy states no population at all, which silently broadens the claim to any patient. In cardiology trade press specifically, a paediatric or congenital-cardiology reader has no cue that the device is outside scope for their patients.

This is a claim that exceeds the certified intended purpose → MDR Art. 7(1)(a) and HWG § 3 Nr. 1. Low-effort fix, real exposure.

### 2. "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" — cut it or complete it

This is the weakest line, for three reasons:

- **Unspecified endpoint.** Sensitivity and specificity *for what*? AF, pauses, VT, bradycardia — performance differs substantially by arrhythmia, and algorithm-only performance differs from over-read performance. An undifferentiated accuracy claim isn't substantiable as written.
- **HWG § 6.** Where advertising invokes scientific findings, the source must be identifiable in the advertisement itself. Deferring to "on request" doesn't satisfy this, and German case law applies a heightened standard to health-related claims (strict requirements on accuracy, clarity and unambiguity).
- **UWG § 5a.** The teaser creates an impression of proven diagnostic accuracy while withholding the information a professional would need to assess it — that's the shape of a misleading omission, not a cure for one.

Either state the figures properly (arrhythmia type, n, reference standard, CI, citation) or drop the sentence. A half-claim is in a worse position than no claim.

### 3. "up to 14 days" — verify against the IFU, and check it's realistically attainable

Duration isn't part of your intended purpose, so it's a standalone performance claim requiring its own substantiation: adhesion, battery, data integrity and skin biocompatibility validated across the full 14 days. Two checks:

- The figure must not exceed the maximum wear time stated in the IFU.
- "Up to" claims at the exact ceiling invite challenge — the maximum must be achievable by a relevant proportion of users in normal conditions, not a best-case bench figure.

### 4. Terminology traps in the German translation

- **"detection" must not become "Diagnose"/"Diagnostik."** Use *Erkennung* or *Detektion von Herzrhythmusstörungen*. This is the single most common drift in DE localisation of this claim type.
- **"healthcare professional" must not become "Arzt."** Use *medizinisches Fachpersonal*. Narrowing to physician misstates the certified condition of use.
- Where wording tracks the intended purpose, lift it verbatim from the approved German IFU rather than translating fresh.

### 5. "continuous" was dropped

Minor, and it costs you a selling point. Reinstating it improves alignment with the intended purpose at no risk.

### 6. Channel warning if this copy is reused

§ 11 HWG doesn't apply to Fachkreise, which is why the current copy survives. If the same text moves to a publicly accessible website or the open-access version of the trade title, the sensitivity/specificity reference becomes directly problematic under § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 2. Gate any online reuse behind a Fachkreis verification.

---

## Revised copy (DE)

> Kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung über bis zu 14 Tage. Zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen bei Erwachsenen unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal.
>
> *[Optional, only if completed:] Sensitivität X % (95 %-KI …), Spezifität Y % für die Detektion von Vorhofflimmern gegenüber [Referenzstandard]; [Autor], [Publikation], [Jahr].*
>
> [Produktname] ist ein Medizinprodukt der Klasse IIa. CE [NB-Nummer]. Hersteller: […]. Zweckbestimmung, Warnhinweise und weitere Informationen entnehmen Sie bitte der Gebrauchsanweisung.

The manufacturer/CE/IFU footnote isn't a statutory Pflichtangabe for devices the way § 4 HWG is for medicinal products, but it's standard practice in German trade press and materially strengthens the Art. 7 position.

---

## Needs verification before sign-off

I can't confirm these from the copy alone:

1. Does the IFU state a maximum wear time of 14 days, and is 14 days validated (adhesive, battery, signal integrity, biocompatibility)?
2. Do sensitivity/specificity data exist, and for which specific arrhythmia and reference standard?
3. Is the CE certificate issued and the intended purpose in the copy identical to the certificate scope? (Advertising ahead of conformity assessment engages HWG § 3a.)
4. Where will this run — Fachkreise-only, or also open web?

One positioning note: if the ad appears adjacent to AF screening content, "detection of cardiac arrhythmias" may be read as supporting screening in asymptomatic populations. Unless your clinical evaluation covers that, keep placement away from screening context.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

The core indication sentence is close but **not compliant as written**. Two changes are mandatory before placement (population restriction, and the sensitivity/specificity teaser); three more are strongly advisable. Nothing here is unfixable — it's a tightening job, not a rewrite.

This is a copy/claims review against MDR Art. 7, HWG and UWG, not legal advice — RA and outside counsel should sign off on the final layout, since placement context (headline, adjacent editorial, online gating) changes the analysis.

---

## Findings, most severe first

**1. "in adults" has been dropped — scope widening (MDR Art. 7(d))**
The authorised intended purpose is limited to adults. The copy says only "For use under healthcare professional supervision in the detection of cardiac arrhythmias," which reads as unrestricted by age and so suggests a use (paediatric/adolescent monitoring) outside the purpose the conformity assessment covered. This is the clearest hard breach. Add **"bei Erwachsenen"**. Non-negotiable.

**2. "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" — two separate problems**

- *Referencing evidence without a citation.* If this points to a publication or any expert statement, **§ 6 Nr. 2 HWG** requires the exact source (Fundstelle) to appear in the advertisement itself; "on request" gives none. If it instead points to internal clinical evaluation data ("data on file"), § 6 Nr. 2 is arguable — but then **§ 5a UWG** (misleading by omission) and **§ 3 HWG** bite instead, because a Fachkreis reader is invited to infer favourable diagnostic accuracy they cannot evaluate. Either way it doesn't survive.
- *The claim is undifferentiated.* Sensitivity and specificity for an arrhythmia detector are meaningless unqualified: they differ per arrhythmia type (AF vs. pause vs. VT), per analysis level (per-patient / per-episode / per-beat), and per reference standard and adjudication method. A bare mention implies a single global accuracy figure the device does not have — **MDR Art. 7(a)/(b)**.

Fix: either state the actual figures with arrhythmia type, analysis level, comparator/reference standard, n, population and CI plus a full citation — or delete the sentence entirely. For cardiology trade press, stating real numbers is the stronger play; this audience discounts "on request."

**3. "up to 14 days" needs to match the IFU and be unambiguous** — verify against technical documentation
Confirm (a) the IFU-specified maximum wear time is in fact 14 days, (b) whether that is *one continuous* wear or cumulative across patch changes, and (c) that 14 days is realistically achievable, not a best-case outlier — German courts treat unsubstantiated "bis zu" claims as misleading under § 5 UWG where the typical result is materially lower. If the IFU caps wear at 7 days, this is an off-label performance claim. Say "kontinuierliche Tragedauer von bis zu 14 Tagen gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung."

**4. No risk information at all — MDR Art. 7(c)**
Art. 7(c) prohibits advertising that fails to inform of a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose. A multi-day adhesive patch has a well-characterised, frequent risk: **skin reaction/irritation at the application site**. A single line plus "Gebrauchsanweisung beachten" discharges this cheaply.

**5. No statement of single-lead limitations — implied diagnostic equivalence**
Positioned in cardiology press alongside "detection of cardiac arrhythmias," single-lead recording can read as interchangeable with multi-lead diagnostics. It is not: no ST/ischaemia assessment, no localisation, higher artefact burden. Add "Ein Einkanal-EKG ersetzt kein 12-Kanal-EKG." This is also your best defence against **§ 3 HWG**.

**6. Missing identification and Fachkreise gating**
No product name, legal manufacturer, or CE/class reference. These aren't § 4 HWG Pflichtangaben (that provision covers medicinal products, not devices), but their absence is out of step with German MedTech practice and weakens you in any UWG dispute. More important: if the trade-press placement also runs **online without access control**, the Fachkreise privilege lapses and the § 11 HWG Publikumswerbung restrictions apply. Require "Nur für Fachkreise" labelling and confirm the publisher's gating for the digital edition.

**7. Language and translation provenance**
For the German market the ad must be in German, and the indication wording must be lifted **verbatim from the German-language IFU/DoC** — not freshly translated from the English intended purpose. A translator-authored variant is the most common way a compliant claim drifts off-label. Note in particular that "healthcare professional" must render exactly as the German IFU renders it ("medizinische Fachkraft" vs. "Angehörige der Heilberufe" — pick the one that is already approved, don't choose).

**8. Minor: "continuous" dropped.** The intended purpose says continuous recording; the copy says only "recording for up to 14 days." Restore "kontinuierliche" for exact alignment.

---

## What the copy gets right

Worth preserving deliberately, because these are the usual failure points:

- **"in the detection of"** rather than "detects" or "diagnoses" — correctly frames the device as supporting the HCP's determination rather than issuing a diagnosis.
- **HCP supervision retained**, matching the intended purpose.
- **No named arrhythmia and no screening language.** Keep it that way. "AF screening," "Früherkennung," asymptomatic populations, or any stroke-prevention adjacency would assert a screening indication your intended purpose does not contain — that's a far worse exposure than anything currently in the draft.

---

## Suggested revision

```
[Produktname] – kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung

Zur Anwendung bei Erwachsenen unter Aufsicht einer medizinischen Fachkraft
zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen.

Kontinuierliche Tragedauer von bis zu 14 Tagen gemäß Gebrauchsanweisung.

Sensitivität/Spezifität je Arrhythmietyp: [Wert, 95 %-KI; n; Referenzstandard]
– [Autor et al., Zeitschrift Jahr;Band:Seiten].

Mögliche Nebenwirkungen: Hautreaktionen im Bereich der Klebeelektrode.
Ein Einkanal-EKG ersetzt kein 12-Kanal-EKG.

Medizinprodukt der Klasse IIa. CE-gekennzeichnet.
Gebrauchsanweisung und Sicherheitshinweise beachten.
Hersteller: [Name, Anschrift].

Nur für Fachkreise.
```

If the accuracy figures can't be published, delete that block rather than replacing it with "Daten auf Anfrage."

---

## To confirm before sign-off

1. IFU maximum wear time — 14 days, continuous or cumulative?
2. Exact German indication wording as it appears in the approved IFU/DoC.
3. Whether sensitivity/specificity data are published (citable) or internal only — this decides between stating figures and cutting the line.
4. Digital placement: is the trade-press website Fachkreise-gated?
5. The headline and any adjacent editorial — a "higher diagnostic yield than 24-h Holter" framing anywhere on the page becomes an implicit comparative claim needing head-to-head evidence, even if the body copy is clean.

## Before the claim pass — two scoping calls

**The German overlay does not apply.** HWG and UWG govern advertising directed at the German market. You've told me this copy runs on the French site only, so HWG § 3, HWG § 11 and UWG §§ 5–6 are out. That matters here more than usual, because two phrases in this copy are textbook German findings — "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" is the exact shape HWG § 11(1) no. 7 catches, and a named-professor endorsement runs at § 11(1) no. 11 / § 3 no. 3(b). **None of those are breaches for a France-only asset.** I've parked them under `Also engaged:` against the condition that the copy gets reused in Germany, because this is copy that will get translated.

**What I cannot assess: French national law.** France has its own advertising regime for medical devices, administered nationally, and it is not in this skill's reference files. Per citation discipline I will not state a French rule I can't cite. So: the endorsement line is the single item I'd route to French counsel first, and I'm flagging it as unassessed rather than clean. My analysis below is **MDR Art. 7 only** — the layer that applies in France because the device is on the EU market.

---

# Device Claims Review: French consumer web page copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Home blood-pressure monitor — Class IIa
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum (ungated public consumer page) — settled, not assumed
**Markets:** France only (EU layer applies; DE layer does not)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 1 cut, 1 reword, 1 to verify, 0 clean.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Ne jouez pas avec votre coeur — mesurez votre tension chaque jour."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** Read as one sentence, the fear premise plus the instruction creates a false impression regarding *treatment* — that daily self-measurement protects the heart. A blood-pressure monitor measures; it does not treat, prevent, or reduce cardiac risk. Art. 7(b) prohibits "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis"; this is the outcome-implication-from-a-monitoring-device shape.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Even if daily monitoring were shown to improve outcomes in some population, this device's contribution is measurement, and the implication of cardiac protection is not curable by data on the em-dash construction.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 and § 3 no. 2(a) — if this copy is ever translated for the German site. The "Nichtverwendung beeinträchtigt die Gesundheit" framing is the highest-frequency § 11 finding there.
**Call:** Cut
**Suggested fix:** see paste-ready copy below.

---

**Claim:** "mesurez votre tension chaque jour"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Not misleading in itself, but it is a measurement-frequency instruction issued to the general public. Whether that tracks the device's assessed intended purpose and IFU is exactly the limb (d) question I can't answer without the intended purpose. If the IFU leaves measurement frequency to the treating physician, consumer copy prescribing daily use suggests a use pattern the conformity assessment did not cover.
**Evidence needed:** The intended purpose from the DoC/technical documentation, and what the IFU says about measurement frequency and who sets it.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) — if the IFU assigns frequency to the physician, or if the intended purpose is framed as physician-directed monitoring rather than self-directed daily screening.
**Call:** Needs rewording (defensively — the reworded version is safe either way)

---

**Claim:** "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue."
**Breach:** none under MDR Art. 7 on the material supplied
**Why:** A bare recommendation ascribes no function or property to the device, and states nothing about treatment or diagnosis. Under Art. 7 alone it stands. **But this is the item I have the least coverage on** — professional endorsement in public-facing device advertising is squarely the kind of thing national regimes regulate, and France's is outside my reference files.
**Evidence needed:** Written, dated recommendation on file; verification that the title "Professeur" and the cardiology qualification are current and correctly stated; the commercial relationship (paid, equity, advisory, gratis) and whether it's disclosed on the page.
**Also engaged:** French national advertising rules for medical devices `[verify]` — not assessed, route to French counsel. Plus HWG § 11(1) no. 11 and § 3 no. 3(b) if the asset is reused in Germany.
**Call:** Verify — do not publish this line on counsel's silence

---

**Drafting note (not a finding):** "coeur" → "cœur".

## Paste-ready revised copy

> Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue.¹
> Surveillez votre tension artérielle à domicile. [Produit] mesure votre pression artérielle et enregistre vos résultats pour votre médecin. La fréquence des mesures et l'interprétation des résultats relèvent de votre médecin traitant. Lisez attentivement la notice.
>
> ¹ *Hold pending counsel and the disclosure check below.*

What changed and why: the fear premise is gone, the causal implication between measuring and heart protection is gone, the frequency instruction is reassigned to the prescriber (which removes the limb (d) exposure whatever the intended purpose turns out to say), and an IFU pointer is added. The intent — get users measuring at home regularly and treat that as serious — survives intact.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" | Intended purpose verbatim from DoC / technical documentation | Regulatory affairs |
| "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" | IFU text on measurement frequency — who sets it | Regulatory affairs |
| All copy | Whether the IFU records a likely risk or limitation (e.g. conditions where readings are unreliable, need for clinical interpretation) that the page should surface | Regulatory affairs |
| "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois" | Signed, dated recommendation; title and qualification verification; commercial-relationship disclosure | Marketing / legal |
| "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois" | Clearance under French national device-advertising rules | French counsel |

**On limb (c):** the copy surfaces no limitation at all. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs on the page, and I won't infer one from the device category — so this is an open question against the IFU, not a finding. The IFU pointer in the revised copy is the proportionate hedge either way.

**Limb (d)** — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I'll cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

## Provisions cited

- **MDR Art. 7(b)** `[verified]` — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md`
- **MDR Art. 7(d)** `[verified]`, contingent — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md`
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7, no. 11; § 3 no. 2(a), no. 3(b)** `[verified]`, not applicable to a France-only asset; listed for reuse risk — `references/hwg.md`
- French national device-advertising rules `[verify]` — not verified by this skill, not assessed

## Limits

It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

**Why:** The pairing creates a false impression regarding treatment — it implies that daily self-measurement protects the heart, and that not measuring endangers it. A blood-pressure monitor measures; it does not treat, prevent or reduce cardiac risk. This is the "outcome implication from a monitoring-only device" shape under limb (b): the copy states nothing factually false and still leaves a clinical impression the device does not support.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. No outcome data would make a measuring device into a protective one; the fix is to stop implying the causal link.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 — squarely, if this copy is ever reused on the German site. "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" is the textbook *Nichtverwendung* framing ("health impaired by not using"), and "mesurez chaque jour" is the *Verwendung verbessert* half. Both halves in one line. Not a finding for France.
**Call:** Needs rewording

---

**Claim:** "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** A bare recommendation asserts no function, property or performance figure, so there is nothing for limbs (a) or (b) to attach to yet. Art. 7 bites only where the copy misleads as to intended purpose, safety or performance — an endorsement does that only if the endorsement itself is untrue or the clinical weight it borrows is manufactured.
**Evidence needed:** That Prof. Dubois exists, holds the stated cardiology qualification, has given written consent to be named, and actually recommends *this* device (not the category). Also: whether the relationship is remunerated or otherwise material, and whether that is disclosed on the page.
**Also engaged:**
- MDR Art. 7(b) — if the recommendation is fabricated, stale, paid-and-undisclosed, or was given for a different product.
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 and § 3 no. 3(b) — Germany only.
- **Not** HWG § 11(1) no. 2. The professional-endorsement prohibition does not apply to devices: § 11(1) closing sentence limits devices to nos. 7–9, 11 and 12. It would not bite even in Germany, and citing it is a false positive.

**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "mesurez votre tension chaque jour"
**Breach:** none identifiable without the intended purpose
**Why:** A daily-measurement frequency is a quasi-clinical instruction. Whether it sits inside the assessed intended purpose, or drifts outside it, depends on what the conformity assessment covered and what measurement regimen the IFU specifies. I cannot call limb (d) blind.
**Evidence needed:** The intended purpose as assessed, plus the IFU's measurement-frequency guidance. If the IFU defers frequency to a healthcare professional, unconditional "chaque jour" is intended-purpose drift, and that is cured by narrowing the claim — not by data.
**Call:** Verify

### Limb (c) — open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation at all. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs on this page — the candidates for a home BP monitor would be things like results requiring clinical interpretation, or accuracy caveats for particular users. I'm not flagging (c) on a risk I inferred from the device category; that would be unfalsifiable. Worth checking against the IFU, and if a likely risk is recorded there, an IFU pointer on the page is usually the proportionate fix.

### Limb (d) — not assessed

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c).

## Suggested fix — paste-ready

> Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue [ajouter la mention de tout lien d'intérêt, ex. « consultant rémunéré par [société] »].
> Suivez votre tension artérielle à domicile, à la fréquence indiquée par votre médecin ou dans la notice d'utilisation.

What changed and why:

- **"Ne jouez pas avec votre coeur" is gone.** Removing the fear/protection framing is what clears limb (b); softening it does not. Any variant that keeps the "your heart is at risk unless you measure" premise reproduces the breach.
- **"chaque jour" → "à la fréquence indiquée par votre médecin ou dans la notice"** — moves the frequency decision to the IFU and the clinician, which keeps the line inside the intended purpose whatever the IFU turns out to say. If the IFU *does* specify daily measurement, you can restore "chaque jour" and cite the notice.
- **Endorsement kept, with a disclosure slot.** Naming a recommending cardiologist is not prohibited for a device. The exposure is in the substantiation and the undisclosed relationship, not in the format.
- **Typography:** "coeur" → "cœur" in any retained copy.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois" | Written consent, current qualification, recommendation covering this specific device, disclosure of any remuneration | Marketing / legal — signed endorsement agreement |
| "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" | Intended purpose as assessed; IFU measurement-frequency guidance | Regulatory affairs — technical documentation, DoC, IFU |
| Whole page | Whether the IFU records a likely risk requiring a user-facing mention | Regulatory affairs — IFU risk/limitations section |
| Whole page | French national advertising requirements for this device class | Fachanwalt / French counsel — outside this skill's scope |

## Provisions cited

- **MDR Art. 7(b)**, **7(c)**, **7(d)** — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- **HWG § 11(1) no. 7**, **no. 11**, **§ 3 no. 3(b)**, and the § 11(1) devices-scoping sentence — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` — cited as *not applicable to France*, retained for market-migration risk only
- UWG §§ 5 and 6 — not engaged; no comparison and no certification/status claim in this copy

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

Additionally, for this asset: **French national law is not covered.** The only layer I verified against here is MDR Art. 7. A France-only consumer page has a French national compliance surface that this review does not touch.
