## Device Claims Review: French consumer product page — home BP monitor

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Home blood-pressure monitor — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Publikum / lay public (ungated consumer web page)
**Markets:** France only (EU). **Not** Germany.

### Which layers apply here

| Layer | Applies? |
|---|---|
| MDR Art. 7 | **Yes** — applies to any device on the EU market, France included |
| HWG §§ 3, 11 | **No** — these are German instruments and the copy does not target Germany |
| UWG §§ 5, 6 | **No** — same reason |

So this review runs on MDR Art. 7 alone. Two consequences worth stating up front, because they cut in opposite directions:

1. The fear-appeal sentence would be a near-textbook **HWG § 11(1) no. 7** hit (health impaired by *not* using the device) and the physician endorsement would engage **§ 11(1) no. 11** / **§ 3 no. 3(b)**. Those are not findings here. I have recorded them under `Also engaged:` against the condition "if the asset is ever localised for DE" — that is the only status they can honestly hold.
2. France has its own national advertising regime for medical devices, and it bears directly on both sentences in this copy. **It is not in the reference files this skill verifies, so I am not going to state its rules.** See *Out of scope* below — this is the largest gap in the review and it is not a formality.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. **1 reword, 1 verify, 1 pending limb (d).**

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.** One clause breaches Art. 7(b) on the face of the copy; the endorsement turns on a French-law question I cannot answer.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Ne jouez pas avec votre coeur"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** The phrase's whole work is the implication that the reader's heart is at risk unless they use this device — it "creat[es] a false impression regarding treatment" from a device that measures and does nothing else. A sphygmomanometer does not treat, prevent, or reduce cardiac risk; pairing the warning directly with "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" presents measurement as the protective act.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. No outcome data would make a monitor protective; the implication has to go.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 — if this asset is localised for the German market
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** Drop the fear frame and let the function stand: "Surveillez votre tension artérielle à domicile, simplement."

---

**Claim:** "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** Art. 7 has no testimonial limb. An accurate, authorised endorsement does not by itself ascribe a function the device lacks or misstate its intended purpose. It is not clean, though — it is unverified, and on a lay page an unqualified specialist endorsement does work that Art. 7(b) can reach if the recommendation is broader than the device's assessed purpose (e.g. if what Prof. Dubois is quoted as recommending is *daily self-monitoring as a clinical practice* rather than this device).
**Evidence needed:** that Prof. Dubois exists as described and holds that title and specialty; written consent to be named commercially; the actual wording and scope of what was recommended; whether the relationship is remunerated, and if so whether it is disclosed.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 11(1) no. 11 and § 3 no. 3(b), UWG § 5(2) nos. 3–4 — if localised for DE. **French national rules on physician endorsement of medical devices — out of scope here, and the reason I cannot clear this line.**
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** Hold this line until the French-law question is answered. If it is retained, tie it to the device and disclose the relationship: "Le Professeur X, cardiologue (hôpital Y), a participé à l'évaluation clinique de ce tensiomètre. Collaboration rémunérée par [société]."

---

**Claim:** "mesurez votre tension chaque jour"
**Breach:** limb (d) **not assessed**
**Why:** A stated measurement frequency is a use recommendation, so it has to be tested against the intended purpose the conformity assessment covered. If that purpose is intermittent or practitioner-directed self-measurement, prescribing a daily regimen to the general public is intended-purpose drift, and drift is not curable by data — it is cured by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment.
**Evidence needed:** the intended purpose as it appears in the DoC/technical documentation, plus whatever the IFU says about measurement frequency.
**Call:** Verify

**Open question on limb (c), not a finding.** The copy surfaces no limitation at all — no pointer to the notice, nothing on interpretation of readings. I am not raising (c), because I have not seen the IFU and I will not infer a likely risk from the fact that it is a BP monitor; a (c) finding built that way would fit every benefit-framed ad ever written. Check the IFU for a recorded likely risk (readings requiring clinical interpretation, conditions affecting accuracy, arrhythmia interference) — if one is there, it belongs in this copy and (c) becomes a real finding.

## Paste-ready revision

Under 50 words, so here is the actual copy, with the endorsement held back pending the French-law check:

> Surveillez votre tension artérielle à domicile, simplement.
> Mesurez-la aux moments recommandés par votre médecin et notez vos résultats : leur interprétation lui revient. Lisez attentivement la notice.

If limb (d) clears and the IFU supports a daily regimen, "aux moments recommandés par votre médecin" can become "chaque jour, à heure fixe" — but not before.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" | Intended purpose as assessed; IFU measurement-frequency wording | RA / technical documentation owner |
| (c) open question | Whether the IFU records a likely risk for lay self-use | RA / IFU author |
| "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois" | Identity, title, specialty, written consent, scope of the recommendation, remuneration and disclosure | Marketing + legal |
| Physician endorsement, FR | Whether French rules permit a named-practitioner endorsement on an ungated consumer page | French-qualified counsel |

## Provisions cited

- **MDR Art. 7(b)** — `[verified]`, `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md`
- **MDR Art. 7(c)**, **7(d)** — `[verified]`, same file; raised as open question / not assessed
- HWG § 11(1) no. 7, § 11(1) no. 11, § 3 no. 3(b); UWG § 5(2) nos. 3–4 — `[verified]`, `references/hwg.md`, `references/uwg.md`; **conditional only**, they do not apply to a France-only asset

## Out of scope — read this before acting

France restricts advertising of medical devices to the public and regulates the use of health-professional endorsements in commercial material. Those rules sit in French national law and the French medical professional code; **neither is in this skill's reference files, so I will not state what they require.** Naming the instruments from memory and paraphrasing their effect would be the same act as inventing a citation, minus the visible cite.

What I can tell you is where the risk concentrates: the single highest-risk element in this copy is the named-cardiologist endorsement on an ungated consumer page, and it is high-risk under exactly the layer I cannot check. Take that line to French-qualified counsel before publication. Point me at the French provisions or ANSM guidance and I will run the pass properly.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

Minor drafting note, non-regulatory: "coeur" should be "cœur" on a French-market page.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

**Do not publish as written.** Two of the twelve words' worth of "creative" here are the two things French public advertising for medical devices most squarely prohibits: a named health-professional endorsement, and a fear appeal. Both sit in the same short line, and neither is fixable by softening the wording — they need to come out. The copy is also missing the mandatory statutory mentions entirely.

Scoping note taken: France-only, so I've reviewed against French law (CSP + MDR) and ignored the German HWG. See the geo caveat at the bottom, which is the one place the "France only" framing may not hold by itself.

---

## Blockers

### 1. "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue" — prohibited endorsement

French law bars public advertising for a medical device from referring to a recommendation from scientists, health professionals, or persons whose notoriety could encourage use of the device (CSP, the R.5213-x series governing DM advertising to the public — mirroring the long-standing medicines rule at R.5122-4). This is a categorical ban, not a balancing test. It does not matter whether:

- Prof. Dubois genuinely holds that view,
- the recommendation is sincere and unpaid,
- you add a disclosure of the relationship,
- or you drop the name and say "recommandé par des cardiologues."

Generic versions ("recommandé par les cardiologues", "plébiscité par les professionnels de santé", "n°1 chez les médecins") fall under the same prohibition. **Remove the endorsement entirely.**

There is a second, independent exposure on the doctor's side. A physician lending their name and title to a commercial product risks breaching the code de déontologie médicale (prohibition on using the profession for commercial promotion, and on *compérage*). If there is any payment or benefit flowing to Prof. Dubois, the anti-gift regime and the French Sunshine transparency obligations (CSP L.1453-1 et seq.) apply regardless of whether the name ever appears in the copy — so **don't treat deleting the line as closing the file.** Check whether a contract, fee, or in-kind benefit exists and whether it's been declared.

### 2. "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" — prohibited fear appeal

DM advertising to the public must not suggest that the person's health could be affected if they do not use the device, and must not be presented in an alarming manner. "Don't gamble with your heart" is a direct instance of exactly that construction: it frames non-use as a cardiac risk.

There's a compounding misleading-claims problem under **MDR (EU) 2017/745, Article 7**. The line implies the monitor protects your heart. It doesn't. It measures blood pressure; it neither treats nor prevents cardiovascular disease. Ascribing functions the device does not have, and creating a false impression regarding treatment or prevention, are both explicitly prohibited by Art. 7.

### 3. Missing mandatory mentions

The copy contains no product name, no intended purpose, and none of the statutory wording required for public DM advertising (per the arrêté on advertising for medical devices). You need substantially this, verbatim-adjacent:

> *Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE, dont la conformité a été évaluée par [nom de l'organisme notifié]. Lire attentivement la notice.*

Class IIa means a notified body was involved, so **the notified body's name must be filled in** — it isn't optional for your class. Add "Demandez conseil à votre médecin ou à votre pharmacien" as well.

---

## Serious, below blocker level

### 4. "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" — contradicts HAS guidance

This instructs a measurement frequency that French clinical guidance does not support. HAS recommends the **règle des 3** for automesure: three measurements in the morning, three in the evening, three consecutive days, in the run-up to a consultation — not indefinite daily self-measurement. Open-ended daily measurement in an unsupervised consumer population drives health anxiety and reactive self-management off single readings.

Two consequences: it's a usage claim that almost certainly isn't supported by your IFU (check it), and it edges toward encouraging self-diagnosis without medical advice. Replace with the règle des 3 framed around a doctor's advice.

### 5. Confirm reimbursement status

Public advertising is prohibited for devices whose cost is covered by assurance maladie. Home BP monitors are generally not reimbursed for the general public, so this is most likely fine — but if any variant of this SKU is listed on the LPPR, the whole page is unlawful irrespective of wording. Worth a five-minute check by your regulatory lead.

---

## Suggested rewrite

> **[Nom du produit] — tensiomètre électronique de bras pour l'automesure à domicile**
>
> Suivez votre tension artérielle chez vous, simplement.
>
> Votre médecin vous a recommandé l'automesure ? [Nom du produit] applique la règle des 3 : 3 mesures le matin, 3 le soir, 3 jours de suite, et transmettez les résultats à votre médecin.
>
> *Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE, dont la conformité a été évaluée par [organisme notifié]. Lire attentivement la notice. Demandez conseil à votre médecin ou à votre pharmacien.*

This keeps the motivational pull (routine, simplicity, partnership with your doctor) without borrowing authority from a named clinician or leaning on dread.

---

## Two things to confirm before sign-off

**Geo-scoping.** "France only" is a business intention; a public, ungated, French-language page is reachable from Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland and Quebec, each with its own DM advertising regime — Belgium's in particular restricts endorsements similarly. Confirm with engineering whether the page is actually geo-restricted or merely hosted on the `.fr` domain. If it's the latter, the "not used in Germany" framing doesn't fully bound your exposure. (It doesn't change my analysis above — the French rules already block the copy — but it matters for the rest of the page.)

**Article numbering.** I'm confident in the substance of the prohibitions and in the MDR Art. 7 analysis. I'd have your regulatory affairs or external counsel confirm the precise current CSP article references and the exact mandatory-mention wording against the consolidated text before you rely on them in a written approval record — that series has been renumbered before, and the mandatory statement must be quoted exactly.

Worth noting: prior ANSM authorisation (visa PP) is **not** required for Class IIa public advertising — that obligation attaches to classes IIb and III. So the fix path here is a copy rewrite, not a filing.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict: don't publish as written

Two of the three elements in this copy hit hard prohibitions in the French medical-device advertising regime, and the ad is missing its mandatory mentions entirely.

---

### 1. The named physician endorsement — remove it

Public advertising for a medical device in France may not refer to a recommendation from scientists or health professionals. This mirrors the long-standing medicines rule (Art. R.5122-4 CSP) and is carried through the DM advertising regime (Art. L.5213-1 et seq. / R.5213-1 et seq. CSP) and ANSM's recommendations on DM advertising. "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue" is the textbook prohibited form — the *Professeur* title makes it worse, not better, because the authority weight is the whole point of the sentence.

Two knock-on exposures:

- **The physician's own liability.** The Code de déontologie médicale (Art. R.4127-20) requires a doctor to oppose the use of their name or title for advertising purposes. You would be putting a named cardiologue in front of the Ordre.
- **Transparency / anti-cadeaux.** If Prof. Dubois received anything of value, you have obligations under Art. L.1453-1 CSP (publication on transparence.sante.gouv.fr) and the anti-cadeaux regime, and an undisclosed paid endorsement is independently a misleading omission under the Code de la consommation. Disclosing it does not cure the prohibition above — the endorsement is out either way.

**Compliant substitute for the credibility you're buying:** cite objective validation instead of a person — clinical validation to ISO 81060-2, or listing on a recognised validated-device registry (STRIDE BP / ESH). That is factual, verifiable, and permitted.

### 2. "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" — fear appeal, and an overclaim

Two separate problems:

- **Fear-based inducement.** The line's whole mechanism is "something bad happens to your heart if you don't use this." French DM advertising must present the device objectively and support proper use; suggesting the user's health will suffer without the product is precisely what the regime excludes.
- **MDR Art. 7 (Reg. (EU) 2017/745).** A blood-pressure monitor *measures*. It does not protect your heart or prevent cardiac events. Implying a protective benefit attributes a function and performance the device does not have and creates a false impression about prevention. Art. 7 applies regardless of market and is enforceable by ANSM as competent authority.

### 3. "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" — unsubstantiated, and contrary to French guidance

Indefinite daily self-measurement addressed to the general public is a clinical recommendation, and it isn't the one French practice uses: HAS guidance on automesure tensionnelle is the *règle des 3* — three measurements morning, three evening, over three consecutive days, ahead of a consultation. Telling an untargeted consumer audience to measure daily promotes use that guidelines don't support, risks driving anxiety and over-measurement, and is a claims-substantiation gap you'd have to defend to DGCCRF or ANSM. Either substantiate the frequency for a defined population or defer to the prescriber.

### 4. Missing mandatory mentions

A public DM advertisement in France must carry the regulated-product statement, the CE marking reference, the instruction to read the notice, and manufacturer identification — the standard wording being *"Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. Lire attentivement la notice."* plus the fabricant/mandataire. None of it is present. The copy also never states the device's intended purpose.

---

### Two things to verify before signing off

- **Reimbursement status.** Public advertising is prohibited for devices taken in charge by the assurance maladie. Autotensiomètres are generally not on the LPPR, so this is likely clear — but confirm for your specific reference.
- **Prior authorisation (visa).** Certain DM categories require an ANSM visa before public advertising, per the arrêté listing them. I'd have regulatory counsel confirm whether your product falls inside that list rather than assume it doesn't — that's a pre-publication gate, not a post-hoc fix.

### One scope note

You've scoped this to France, and I've reviewed it on that basis. Worth flagging only this: an ungated French-language page is routinely reached from Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland and Canada, and "we don't use it in Germany" doesn't limit exposure unless the page is actually geo-restricted. If it isn't, the market scoping is an intention rather than a control.

---

### Suggested replacement

> **Tensiomètre [Marque X] — l'automesure tensionnelle à domicile**
>
> L'automesure permet de suivre votre tension artérielle dans les conditions de la vie quotidienne et de transmettre vos relevés à votre médecin. Demandez à votre médecin ou à votre pharmacien si l'automesure est adaptée à votre situation et selon quel rythme la pratiquer.
>
> Validé cliniquement selon la norme ISO 81060-2. [Référencé sur STRIDE BP, si exact.]
>
> Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. Fabricant : [X]. Lire attentivement la notice.

Minor copy point while you're in there: `coeur` should be `cœur`. On a consumer health page the missing ligature reads as carelessness.

I've flagged the regulatory framework and where the lines fall, but the visa question and the final sign-off should go through your regulatory affairs function or French counsel — that's a gate I can't close for you.

## Verdict: do not publish as written

Two hard blockers, plus missing mandatory mentions. All are fixable, but the first one can't be softened — it has to come out.

---

### 1. "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue" — remove it

Public-facing advertising for a medical device in France may not rely on a recommendation from scientists, health professionals, or persons whose notoriety could encourage use of the device (CSP art. R.5213-1 et seq., the prohibitions transposing the same logic as art. R.5122-4 for medicines). A named cardiologist, and a *professeur* at that, is the textbook case. There is no disclaimer, no "à titre personnel", and no disclosure of the commercial relationship that cures this on an ungated consumer page.

Three knock-on exposures, each independent of the ad rules:

- **The physician's own liability.** Lending one's name to commercial promotion breaches the code de déontologie médicale (CSP art. R.4127-13 and R.4127-19). The Ordre des médecins can act against Prof. Dubois regardless of what happens to you.
- **Anti-cadeaux / transparence.** If Dubois is compensated in any form, the benefit falls under the anti-gift regime (CSP art. L.1453-3 et seq., authorisation or declaration depending on amount) and the link must be published under art. L.1453-1. Confirm what contract exists before anyone touches this line again.
- **If "Professeur Dubois" is composite, illustrative, or not a real practising cardiologist**, you add a misleading commercial practice under art. L.121-2 code de la consommation and MDR art. 7 — a DGCCRF matter, not just an ANSM one.

Note that swapping in a celebrity instead of a doctor does **not** fix this; the prohibition covers notoriety-based endorsement too. What you *can* do is make a factual, non-endorsement reference to clinical practice (e.g. that home self-measurement is part of recommended hypertension follow-up), provided it isn't framed as a third party vouching for your product.

### 2. "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" — fear appeal, and it implies self-measurement substitutes for a consultation

Two separate problems in one clause. DM advertising to the public may not use elements likely to provoke fear, nor suggest that a medical consultation or examination is superfluous. "Don't gamble with your heart — measure daily" does both: it frames non-use as a cardiac risk, and it positions the device as the protective act. Rewrite around what the device actually does (track, record, share with your doctor), not around what happens if you don't buy it.

Also: **cœur**, not *coeur* — use the ligature.

### 3. "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" — unsupported usage claim

Daily indefinite self-measurement is not what French practice recommends. HAS/SFHTA guidance is the *règle des 3* — three measurements morning, three evening, three consecutive days, before a consultation or for a defined follow-up period. Promoting a different usage pattern than the one supported by your IFU and by clinical guidance is a claim about performance/use that engages MDR art. 7, and clinically it drives over-measurement anxiety in exactly the population you're selling to. Align the frequency with your notice; if the notice says something else, the notice wins.

### 4. Mandatory mentions are absent

Public DM advertising must carry, at minimum (CSP art. R.5213-1, from décret n° 2012-743): the device's commercial name/reference, its intended purpose, and an express invitation to read the instructions in the notice or on the labelling carefully. The ad must also be identifiable as advertising and the product identifiable as a medical device. If the fragment you sent sits on a page that already carries the ANSM-style block, fine — but I don't see it here, so confirm.

### 5. Two things to verify before publication

- **Reimbursement status.** Advertising to the public is prohibited for devices taken in charge by the compulsory health insurance schemes (CSP art. L.5213-3), subject to the exceptions set by arrêté. Most consumer autotensiomètres are not on the LPPR, but confirm for this SKU.
- **Prior ANSM authorisation (visa).** Devices on the "risque important" list (CSP art. L.5213-4, arrêté du 24 septembre 2012) need an ANSM visa before any public advertising. I am not certain whether home blood-pressure monitors / self-monitoring devices fall within that list — check it against the current arrêté rather than taking my word, because if they do, the whole page needs a visa and not just a copy edit.

---

### Suggested compliant rewrite

> **[MARQUE MODÈLE] — autotensiomètre brassard pour la mesure de la pression artérielle à domicile**
>
> Suivez votre tension chez vous et partagez vos relevés avec votre médecin. Pour un suivi fiable, la pratique recommandée est de 3 mesures le matin et 3 mesures le soir, 3 jours de suite, avant votre consultation.
>
> *[MARQUE MODÈLE] est un dispositif médical de classe IIa, marqué CE [n° organisme notifié], fabriqué par [fabricant]. Lisez attentivement la notice avant utilisation. Demandez conseil à votre médecin ou à votre pharmacien. [Mois/année de la mention].*

Adjust the measurement protocol to match your IFU — I've written the HAS/SFHTA pattern, but your notice governs.

---

I've kept this to France as you scoped it. One flag only, since you mentioned it: the professional-endorsement line would also be independently unlawful under §11 HWG in Germany, so if this page is ever localised, fixing point 1 now saves you doing it twice.

# Device Claims Review: Congress booth panel

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Sirolimus-eluting coronary stent — stated Class IIb, CE marked, notified body involved
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (interventional cardiologists, congress booth) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply
**Markets:** DE (EU)

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 2 verify, 0 clean.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

Because the audience is Fachkreise, § 11 is out of scope here — raising § 11 nos. 7/9/11 against this panel would be a false positive. HWG § 3 still applies in full, as does MDR Art. 7 and UWG § 5.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "delivers sustained drug release across the full lesion"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`; HWG § 3 no. 1 `[verified]`; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** "Across the full lesion" states a capability with no qualifying condition. A stent covers the treated segment only within its labelled length and diameter range; whether it covers "the full lesion" is a function of lesion length and operator sizing, not a property of the device. Art. 7(a) prohibits "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have"; HWG § 3 no. 1 covers "Wirkungen [...], die sie nicht haben"; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 reaches "Zwecktauglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse". A cardiologist reading this panel is the exact reader who will infer complete drug coverage of the lesion, including no geographic miss.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the unconditional form — this is cured by wording, not by data. If you want to keep a coverage claim, you need the labelled length/diameter range and any drug-distribution data at the stent edges.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) — if the assessed intended purpose is limited to, e.g., de novo lesions in native coronaries within a defined length range, "full lesion" unqualified suggests use in long diffuse disease, bifurcations or in-stent restenosis. Cannot confirm without the intended purpose.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "sustained sirolimus release across the treated segment, in lesions within the labelled stent length range"

---

**Claim:** "Approved and available now" — the word *approved*
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 `[verified]`
**Why:** § 5(2) no. 4 covers "Aussagen oder Symbole, die [...] sich auf eine Zulassung des Unternehmers oder der Waren oder Dienstleistungen beziehen". This device holds a CE certificate issued following conformity assessment with notified-body involvement. It does not hold an "approval". The distinction is not pedantic in Germany: *Zulassung* is the term of art for medicinal-product marketing authorisation, and an English "Approved" on a booth panel translates straight into it for this audience. Unqualified, it also carries no scope — it does not say approved by whom, under what, or for which sizes and indications.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Cured by naming the actual regulatory status.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 3 (Status of the *Unternehmer*) if the surrounding booth material presents "approved" as a company-level status rather than a product one.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "CE marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. Notified body [name], [four-digit NB number]."

---

**Claim:** "delivers sustained drug release"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A sustained-release claim for a sirolimus-eluting stent is ordinary and not misleading on its face. But "sustained" is undefined — it rests on elution kinetics I have not seen, and under UWG § 5(2) no. 1 the expected results of use are a wesentliches Merkmal. For a Fachkreise audience the naked adjective is also weaker than the number.
**Evidence needed:** Elution profile from the technical documentation — release duration and the in-vivo or in-vitro basis for it.
**Call:** Verify (and strengthen)
**Suggested fix:** "sustained sirolimus release over [X] days" — cite the release duration from the technical file.

---

**Claim:** "available now"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Availability is expressly a wesentliches Merkmal under UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Verfügbarkeit"). Not misleading on the material supplied, but it is a hard factual assertion made at a congress where cardiologists may act on it.
**Evidence needed:** Confirmation that the full labelled size matrix is orderable in Germany on the date the booth is staffed — not "launching", not partial sizes.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — if only part of the size range ships now, or German availability trails the CE certificate.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** "Available in Germany from [date] in [size range]." Or drop to "Available now in Germany" only if the whole matrix genuinely ships.

---

### Limb (c) — open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation, contraindication or IFU pointer. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — I have not seen it, and I won't infer one from the fact that this is a drug-eluting stent, because that would make the finding unfalsifiable. Worth checking against the IFU.

Context on proportionality: a congress panel for interventional cardiologists is not expected to carry patient-facing safety text. Where (c) bites on an asset this short, the proportionate fix is a pointer, and I've included one in the revised copy below.

### Premise worth checking: the stated class

You've given the device as Class IIb. A drug-eluting coronary stent sits at the intersection of the implantable and ancillary-medicinal-substance classification rules, and I'd expect to see Class III. I can't resolve that here — MDR Annex VIII is not in this skill's reference files, so I will not state the classification rule as verified `[verify]`. Confirm the class on the certificate with your notified body. It matters for copy because any class or certification statement you add to a panel is a UWG § 5(2) no. 4 claim, and stating IIb on a Class III device would breach it independently of everything above.

## Paste-ready revised copy

> Our sirolimus-eluting stent provides sustained sirolimus release over [X] days across the treated segment, in lesions within the labelled stent length range.
>
> CE marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. Notified body [name], [NB number]. Available in Germany from [date] in [size range].
>
> Please consult the Instructions for Use for indications, contraindications and warnings.

Four bracketed values to fill from the technical file and the certificate.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "sustained drug release" | Elution duration + basis (in-vivo/in-vitro) | R&D / technical documentation owner |
| "across the full lesion" | Labelled stent length and diameter range | RA / labelling |
| "Approved" | Certificate: issuing notified body, NB number, scope, class | RA / QA |
| "available now" | German availability date and which sizes ship | Commercial / supply chain |
| Limb (c) | IFU: likely risks, contraindications, warnings | RA |
| Intended purpose | Verbatim from DoC / technical documentation | RA — see below |

## Limb (d) — not assessed

Limb (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is **not assessed**: I have not seen the intended purpose. It is the limb device marketing trips most often, so paste it from the technical documentation or DoC and I will cover it. Everything above reviews limbs (a), (b) and (c). The specific thing I'd check it against is "across the full lesion" and whatever lesion types and vessel dimensions the conformity assessment actually covered.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1 — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11 — `references/hwg.md` — considered and **not applied** (Fachkreise) `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- MDR Annex VIII classification rules — **not verified by this skill** `[verify]`

One scope note on the audience: this holds as long as the panel stays on the booth. If the same wording is reused on an ungated product page or in patient-facing material, § 11 needs re-checking, and "Approved and available now" reads differently to a lay reader than to a cardiologist.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

There is no "approval"/Zulassung for a medical device in the EU — a Class IIb device carries a CE mark following notified-body conformity assessment. "Approved", and its German rendering "zugelassen", imports an authorisation concept that belongs to Arzneimittel and that this device does not hold. The word also carries no scope, so the reader cannot tell what was assessed.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — the accuracy of the underlying certificate does not cure the wrong status word. Cured by naming the actual status.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) — if the CE certificate scope is narrower than the lesion/vessel range the booth copy implies. Cannot be assessed without the intended purpose.
**Call:** Needs rewording

---

**Claim:** "delivers sustained drug release **across the full lesion**"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) [verified]; HWG § 3 no. 1 [verified]
**Why:** Art. 7(a) prohibits "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". A stent elutes drug from its stented segment; coverage of the *full lesion* is a function of operator sizing and placement, not a property of the device. Where the lesion exceeds the deployed length, or where there is geographic miss, the device does not do what the panel states it does. HWG § 3 no. 1 is the same test in German law ("Wirkungen beigelegt werden, die sie nicht haben").
**Evidence needed:** n/a — no elution data cures this, because the defect is the reference frame. Cured by restating coverage against the **stented segment**, which is what the device controls.
**Call:** Needs rewording

---

**Claim:** "**sustained** drug release"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Not misleading on the material supplied. "Sustained" is standard DES vocabulary, but it is unquantified, and § 5(2) no. 1 reaches "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" and the results of "Tests". An open duration against a documented elution profile is an open question for the technical file, not a breach.
**Evidence needed:** Pharmacokinetic / elution-profile data from the technical documentation — the release period actually characterised, and the conditions under which it was measured.
**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "available **now**"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** § 5(2) no. 1 lists **Verfügbarkeit** expressly. Accurate on its face as far as I can tell; becomes a finding only if the device is not in fact orderable and deliverable in Germany on the congress dates, or if only some sizes in the matrix are.
**Evidence needed:** Confirmation from commercial/supply that the full size matrix is releasable in DE on the booth dates. If only part of the range is, say which.
**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "Our **sirolimus-eluting** stent"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A composition statement. HWG § 3 no. 3(a) (Zusammensetzung oder Beschaffenheit) would bite only if the drug is not sirolimus or not a sirolimus formulation as documented. No reason on the material supplied to think it is wrong.
**Call:** OK

---

## Open question — limb (c)

The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a **likely** risk that belongs on this panel, so I'm not recording a (c) breach — I won't infer one from the device category, because that reasoning would condemn every benefit-framed ad and tells you nothing.

Worth checking against the IFU. For a congress panel aimed at Fachkreise, the proportionate fix where (c) genuinely bites is an IFU pointer, not patient-facing safety text — cardiologists are not the audience the limb is written to protect, and trade copy of this length isn't expected to carry a risk section. I've included the pointer in the revised copy below regardless; it is cheap and it closes the question.

## Considered and not raised

- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a) (guaranteed success)** — "delivers" asserts a technical output, not certainty of a clinical Erfolg. Doesn't bite here. It would if the panel added an outcome promise (e.g. restenosis or TLR framing stated as assured).
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(b) (no harmful effects)** — nothing in the copy reassures about absence of side effects.
- **HWG § 11** — Fachkreise, so out of scope entirely. One caveat: if this panel is visible from an area of the congress open to press, patient advocates or the public, the audience anchor changes and nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 come back into play. Worth confirming the hall is registration-gated.
- **UWG § 6** — no comparator, express or implied. Not comparative advertising.

## Revised copy — paste-ready

> Our sirolimus-eluting stent provides controlled drug release over [X days] across the stented segment.
> CE marked, Class IIb (notified body [NB number]). Available in Germany now.
> Please consult the Instructions for Use for indications, contraindications and warnings.

| (c) omission | IFU — likely risks, contraindications, warnings | RA |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), 7(c), 7(d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1, no. 3(a) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11 — considered and **not applied**: audience is Fachkreise — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) no. 1, § 5(2) no. 4 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 6 — not engaged; the copy makes no comparison, express or implied

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

One scope note on the "Approved" finding: how German courts treat *zugelassen* for CE-marked devices is a case-law question this skill does not verify. The finding above rests only on the statutory text of UWG § 5(2) no. 4.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Premise check first

**"Class IIb" is almost certainly wrong for this device.** Under MDR Annex VIII, a coronary stent is in direct contact with the central circulatory system (Rule 8 → Class III), and a device incorporating a medicinal substance with ancillary action is Class III under Rule 14. A sirolimus-eluting coronary stent lands in Class III on both counts, with the drug component requiring consultation of a medicines competent authority/EMA in the conformity assessment.

This doesn't soften any finding below — it hardens them (Class III = higher scrutiny, more exposure if a claim outruns the certificate). But confirm the classification on the certificate before this copy is printed, because internal documents describing a Class III stent as IIb is a finding an auditor will pull on. Review below assumes the device is lawfully CE marked with a valid certificate.

---

## Findings

### 1. "Approved" — high severity
There is no such thing as *approval* for a medical device in the EU. Devices are CE marked following conformity assessment; "Zulassung/zugelassen" is the term of art for medicinal products under the AMG. In the German market this is a well-worn irreführende-Werbung trap: it implies an authority reviewed and endorsed safety and efficacy, which no one did.

- **Basis:** MDR Art. 7(b) (false impression as to properties); § 3 HWG (Irreführung); § 5 UWG; the MPDG's misleading-claims provision (§ 14).
- **Fix:** "CE marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745" / "CE-gekennzeichnet gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745". Never "zugelassen", never "amtlich geprüft".
- **Related:** do **not** name or logo the notified body ("TÜV-zertifiziert", "certified by [NB]"). Notified body involvement is a regulatory fact, not an endorsement, and presenting it as a quality seal is itself misleading. Cite the CE mark, not the certifier.

### 2. "across the full lesion" — high severity
This is the most exposed phrase in the copy. It reads as an absolute coverage claim — uniform drug delivery over the entire lesion, whatever the lesion is — and does two things at once:

- **Overclaims performance.** Complete lesion coverage is not something a stent guarantees; geographic miss is a recognised clinical phenomenon driven by sizing and deployment, not eliminated by the device. → MDR Art. 7(a)/(b).
- **Implies use outside the approved intended purpose.** Your sizing matrix covers a defined diameter and length range. "Full lesion" invites the cardiologist to read this as suitable for long, diffuse or bifurcation lesions that the conformity assessment may not cover. → MDR Art. 7(d), the provision specifically aimed at suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose.

**Fix:** replace the coverage claim with the actual size range and indicated lesion length from the IFU. Specificity is both safer and more persuasive to this audience.

### 3. "sustained drug release" — medium
Directionally fine if it mirrors the IFU, but as written it is unquantified and unsourced. Interventional cardiologists at a booth will ask "over what period, measured how" — and § 6 HWG requires that any reference to studies, expert opinions or literature names the author, the publication and the date.

**Fix:** quantify it and cite it — "controlled sirolimus release over X days (pharmacokinetic data, [author, study, year])". Use the release-kinetics wording from the IFU/technical documentation verbatim where you can; don't paraphrase upward.

### 4. No reference to risks or to the IFU — medium
MDR Art. 7(c) makes it a prohibited claim to fail to inform of a likely risk associated with normal use. A short promotional block obviously can't carry a full risk profile, and unlike medicinal products there is no § 4 HWG Pflichtangaben box for devices — but silence plus two strong efficacy claims is the pattern that triggers Art. 7(c).

**Fix:** standard IFU pointer, on the same panel and legible, not in 4pt on the back.

### 5. "available now" — verify before use
Factual claim, so it's only a problem if untrue — but "now" is a commitment that all indicated sizes are orderable in Germany on the day of the congress. Partial launch, restricted size availability, or shipping against a certificate not yet in force makes this misleading, and pre-CE promotion is separately prohibited.

**Fix:** confirm with commercial ops. If launch is staged, say so: "Ab [Monat] in Deutschland verfügbar" or name the available sizes.

### 6. Booth access — practical, worth a decision
Your Fachkreise framing is what keeps § 11 HWG (which restricts advertising directed at the general public) off the table, and it's the right framing for a congress. But German congress halls are not reliably closed to press, industry visitors and patient-organisation attendees. If the booth is walk-up accessible, mark the panel "Nur für Fachkreise" / "For healthcare professionals only" and be able to show the access-control arrangement. Same file: if giveaways are on the stand, § 7 HWG applies to those independently.

---

## Revised copy

**English (congress use):**

> **[Brand] sirolimus-eluting coronary stent**
> Controlled sirolimus release over [X] days ([author, study, year]).
> Available in diameters [X–Y] mm and lengths [A–B] mm.
> CE marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. Available in Germany from [date].
> *For healthcare professionals only. Please consult the Instructions for Use for the full intended purpose, indications, contraindications, warnings and potential adverse events.*

**German:**

> **[Marke] Sirolimus-freisetzender Koronarstent**
> Kontrollierte Sirolimus-Freisetzung über [X] Tage ([Autor, Studie, Jahr]).
> Verfügbar in Durchmessern von [X–Y] mm und Längen von [A–B] mm.
> CE-gekennzeichnet gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745. Ab [Datum] in Deutschland verfügbar.
> *Nur für Fachkreise. Zweckbestimmung, Indikationen, Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweise und mögliche unerwünschte Wirkungen entnehmen Sie bitte der Gebrauchsanweisung.*

---

## Before sign-off

1. Confirm the risk class and the scope of the CE certificate (MDR certificate, or an MDD legacy certificate running under the Art. 120 transitional provisions — the latter constrains you further, since no significant change in design or intended purpose is permitted).
2. Pull the IFU intended-purpose and sizing text and check every claim word-for-word against it.
3. File the substantiation for the release-kinetics claim in the claims/marketing dossier with the citation as printed.
4. Have the German wording checked by German-qualified regulatory or legal counsel before print — the terminology distinctions here (zugelassen vs. CE-gekennzeichnet especially) are where German competitor Abmahnungen under the UWG typically originate.

I've flagged the classification discrepancy as the one thing that should be resolved rather than assumed; everything else above is actionable as written.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not ready to run in Germany as written. Two hard blockers ("Approved", "across the full lesion"), one omission (no risk/IFU reference), and one factual item I'd want confirmed before anything goes to print.

---

## Findings

**1. "Approved" — blocker.** EU medical devices are not *approved*; they undergo conformity assessment and carry a CE mark. The German rendering is the real danger: "zugelassen" is the term of art for a medicinal-product marketing authorisation and would imply an authority review this device never had. Misleading under MDR Art. 7(b), HWG § 3, UWG § 5, plus the Täuschungsschutz provisions of the MPDG.

Use: *"CE-gekennzeichnet gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745, Benannte Stelle [NNNN]."* Avoid "TÜV-geprüft"-style framing that presents the notified body as an endorser — the NB identification number belongs next to the CE mark, not in a quality claim.

**2. "across the full lesion" — blocker.** This reads as a coverage/outcome claim (no geographic miss, uniform delivery over any lesion) rather than a drug-release characteristic. Whether the stent covers the full lesion depends on sizing and operator technique, and the IFU will specify a bounded lesion-length and vessel-diameter range. Ascribing a property the device does not have, and suggesting use beyond the assessed intended purpose — MDR Art. 7(a) and 7(d), HWG § 3.

Replace with the indicated ranges from the IFU. If you want to keep a uniformity message, it has to be tied to specific elution data and labelled as in vitro/preclinical where that's what it is.

**3. "sustained" is unsubstantiated.** German courts apply a high evidentiary bar to health-related claims (gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis), and the burden sits on the advertiser. Give a number and a source: release over X days, cite the study. If you cite literature at the booth, HWG § 6 requires accurate attribution — author, publication, date — and verbatim quoting.

**4. No risk or IFU reference — MDR Art. 7(c).** A pure benefit claim with nothing about stent thrombosis, restenosis, DAPT requirements or contraindications is exposed, even to Fachkreise. Add the standard IFU pointer.

**5. "available now" — verify it's literally true for Germany today.** If launch is staged or the certificate is still in progress, this is UWG § 5/5a. Also confirm whether the certificate is MDR or a legacy MDD certificate under transitional provisions — if legacy, you cannot describe the device as MDR-certified.

**6. Factual check: the Class IIb designation looks wrong.** A drug-eluting coronary stent is in direct contact with the central circulatory system and incorporates an ancillary medicinal substance (sirolimus), which points to Class III under MDR Rules 8 and 14 — with a medicines-authority consultation in the conformity assessment. If the device really is certified as IIb, that's worth resolving before any regulatory claim is printed; if it's a slip in the brief, no harm, but the copy shouldn't state a class either way.

---

## Suggested rewrite

**DE (Fachkreise):**
> Sirolimus-freisetzender Koronarstent mit kontrolliertem Freisetzungsprofil über [X] Tage ([Quelle: Studie/Daten]). Indiziert für Läsionslängen von [X–Y] mm bei Gefäßdurchmessern von [A–B] mm.
> CE-Kennzeichnung gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745, Benannte Stelle [NNNN]. Ab sofort in Deutschland verfügbar.
> Nur für Fachkreise. Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung: Indikationen, Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweise und Vorsichtsmaßnahmen.

**EN (if the congress runs in English):**
> Sirolimus-eluting coronary stent with a controlled release profile over [X] days ([data source]). Indicated for lesion lengths [X–Y] mm in vessels [A–B] mm. CE marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745, notified body [NNNN]. Available in Germany now. For healthcare professionals only. Refer to the Instructions for Use for indications, contraindications, warnings and precautions.

For the German market, run the German version as the primary — and have the translation reviewed specifically for "zugelassen," which is the single word most likely to be introduced by a translator and most likely to draw an Abmahnung.

---

## Two booth-context notes, adjacent to the copy

- Giveaways and hospitality are constrained by HWG § 7 and §§ 299a/299b StGB — keep to geringwertige Kleinigkeiten and check against the MedTech Europe / BVMed code your company follows.
- If the congress admits press or the general public to the exhibition floor, Laienwerbung restrictions come into play for material that can be picked up freely. Worth confirming the floor is Fachkreise-gated.

The realistic enforcement route here is a competitor UWG action via the Wettbewerbszentrale, not an authority inspection — which in practice means the bar is whatever a rival's counsel thinks they can win on. "Approved" is exactly the kind of word they look for.

This is a regulatory-copy review, not legal advice; your Regulatory Affairs and legal teams should sign off on the final German text.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Two of the three sentences carry real risk. The "Approved" claim is the one I'd block before the booth ships.

---

## Findings, ranked

### 1. "Approved" — misrepresents regulatory status (block)

A Class IIb device is **CE marked** following conformity assessment with notified body involvement. It is not "approved," and it must never be rendered in German as *"zugelassen"* — that term is reserved for medicinal products with a marketing authorisation. Because this is a sirolimus-eluting stent (an ancillary medicinal substance under MDR Art. 1(9)), the drug framing makes the reader *more* likely to hear "approved" as a pharma-style authorisation, not less.

Exposure: MDR Art. 7(b) (false impression as to properties/status), § 3 HWG (irreführende Werbung), § 5 UWG — and § 5 UWG is the practical threat, because German competitor enforcement via Abmahnung is fast and cheap for the complainant.

Second-order point: don't overcorrect into *"CE-zertifiziert!"* as a headline selling point either. CE marking is a legal precondition for placing the device on the market, and promoting a statutory requirement as a competitive advantage is **Werbung mit Selbstverständlichkeiten** — itself misleading under § 5 UWG. State the status factually, in small type, as context rather than benefit.

Also: do not name or logo the notified body. A certificate is not an endorsement, and presenting it as one is its own Art. 7 problem.

### 2. "across the full lesion" — performance overclaim

The device covers the **stented segment**, not "the lesion." Whether the lesion is fully covered depends on operator sizing and on whether your longest available length exceeds the lesion — geographic miss is a recognised phenomenon this audience knows well. As written the claim is unconditionally false for any lesion longer than your longest stent, which is exactly the kind of falsifiable absolute that invites a challenge.

This also brushes MDR Art. 7(d): it hints at use beyond the intended purpose covered by the conformity assessment (e.g. long-lesion or full-metal-jacket strategies) unless your intended purpose and clinical evidence actually cover that.

Fix: "along the full length of the stented segment."

### 3. No risk balance, no IFU reference — MDR Art. 7(c)

Art. 7(c) prohibits claims that mislead by **failing to inform the user of a likely risk**. Pure-benefit copy for a DES, with no pointer to stent thrombosis, restenosis, DAPT requirements, or sirolimus/polymer hypersensitivity, is the textbook shape of that problem.

Fachkreise status does not exempt you. Note that § 4 HWG *Pflichtangaben* do **not** apply here — that provision covers Arzneimittel, and your product remains a device — so the IFU reference is doing the work instead. It is cheap and it is expected.

### 4. "sustained" and "delivers" — undefined, and too certain

"Sustained" needs a number and a source: sustained over how many days, measured how. If the underlying data is in-vitro elution kinetics, the copy must not let a cardiologist read it as a clinical outcome — release kinetics are not patency, TLR, or MACE.

"Delivers … across the full lesion," unqualified, edges toward suggesting assured success, which § 3 Nr. 2a HWG addresses directly. Attach a footnote and a data reference.

### 5. Device not identified

"Our sirolimus-eluting stent" is too loose. Claims attach to a specific device with a specific intended purpose and a specific certificate. Generic phrasing lets the claim spill onto line extensions or sizes that are not certified or not launched. Name the product and system.

### 6. "available now" — substantiate

True only if the device is actually placed on the German market and orderable in the advertised sizes. If availability is partial, or if you are relying on MDR Art. 120 transitional arrangements rather than a fresh MDR certificate, say what is actually true. Advertising stock you cannot supply is a Lockangebot issue under § 5a UWG.

---

## Suggested rewrite

**English**

> **[PRODUCT NAME] Sirolimus-Eluting Coronary Stent System**
> Sustained sirolimus release over [X] days along the full length of the stented segment.¹
>
> CE marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. Available in Germany in diameters [X–Y] mm and lengths [X–Y] mm.
>
> ¹ [In vitro elution data / Study name, citation — data on file]
> For healthcare professionals only. Please consult the Instructions for Use for full indications, contraindications, warnings, precautions and adverse events.

**German**

> **[PRODUKTNAME] Sirolimus-freisetzendes Koronarstentsystem**
> Anhaltende Sirolimus-Freisetzung über [X] Tage über die gesamte Länge des stentversorgten Segments.¹
>
> CE-Kennzeichnung gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745. In Deutschland verfügbar in den Durchmessern [X–Y] mm und Längen [X–Y] mm.
>
> ¹ [Quelle / Daten auf Anfrage]
> Nur für Fachkreise. Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung mit Angaben zu Indikationen, Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweisen, Vorsichtsmaßnahmen und Nebenwirkungen.

---

## Before the booth opens

- **Fachkreise gating.** Fachkreise treatment holds only if the booth is in an access-controlled area restricted to HCPs. If the hall is open to the public or to press at any point, § 11 HWG restrictions bite and the copy needs reworking. Confirm the congress access model in writing.
- **Substantiation file.** German courts apply a strict evidentiary standard to health-related advertising — the advertiser bears the burden, and the expected standard is *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis*. Have the CER extract, elution data and any cited trial in a booth-accessible dossier.
- **Claims-to-CER traceability.** Every number in the footnote should map to a specific section of the clinical evaluation and be consistent with the IFU wording.
- **IFU language.** German-language IFU is the default requirement; the professional-user exception under the MPDG is narrower than people assume. Worth confirming with your regulatory lead rather than assuming English suffices — I'd flag this as a check, not a finding.
- **Booth conduct.** Giveaways and hospitality fall under § 7 HWG and the MedTech Europe / BVMed codes, separately from this copy.

This is a regulatory copy review, not legal advice — item 1 in particular should go past your regulatory affairs lead before print.

Both anchors are supplied, so this is a full four-limb review.

# Device Claims Review: headline + subline (14 words)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Class I reusable surgical retractor — Class I, self-certified (no notified body indicated)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure during open procedures"
**Audience:** Fachkreise (hospital procurement) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply; § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU-wide MDR Art. 7 applies regardless)

## Summary

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 1 substantiate-or-cut, 0 OK as written.

**No confirmed breach on the material supplied.** Both lines are soft claims that sit just short of the statutory hooks — but both rest on facts I haven't seen, and the second carries a structural defect that evidence cannot cure if the implied comparison is read as comparative advertising.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** "Actually" carries an implicit comparison — *unlike the retractors you use now*. If that makes competitors or their goods **erkennbar** within UWG § 6(1) [verified], the comparison is tested against § 6(2) and fails **no. 2** on its face: "enjoyment" is not an *objektiv, wesentlich, relevant, nachprüfbar und typisch* characteristic, and there is no named comparator for the reader to check against. On the copy alone I cannot conclude a competitor is recognisable — the line disparages the whole product category rather than an identifiable rival — so I am not recording it as a breach.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. If the line is comparative, § 6(2) no. 2 asks what the *reader* can verify, not what you hold. A user-satisfaction study would not fix an undefined comparator or a subjective criterion. The fix is objective, checkable attributes.
**Also engaged:**
- UWG § 6(2) no. 2 [verified] — if the implied comparison makes competitors recognisable to this procurement audience.
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — "Vorteile", "Beschaffenheit": an unverifiable handling-superiority claim directed at a buyer, if it is geeignet under § 5(1) to move a procurement decision.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix (paste-ready, DE):**

> **Ergonomie für lange Eingriffe.** Griffgewicht [X] g, rutschfeste Riffelung, [N] Aufbereitungszyklen validiert.
> Zweckbestimmung: manuelle Retraktion von Gewebe zur Aufrechterhaltung der Exposition des Operationsgebiets bei offenen Eingriffen. Gebrauchsanweisung beachten.

**(EN equivalent):** "Built for long procedures. [X] g, non-slip knurled grip, validated for [N] reprocessing cycles."

---

**Claim:** "Surgeons love it."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** It ascribes no therapeutic effect (HWG § 3 no. 1 [verified] not engaged) and no function or property beyond the intended purpose. It is an aggregate assertion of user satisfaction — close to puffery, but phrased as a statement of fact about a body of clinicians, which is what keeps it inside § 5(2) no. 1's reach if nothing sits behind it.
**Evidence needed:** The basis for the aggregate. A user-satisfaction survey, evaluation-loan feedback, or post-market surveillance user feedback — with N, sites, date, and question wording. If there is no dataset, this is a rhetorical flourish stated as fact to a purchaser, and it should come out rather than be defended.
**Also engaged:**
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — if no evidentiary basis exists for the aggregate satisfaction assertion.
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 [verified] — **only if this copy also runs on an ungated public page.** Then the audience is Publikum, not Fachkreise, and an aggregated third-party endorsement is testable for *irreführend*. Note: testimonials are not flatly prohibited for devices; no. 11 bites only where they are missbräuchlich, abstoßend or irreführend.
**Call:** Needs substantiation (or cut)
**Suggested fix (paste-ready, DE):**

> In einer Anwenderbefragung an [M] Kliniken bewerteten [X] von [N] Chirurgen die Handhabung mit "gut" oder "sehr gut" ([Quelle, Monat/Jahr]).

If that dataset does not exist, delete the line. Do not soften it to "Chirurgen schätzen …" — same claim, same hook, less defensible.

---

## Limbs I checked and cleared

- **Art. 7(a)** [verified] — no function or property is ascribed at all. Nothing to overclaim.
- **Art. 7(b)** [verified] — no treatment or diagnosis impression. A retractor makes no diagnostic or therapeutic representation here.
- **Art. 7(d)** [verified] — **clear.** No user population, setting, or indication is suggested, so there is no intended-purpose drift. Worth naming the inverse problem, as a drafting note and not a finding: the copy communicates no intended purpose whatsoever. For a procurement reader comparing retractors, 14 words of feeling carry no decision content.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** [verified] — I am **not** citing this. "You'll enjoy using it" is a promise about the buyer's experience, not an *Erfolg* in the therapeutic sense the provision addresses. Stretching it there would be a false positive.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(b), no. 3(b)** [verified] — no no-harmful-effects claim, no claim about the maker's credentials or track record.
- **HWG § 11** [verified] — does not apply to Fachkreise. See the channel caveat above.
- **HWG § 3a** — Arzneimittel only. Not applicable to a device.
- **UWG § 5(2) nos. 3, 4** [verified] — no class, certification, notified-body or approval claim is made. Clean. (If a CE badge or "Class I" mark appears in the layout I haven't seen, no. 4 comes back into play.)

## Open question on Art. 7(c) — not a finding

The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a **likely** risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs in this asset. I am deliberately not inferring one from the device category — retraction injury, reprocessing failure and the like are plausible, but flagging copy for omitting a risk I guessed at makes the finding unfalsifiable.

Check the IFU's warnings and reprocessing sections. Two candidates to look for, given this is a **reusable** device retracting tissue: validated reprocessing limits (cycle count, method) and any retraction-force or duration warning. For trade-press or brochure copy at this length, the proportionate fix where (c) genuinely bites is an IFU pointer — "Gebrauchsanweisung beachten" — which the suggested rewrite already carries.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Surgeons love it." | Satisfaction survey or PMS user feedback: N, sites, date, question wording | Marketing / PMS lead |
| Rewrite attributes ([X] g, [N] cycles) | Weight from drawing; reprocessing validation report cycle count | R&D / QA |

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 0 reword, 0 substantiate, 1 verify, 1 OK.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Surgeons love it."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** An aggregate satisfaction/preference statement. It ascribes no function, property, therapeutic effect or clinical outcome to the device, so MDR Art. 7(a)/(b) and HWG § 3 no. 1 are not engaged on the face of it. It is not a claim about the manufacturer's credentials or track record, so § 3 no. 3(b) is not engaged either.
**Evidence needed:** Whatever the statement rests on — a user survey, evaluation-unit feedback, reference customers. Needed only if the claim is presented to procurement as measured rather than as promotional register.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("wesentliche Merkmale … Vorteile", and "Ergebnisse oder wesentliche Bestandteile von Tests") — **if** the claim is placed next to, or derived from, a satisfaction survey or evaluation data. Presenting a figure-backed preference claim without its basis, or generalising a small evaluation to "surgeons", would be zur Täuschung geeignet. As bare copy with no number attached, it is not.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** Not required. If you want it substantiated rather than promotional: "Rated easier to hold at depth by 18 of 20 surgeons in our 2026 evaluation programme (n=20, three centres)." — only if that data exists and you publish n and setting.

---

**Claim:** "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A handling/ergonomics preference statement about the assessed use. It does not suggest a user population, setting or indication outside "manual retraction of tissue … during open procedures", so **limb (d) is assessed and clear** — the copy describes no use at all, which is what keeps it clear. No treatment or diagnosis impression arises, so (b) is not engaged. The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a **likely** risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs here. Two places to look, both specific to what you described: retraction pressure/duration limits, and the reprocessing and inspection constraints that attach to a *reusable* instrument. I am not raising (c) as a breach: I would be inferring the risk from the device category rather than from your material, and a (c) finding built that way is unfalsifiable.

Both lines are preference register with no product content. # Device Claims Review: trade headline (13 words)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Reusable surgical retractor — Class I

## Summary

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword recommended, 1 to substantiate, 0 clean as written.

**No breaches identified** against MDR Art. 7, HWG § 3, or UWG §§ 5–6 on the material supplied. The copy stays inside the intended purpose and claims no clinical effect, which is what keeps it out of trouble. The exposure here is thin and sits in two places: whether "Surgeons love it" rests on anything, and whether "actually" imports a comparison you can't defend.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below

## Findings

### Claim 1 — "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using."

**Breach:** none
**Why:** No function or property bearing on intended purpose, safety or performance is asserted, so the Art. 7 gateway ("may mislead the user or the patient **with regard to the device's intended purpose, safety and performance**") is not engaged. No use outside manual retraction is suggested, so limb (d) is clear. HWG § 3 no. 1 needs a claim of *therapeutische Wirksamkeit oder Wirkungen* — enjoyment of handling is not one.
**The live risk is "actually."** It implies that other retractors are not enjoyable. UWG § 6(1) reaches indirect identification, but it requires a **Mitbewerber** to be made *erkennbar*. An undifferentiated swipe at the whole market identifies no one, so § 6 does not engage on this line standing alone. It does engage the moment the line sits next to a named competitor, a comparison table, or a context where procurement can tell who is meant — and then § 6(2) no. 2 fails, because "enjoy" is not *objektiv* on a *nachprüfbare* characteristic. **That failure cannot be cured by evidence**; a satisfaction study you hold does not make the claim checkable by the reader. The fix is to name the comparator or drop the comparison.
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the claim as written. If the comparator becomes identifiable, no evidence cures it.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 — if this headline runs on a page or panel where a specific competitor is recognisable.
**Call:** Needs rewording (cheap insurance, not a breach)
**Suggested fix:** drop the implied comparison and anchor to a property you can support from the design file:

> "Balanced handle, polished blade edges — controlled manual retraction through long open procedures."

### Claim 2 — "Surgeons love it."

**Breach:** none
**Why:** An aggregate user-satisfaction assertion, not a performance or clinical claim. Nothing in HWG § 3 bites: no efficacy claim (no. 1), no promise that *ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann* (no. 2(a)), no claim that *keine schädlichen Wirkungen* follow from use (no. 2(b)), no claim about the maker's *Person, Vorbildung, Befähigung oder Erfolge* (no. 3(b)).
**But it is stated as a fact about a population.** If nothing sits behind it, it is capable of being *zur Täuschung geeignete Angaben* about *wesentliche Merkmale* / *von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse* under UWG § 5(2) no. 1, subject to the § 5(1) materiality filter (*geeignet, den ... Marktteilnehmer zu einer geschäftlichen Entscheidung zu veranlassen*). Procurement does buy partly on surgeon acceptance, so the filter is unlikely to rescue it.
**Evidence needed:** the survey, evaluation, or trial-use feedback the claim rests on — n, site count, date, and the question asked.
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix (substantiated version):**

> "Rated better than their current retractor by 27 of 31 surgeons across 4 hospitals (evaluation, 2026)."

**Suggested fix (if no data exists) —** make it a claim about your process, not about surgeons' feelings:

> "Developed with surgeons in open general and vascular procedures."

## Two false positives I am not raising

Worth stating explicitly, because both are the obvious calls on this copy and both are wrong here:

- **HWG § 11(1) no. 11 (Äußerungen Dritter).** "Surgeons love it" is testimonial-shaped, but § 11 applies only *außerhalb der Fachkreise*. Hospital procurement is Fachkreise, so § 11 does not apply at all. Even where it does, no. 11 catches testimonials only where *missbräuchlich, abstoßend oder irreführend* — they are not flatly prohibited for devices.
- **MDR Art. 7(a).** Preference and enjoyment are not "functions and properties" in the sense the gateway clause requires. Stretching (a) to cover tone would make every adjective a finding.

**Limb (c) — failing to inform of a likely risk.** The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a *likely* risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs in this asset. Worth checking against the IFU — reprocessing constraints and retraction-pressure cautions are the places I'd look first, though I'm naming those as *where to look*, not as findings. Proportionality matters: a 13-word trade headline is not expected to carry safety text, and an IFU pointer is the usual proportionate fix where (c) genuinely bites.

**Audience gating.** A B2B claim anyone can read is not automatically Fachkreise. If this headline runs on an ungated web page or an open trade-show panel, § 11 comes back and Claim 2 needs re-checking against no. 11. Confirm the placement.

**Certification claims.** The copy makes none, so UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4 are not engaged. If a CE badge, class statement, or notified-body reference gets added alongside it, the claim has to match the certificate exactly. Check it with your RA function before any badge goes on the asset. `[verify]`

| Limb (c) check | IFU: likely risks, reprocessing limits, cautions | RA |
| Placement | Is the asset gated to Fachkreise? | Marketing |

## Bottom line

Don't run it as-is. Two sentences, two substantiation problems, and zero content for the audience you named. The fix isn't heavy — it's swapping unprovable affect claims for verifiable ones.

---

## Claim by claim

**"Surgeons love it."**

This reads as a factual assertion about general professional acceptance, not puffery. German courts treat quantifiable-sounding acceptance claims as objektiv nachprüfbar, and in the health sector the Strengeprinzip puts the burden of proof on you — you must hold the evidence *before* publication, not produce it after an Abmahnung.

- If you have a user survey: usable, but name n, population, period, and who ran it.
- If you have individual testimonials: **§ 6 HWG** applies regardless of audience — the endorsers must be fachlich berufen, and author plus date must be disclosed.
- If it's an internal impression from a few sales conversations: cut it. There's nothing to defend.

One genuinely helpful thing about your audience: because hospital procurement counts as **Fachkreise** under § 2 HWG, the hard bans in **§ 11 HWG** (Gutachten, Dankschreiben, Äußerungen Dritter, Vorher-Nachher etc.) are off the table. Testimonials are *not* per se prohibited here. The constraint is substantiation and § 6 formalities, not prohibition — so don't over-correct into sterility.

**"The retractor you'll actually enjoy using."**

"actually" is doing the damage. It carries an implicit "unlike the ones you currently use" — an unqualified superiority claim over the entire category.

Be precise about the real exposure, because the obvious statute doesn't bite:

- **§ 6 UWG (vergleichende Werbung)** and **§ 4 Nr. 1 UWG (Herabsetzung)** both require an *identifiable* competitor. In a fragmented retractor market, no individual competitor is identifiable, so these likely don't apply. Don't rewrite as though they do.
- What does apply: **§ 5 UWG** and **§ 3 HWG** — misleading superiority (Alleinstellungsbehauptung) without a substantiated performance basis. That's the actionable risk.
- Realistic enforcement vector is an Abmahnung from a competitor, the Wettbewerbszentrale, or Integritas — not an authority action. Fast, cheap for them, expensive for you.

**MDR Article 7:** the claims are about user satisfaction, not clinical performance, so Art. 7(a) ("functions and properties which the device does not have") is a stretch here. But note the quieter obligation: under **Annex XIV Part A**, your clinical evaluation must cover the claims you make. Every promotional claim needs a traceable line back into the technical documentation. "Surgeons love it" currently has none.

---

## What's missing for the actual audience

Procurement doesn't buy on enjoyment. For a **reusable** Class I instrument, the decision variables are lifecycle cost and reprocessing burden. Nothing in this copy touches them.

Also worth confirming with your RA colleagues: a reusable surgical instrument is Class I under **Annex VIII Rule 6**, but it's **Class Ir** — **Art. 52(7)(c)** requires Notified Body involvement limited to reuse aspects (cleaning, disinfection, sterilisation, maintenance, functional testing, and the related IFU). If that NB certificate is in place, it's a real differentiator you're not using. If the copy anywhere implies broader CE certification than the Ir scope, that itself becomes a § 3 HWG issue.

Concrete substance to lead with instead: validated reprocessing per ISO 17664 with the cycle count actually supported by your test report; material and corrosion behaviour; weight/handling data; UDI-DI and availability; instrument-set compatibility.

---

## Rewrite options

**If you hold survey data:**

> Wundspreizer zur manuellen Retraktion von Gewebe und Freihaltung des Situs bei offenen Eingriffen.
> In einer Anwenderbefragung (n = 120 Chirurginnen und Chirurgen, DACH, 03/2026) bewerteten 87 % die Handhabung mit „gut" oder „sehr gut". Methodenbericht auf Anfrage.

**If you hold no survey data:**

> Wundspreizer zur manuellen Retraktion von Gewebe und Freihaltung des Situs bei offenen Eingriffen.
> Validierte Aufbereitung nach ISO 17664, belegt für [X] Zyklen. Ein Instrument statt Set — reduziert Siebbestückung und Aufbereitungsaufwand.

Keep the numbers only if the test report carries them; a placeholder that ships unfilled is worse than the original copy.

**On language:** English promotional material to German Fachkreise is generally fine. The German-language requirement (**MDR Art. 10(11)**, **§ 8 MPDG**) hits Kennzeichnung and Gebrauchsanweisung, not advertising. That said, procurement documentation lands better in German, and mixed-language claim sets are where translation drift creates new Irreführung risk.

Two open items only your team can close: whether the survey exists, and whether the Ir certificate is in hand. Everything above assumes your RA/Legal function signs off on the final wording — my read is on the claim structure, not a substitute for that review.
